News.title: Inside Legacy funeral home of horrors where director Robert Bush left bodies piled up
News.content:
Shaken police officers called to a funeral parlour likened to a 'horror scene' described it as ‘strange and weird’. Walking slowly around the Legacy Funeral Services premises by torchlight, the police officers sounded concerned and disturbed by what they saw.

The public-facing front of the building featured a perfectly respectable waiting room and chapel. But the order and dignity turned to into chilling chaos and a callous disregard for the dead and the grieving behind the scenes of Robert Bush's Legacy Independent Funeral Directors.

Bags of belongings, screwed up paperwork, charity donation envelopes, old scrap cars, a hearse, car seats and a sink labelled ‘dirty area’ full of scissors and waste were discovered.

View 8 Images Four motorbike leathers were treated with more respect than the dead (Image: Humberside Police)

‌



In another room was a single comfy chair with a foot rest in front of a screen. Disturbingly families have told of their fears Bush was watching them as they visited their loved ones.

There is also a book about a road trip to America and disturbingly what looked like four motorbike leathers and helmets hanging neatly from the wall. They appeared better cared for than than the 35 bodies stored nearby. One even appeared to have Legacy branding on it like some kind of sponsor or advertising.

View 8 Images Two motorbikes were found in the workshop of the Hessle Road premises (Image: Humberside Police)

‌



Angry face car bonnets, often used in stock car racing, were also stored in the vast building, along with superbikes which were pictured in the workshop of the Hessle Road premises. Katie Woolston, 28, who had gone to Legacy after her fourth miscarriage and now also fears her child was dumped in a bin by Bush, said: "People's loved ones were in the building, so why on earth was he storing motorbikes and cars in there?"

View 8 Images Police found chaos in the back rooms at Legacy (Image: Humberside Police)

Forensic scientist and former funeral director Dr Richard Lloyd told the court during Bush's sentencing for 67 offences that the Hessle Road site was "in a lamentable state." He said there was a "wholly inadequate approach to care for the deceased" at the mortuary. The court also heard there was a large amount of unidentified clothing, which was likely for dressing the deceased, meaning the service was routinely not carried out.

‌



View 8 Images Piles of clothes, believed to have been left for the deceased to be dressed in, were found at the site (Image: Humberside Police)

During his police interview Robert Bush proudly boasted to police about his chapel at the Hessle Road premises. It was the only neat area along with the kitchen families used for teas and coffees. He told officers: “It seats about 70 people, it’s got a lectern, the coffin sits at the front.”

He described how they had a vicar “the same as a crematorium” and a celebrant with a slide show on a screen. But the police officers who arrived at Legacy March 6, 2024, found behind the spotless and ornate ivory sofa front was a back room scene of horror and chaos.

‌



View 8 Images Public-facing areas looked clean and well organised (Image: Humberside Police)

They found a large number of human bodies - 17 had putrified - within a dirty cold storage area which had a large sliding door at one end. There was racking along both sides, three racks high with bodies stored on the racks on both sides of the room in an "undignified manner".

As the prosecutor said this week: “The vast majority were uncovered and in varying states of decomposition; there was a further naked body lying on a stretcher on the floor. In addition, there was one sealed wooden coffin and four sealed cardboard coffins.

‌



View 8 Images Though in front of the desk looked somewhat neat and organised to customers, behind the desk told the truth about the funeral home (Image: Humberside Police)

“There was evidence of human putrefaction, visible on the floor, and a mop and bucket in the corner of the room, which contained further evidence of putrefaction. Many of the bodies had hospital identity bracelets on their wrists and/or ankles, some had biological hazard bracelets, while others had no identifying markers.”

Dr Lloyd's report on the conditions in the premises detailed how containers of ashes were found all over the premises, with most "stored in an undignified manner". Some were stacked chaotically on shelves or on the floor where damp had caused mould to grow on the boxes. In some instances, ash was found on desk surfaces, in empty and unidentified boxes and, in one room, strewn across the floor.

‌



View 8 Images Bags of ashes were found on the floor of the Hessle Road branch (Image: Humberside Police)

Officers had been flagged down in the street by funeral directors who’d been called in to collect a body for Bush when he was away in the US. Gary Pickering and Steve Emmerson - Directors of Evergreen Funeral Directors were left “shaken” by the discovery which one of Bush's casual workers had told them was like something from a ‘horror scene.’

“Putting it simply, they were shocked by what they saw…but then saw a passing police car, which they flagged down, and they spoke to PC Crosher. The officer described the witnesses as being shaken as they relayed the details to him,” the prosecutor said.

View 8 Images Bush had started making his own coffins (Image: Humberside Police)

‌



“Three police officers then attended Mr Bush’s premises at Hessle Road, where they found a large number of human bodies within a cold storage area of the premises...Many of the bodies had hospital identity bracelets on their wrists and/or ankles, some had biological hazard bracelets, while others had no identifying markers. There was also evidence of personal possessions with some of the deceased and other personal effects on the floor and on shelving.”

Families had complained about a bad smell coming from the premises with one relative noticing mould on his gran's coffin. Photographs show one room full of wood cuttings after Bush started making his own PDF coffins to save money.

News.title: Cruel Legacy funeral director Robert Bush laughed as he told police his industry was 'highly unregulated'
News.content:
Twisted undertaker Robert Bush laughed about the lack of regulation in the funeral industry when he was quizzed by police about his cruel crimes, new footage has shown.

Humberside officers arrested him after finding 35 bodies stored in his Legacy Funeral business in Hull and asked him who his ‘governing body' is. Bush scoffed that he hadn't been inspected since Covid telling them: “I know! We are a highly unregulated industry.”

“When you join the National Association of Funeral Directors you have an inspection to put a certificate on your wall, but they just come and check. But they are also checking if you’ve got cushions on your sofa and how many leaflets you have,” he told them, appearing relaxed and sipping coffee during his police interviews.

“They have been round and it’s only covid times they kind of rescinded that, until then, they came around and did spot inspections and things. But if you didn’t come up to scratch, there wasn’t a penalty, you were just not in their association any more.”

‌



View 5 Images Bush said he got into trouble because of debt and denied having a luxury lifestyle.

His comment will add fuel to the victims’ calls for urgent regulations to be brought in. Families whose loved ones were left at the funeral home for up to two years and those given fake ashes and some none at all, have been calling for action as they tell Bush’s sentencing hearing how they've suffered PTSD, nightmares and suicidal thoughts.

Bush, 48, has already pleaded guilty to 67 offences after police removed 35 bodies and a quantity of ashes from Legacy Independent Funeral Directors, in Hull. He is due to be sentenced on Friday. He was arrested at Heathrow on a plane in March 2024 and released on bail. He was then rearrested in July 2024, but still did not seem to grasp the horror of his crimes and told police: “I’m no Che Guevara!”

He answered the door in his dressing gown with his two Bichon dogs barking at his feet. "Rob, we’ve come to arrest you," a female officer tells him and he replies: "Right." As he’s read his rights, Bush puts his head in his hands and tells the two officers: “I don’t understand. I’m not like an international…you know I’ve been arrested off a plane by gunpoint. I’ve been taken out. It’s like I’m Che Guevara or something. I’m not that complicated."

‌



View 5 Images 'I'm not Che Guevara' Bush protests

He told police who arrived at his home: “I’ve said so many times ‘let me help you’. I will unravel whatever it is. I will come down and talk to you. Four months have gone by...I know I’m not good at accounting and my handwriting is bad and all that. I’m sure there are times when you’ve looked at things and thought ‘I don’t’ know what that means'. But not once have I had a question since I’ve been released. I don’t understand it.”

He’s told by the officer how their questions need to come in an interview and he counters: “I was expecting to have interview after interview. It feels vindictive the way this has been done...I’ve been compliant from the word go. I’ve come back early on my own accord. I’ve been taken off a plane at gunpoint. Massive Met Officers with their guns. We were coming home. I told you we were coming home. You knew all our travel plans and everything.”

Sitting on his stairs, with his head in his hands, he appears frustrated and adds: “I’ve been compliant from the off. I’ve been here all this f**king time.”

‌



View 5 Images Bush slumps at the bottom of his stairs complaining about his treatment

His reaction was a far cry from his first police interviews when he seemed relaxed and chatty with officers. He appeared the most bothered about the impact it will have on his own family, rather than the hundreds of people affected by his crimes. He is keen to point out the crimes are all down to him and did not involve his wife and daughter.

“The whole thing has been a crescendo of poor choices, situations, debt. It’s all on my shoulders, I am solely responsible for the whole event. Which obviously has implications of my future and how my family’s future will be," he says. When asked how many bodies were in your storage facility, he admits: “Quite a lot. A good 30.

"There's a portion of them that are new, so haven’t done the funeral yet, ummm, there are a couple, a few more that we have only recently done. And then the others I was, well the plan was to get them cremated as soon as I could afford to do so. “

‌



View 5 Images Bags of ashes were found at Hessle Road in Hull (Image: Humberside Police)

When asked why he had not cremated the bodies, he told them he blamed his “debts” and “cash flow problems”. The officer asks: ‘So in your own mind you would catch up eventually?’ He then laughs strangely before adding: “They weren’t meant to stay with me forever. The oldest one was the paperwork I needed, I didn't have, otherwise I would have…I chased it but it was too far down the line.

“I should have contacted bereavement services and told them what had happened but then I would have revealed everything and I’d be sat here talking to you. I didn’t want them to be with me. I wanted to make things right. I know that this has hurt people and I am, I am so sorry for the hurt caused. But I never wanted this to be like this. It wasn’t my plan, it was poor choices.

“This is just a problem I was hoping to resolve without causing the hurt I know it has caused. I wanted to continue my business. You know I wanted to continue helping people. I always enjoyed being a funeral director…It was a real privilege but this has been as I am sure you can imagine, distress it caused (to) myself, I caused myself…”

‌



During his interviews he moaned about his high energy bills and how body bags were ‘surprisingly expensive things”. He told how he’d taken to making his own coffins after being shown how to by a joiner. But he was still buying superbikes and going on luxury holidays. When he was arrested he just returned from Arizona where he’d gone to watch motorcycling races.

He shared his passion for luxurious fast super bikes, which he owned several of, with his daughter and four full leathers with helmets were stored in his Legacy premises. About his spending habits, he said: “I wouldn’t say we had an exorbitant lifestyle, we tried to still live but generally the biggest problem was having branches I couldn’t afford to have but couldn’t give away.

"Then I had electric and gas, which was as much as the rent. Then Hull city council was coming at me and then the other crematoriums did the same when they got wind of that. So everywhere I go I have to pay in advance.”

View 5 Images Bush was more relaxed during his police interview and said he didn't mean to 'hurt' anyone

‌



Stroking his beard he replied: “I never intended for any of this…I suppose, opportunities that were maybe poor choices that maybe I’d taken them to try to fire-fight one problem over another. But mostly it’s always been financial problems. Debt has led to this. A continuous onslaught of financial crisis.”

Sipping from a plastic coffee cup and picking his nails he was asked how many bodies the facility could hold. He replied: “I think about 45 trays. I know we say spaces but they are not all either fit for purpose…”

The ‘opportunities’ for Bush to save money came when funerals were held in his own chapel and they would keep the coffin themselves - telling families the cremation would happen at a later date. He explained: “It presented an opportunity that I didn’t have to maybe do it immediately and if I held onto them for a little bit, it backfilled another one, and to catch up but I didn’t catch up.”

And he bemoaned the struggles of the funeral industry: “Since January it has been very quiet for everybody but before that in a good month you would be looking at 18 to 20 (funerals) a month, since we’ve had Hessle Road. Before that 1 or 2, was getting pretty dire before then. The last couple of months been more like six or seven. The crematoriums have been quiet too…”

‌



He agreed his bank accounts were “messy” and added: “I just pay the biggest wolf really. I think I ignored problems for too long and hoped that I was going to come up with a magic solution. Either more work would turn up or maybe….I tried a couple of times to do these IVA things but they just want more money off you. They kind of also need structured accounts which I didn’t have. Some of the other mechanisms people might turn to, I wasn’t able to.”

When he was quizzed again in July his solicitor read out a statement on his behalf. “I have never actually prevented the lawful and decent burial of any deceased person whether intentionally or recklessly."

News.title: Dramatic arrest of teenage Norwegian 'hitman' who organised crime gang tasked to kill someone
News.content:
Dramatic arrest of teenage Norwegian 'hitman' who organised crime gang tasked to kill someone

Footballer Johannes Natland, 19, travelled to the UK to carry out an assassination and has now been convicted of a conspiracy to commit murder after a Counter Terrorism Police investigation

Norwegian hitman guilty of murder plot for gang linked to Iran

A teenager who travelled to Britain from Norway to carry out a "hit" for a Swedish gang has been found guilty of conspiracy to murder.

Johannes Natland was thwarted when police swooped to arrest him in a hotel room in Huddersfield, West Yorkshire, after being found to be in possession of two firearms and 19 rounds of ammunition. The Old Bailey heard how the talented footballer, 19, had been tasked by organised crime group Foxtrot Network to carry out criminal activity on behalf of the Iranian regime.

The murder target of the Scandinavian group, which has been sanctioned by the UK government, has never been identified. Following a retrial, Natland heard the jury's unanimous guilty verdict today after they deliberated for more than 17 hours. He showed no emotion in the dock as the decision was read out.

View 5 Images Johannes Natland, 19, was arrested in a hotel room in Huddersfield (Image: Metropolitan Police / SWNS)

Natland pleaded guilty to possession of the firearms and ammunition, but had denied the conspiracy charge. CTP London officers uncovered a significant amount of evidence demonstrating that he was fully aware he was being asked to kill someone in the UK.

Prosecutor Alistair Richardson said during the trial that the teenage was "recruited" by the Foxtrot Network, which was described as a Swedish organised crime group, backed by the Iranian regime. It is well known for hiring young killers that Europol has called "violence-as-a-service".

Commander Helen Flanagan, head of Counter Terrorism Policing London, said: “Due to the swift and professional work of CTP London officers, supported by officers from West Yorkshire Police and CTP North East, Natland was arrested before he was able to carry out a murder in the UK.

View 5 Images He wore only boxers when the police raided his room (Image: Metropolitan Police / SWNS)

“This investigation highlights the importance of the strong links with our international law enforcement partners to counter the very real threat of criminal organisations across European borders. We’ve worked particularly closely with colleagues from Norwegian law enforcement authorities and as a result, we have stopped somebody from being assassinated here in the UK.

“Our investigation, which remains ongoing, has also resulted in two lethal weapons and ammunition being taken out of criminal hands and off the streets of the UK which has undoubtedly made the public safer.”

He was arrested in in March 2025 and a bag containing two guns - a semi-automatic pistol and a revolver - and bullets was discovered inside a plastic bag under his bed. He had arrived at Manchester Airport on an emergency passport two days earlier.

5 View 5 Images Two firearms were found under his bed (Image: Metropolitan Police / SWNS) 5 View 5 Images The 19-year-old landed in the UK two days before (Image: Metropolitan Police/PA Wire)

Natland was only prevented from carrying out the hit because Norwegian police arrested the teenager who had recruited him and alerted the UK force.

During the trial, jurors viewed bodycam footage of armed police arresting Natland at Briar Court Hotel in Huddersfield, West Yorkshire, 48 hours after his arrival in the UK. At 5.15am on March 19 last year, officers knocked loudly on his hotel room door saying: “It’s the police, come to the door.”

Natland came out wearing only a pair of boxer shorts and rubbing his eyes as if he had just woken up.

He turned to one of the officers and held his hands up, imitating holding a gun and pretending to shoot him with his empty hands.

Another officer immediately took hold of the defendant’s left hand, put him against the wall and he was arrested on suspicion of conspiracy to murder.

Asked if there were any weapons in his room, he shook his head slightly.

View 5 Images Police released footage of his dramatic arrest (Image: Metropolitan Police / SWNS)

The footage captured an exchange with one of the officers in which a smiling Natland asked if he was “happy”, saying in Norwegian: “That was fun, like.”

He had travelled on a temporary Norwegian passport, he was stopped and spoken to by a Border Force officer.

‌



He told the officer he had come to the UK with just £40 to “visit friends” who he knew online from playing Fortnite and Fifa, the court heard.

Natland was taken to Huddersfield police station where he spoke to a nurse about his history of cannabis use.

After a police interview in which he answered no comment, Natland was escorted back to the custody desk and while waiting to be taken back to a cell, gesticulated with his finger to an officer and said: “Sneaky sneaky.”

Article continues below

A Counter Terrorism Police investigation remains ongoing. In September 2025, a 27-year-old man was arrested on suspicion of conspiracy to commit murder. He has subsequently been released under investigation.

Two men, aged 30 and 27, were arrested in Bradford on 20 May on suspicion of handling stolen goods (a car). They were taken into custody before being released on bail.

News.title: Rambling Donald Trump veers off script and falls asleep during Graham eulogy
News.content:
US President Donald Trump speaks at the funeral of late US Senator Lindsey Graham

Donald Trump struggled to stick to the script and appeared to have difficulty staying awake during the funeral service for Senator Lindsey Graham in Washington DC on Tuesday

Donald Trump once again found himself unable to stick to the script during a eulogy for Senator Lindsey Graham, veering off-topic to joke that the late senator wasn't actually liked by everyone.

"Virtually everyone, Republican or Democrat, liked Lindsey," the US president said during a eulogy for his former rival turned close political ally, who died earlier this month aged 71.

"Well, not everybody," he quipped. "But it sounds good. He was a tough cookie. I have to be honest. I have to veer from this for a second."

Elsewhere during the funeral service on Tuesday, the 80-year-old president appeared to struggle to keep his eyes open after earlier holding closed-door meetings with both Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky.

In a post on X after the meeting, Zelensky said the pair had discussed Trump's recent pledge to allow Ukraine to produce Patriot missile interceptors, as well as "several other ideas that could help".

In a video shared on social media, Netanyahu hailed the meeting as "one of the best conversations I’ve had with the president of the United States". White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt wrote on X: "Both meetings were positive and productive!"

News.title: Andy Burnham makes emotional pledge to fix social care for 'my dad and millions like him'
News.content:
Andy Burnham makes emotional pledge to fix social care for 'my dad and millions like him'

Andy Burnham said risks of failing to reform social care were too great, with around 2million people struggling to access care in England while others see their savings wiped out

View 2 Images Andy Burnham meets a resident as he visits a care home in north London (Image: Getty Images)

Andy Burnham made an emotional pledge to overhaul the crisis-hit social care system to help “my dad and the millions like him”.

‌



The Prime Minister said the risks of failing to reform social care were too great, with around 2million people struggling to access much-needed care in England while others see their savings wiped out to fund help for their loved ones.

‌



He said England’s system is “as unfair as American healthcare”, adding: "The vulnerable pay with everything, and it can completely leave them with nothing."

‌



In an emotional speech at a Jewish Care facility in north London, Mr Burnham described how carers looking after his dad Roy, who has Alzheimer's, could draw out "a moment of his old character" through conversation. He has previously spoken of his heartbreak that his dad doesn't know that he has become Prime Minister.

Assisted dying debate should only come after hospice and care changes, says Andy Burnham READ MORE :

View 2 Images Prime Minister Andy Burnham meets residents and staff members as he visits a care home in north London (Image: Getty Images)

The Prime Minister hit out at politicians that kicked the issue into the long grass for decades - with 22 reviews in the past 30 years. "It's a major dereliction of public duty that Parliament has not faced up to this of all challenges, something so fundamental to life as this," he said.

‌



He added: "I am making this a test of myself whether I can bring forward a solution, or I would never forgive myself, ever."

Mr Burnham wants to create a new national care service, with better pay and training for care workers, and closer ties to the NHS, to ease pressure on hospitals.

He said an independent review by Baroness Casey would be brought forward to next summer, instead of 2028, alongside a national consultation with the public about the kind of system they want to see.

‌



He also kicked off cross-party talks with the Tories and the Liberal Democrats to try to find consensus on an issue that has bedevilled politicians for decades.

Efforts to reform social care have repeatedly been torpedoed by rows over how to fund it. While Mr Burnham was Health Secretary in Gordon Brown's government, plans to allow people to defer payment until after they died were floated - but sparked a backlash, with the Tories branding it a "death tax".

Theresa May abandoned plans to get people to pay more of the costs of their care in 2017, which was dubbed a "dementia tax" by critics.

‌



Mr Burnham said he wanted to stop people having to sell their homes to pay for care, but said there would need to be "difficult decisions” on funding.

He left the door open to tax hikes but said the Government owed it to the public to “do more with what you’ve got”. He signalled that tax rises to pay for social care could be in Labour’s next manifesto, saying: “We will put them before the country at the right time, and we will hopefully proceed with people’s consent.”

He also pointed to the eye-watering bill for social care failings, which cost the NHS around £2.5 billion a year to keep patients in hospital who are well enough to leave because there is no suitable care.

‌



Carers should be the best paid people in society, not the worst, he said, promising reforms to the social care workforce to bring it in line with the NHS.

Mr Burnham said: "I watch sometimes how people communicate with my dad and they're able to catch a kind of a moment of his old character. It comes out because of the way they draw in the conversation and that is an amazing talent to have.

"But also moving from a wheelchair to an armchair, or from there to a bed without distress or discomfort, it is incredibly demanding and skilful what they do and that needs to be recognised."

‌



Describing how many overseas care workers were caring for his father, he said: “I want those carers to know we appreciate you, we appreciate what you are doing to support people here.”

Mr Burnham, who spoke without notes, said he was prepared to stake his political reputation on the plans.

“This is huge for me,” he said. “I know this will require me to put what political capital I have on the table and it could wear down that political capital in some ways.

‌



“But I’m prepared to do it. I’m prepared to do it because this has gone on too long. The risks of failing to act are too great.”

Appearing visibly emotional, he said: "I am going to do all of those things for my dad and the millions like him up and down the country."

Lib Dem leader Sir Ed Davey, who cares for his disabled son, said he felt hopeful after constructive talks. "Everyone will have to accept things we might not like in order to work together - but I think that’s what the public want and expect us to do," he said.

Article continues below

Shadow health secretary Stuart Andrew, who represented the Tories at the talks, said: “The Conservatives are ready to work with Labour on serious proposals to reform social care.

“But Burnham needs to produce the detail, and pledge not to raise taxes or increase borrowing to pay for change.”

News.title: France wildfires live: 42C heatwave threatens nuclear plant after shock arrests
News.content:
A scorching heatwave threatens to force the closure of the Golfech nuclear power plant in south-west France just days after operations at the site resumed following a 17-day shutdown

A scorching heatwave threatens to worsen wildfires and force the closure of a nuclear power plant in south-west France just days after it came back online.

The Golfech nuclear power plant was shut down for 17 days after temperatures in the River Garonne, from which the plant draws water to cool its reactors, approached the regulatory limit of 28C. But France's latest heatwave - which will see temperatures in the region soar to 42C today - could force state-owned electricity company EDF to shut the plant down again.

Meanwhile, astonishing arrests have been made as firefighters continue to battle wildfires that have ravaged 42,000 hectares of south-west France and spread into parts of the Bordeaux metropolitan area. More than 220,000 people in the Gironde region have been evacuated over the past week in what has been France's largest peacetime evacuation.

But while many have sought refuge in evacuation centres, a handful of people have instead found themselves in police custody. A man was arrested after allegedly "posing" as a psychologist offering paid counselling sessions to those affected by the fires, French police told Sky News.

Two men were arrested several days ago on suspicion of "stealing food and supplies" intended for those affected by the wildfires, the broadcaster reported. Officers have been standing outside evacuation centres and fire-ravaged areas to keep people safe and ensure restricted zones are protected.

Although the regional prefecture said the wildfires remain "stabilised", with "several flare-ups" brought under control overnight, officials warned weather conditions remain "unfavourable" today.

News.title: Pedestrian dies after being hit by road sweeper in Salford suburb
News.content:
Pedestrian dies after being hit by road sweeper in Salford suburb

The victim, a man aged 64, succumbed to his injuries in hospital following the incident on Cleggs Lane, Little Hulton

View Image The scene of the incident on Cleggs Lane (Image: MEN Media)

A man has died after he was hit by a road sweeper in a Salford suburb.

‌



The incident took place on Cleggs Lane in Little Hulton yesterday morning, with a large number of emergency services sent to the scene. Cleggs Lane was cordoned off by the police shortly after the incident at around 8am.

‌



Greater Manchester Police have confirmed this afternoon that the pedestrian, aged 64, died in hospital yesterday afternoon. Manchester Evening News reports the man had suffered serious and life-threatening injuries.

‌



The driver of the road sweeper, a 39-year-old man, was uninjured. Enquiries into the circumstances of the incident remain ongoing.

Anyone who witnessed the incident or has footage of it is asked to contact the police.

Article continues below

A similar incident took place in October last year in Leicester, when Sardar Joginder Sing Ji, aged in his 80s, died after he was hit by a road sweeper owned by Leicester City Council. A man was initially arrested on suspicion of causing death by careless driving but was later released under investigation.

News.title: Sainsbury's makes major change to Nectar rewards as shoppers save more money
News.content:
Sainsbury's makes major change to Nectar rewards as shoppers save more money

Sainsbury's shoppers can now collect one Nectar point for every £1 spent on Sainsbury’s products through Uber Eats in a major expansion of the loyalty scheme

View Image Sainsbury's shoppers should add their Nectar details when buying products via Uber Eats (stock) (Image: Getty)

Shoppers are being urged to add their Nectar details before ordering food from Sainsbury's via Uber Eats.

‌



In a major expansion of the loyalty scheme, customers can now collect one Nectar point for every £1 spent on eligible Sainsbury’s products through the Uber Eats app or website.

‌



But shoppers must enter their full Nectar card number at checkout, or they will miss out, as points cannot be awarded retrospectively.

‌



The new collection option is available through participating Sainsbury’s stores on Uber Eats, with the wider rollout covering more than 1,300 locations across the UK.

It means customers using the rapid-delivery service for fresh food, household essentials or last-minute purchases can now earn rewards on their orders.

Free apples in Tesco for next few weeks for certain customers at 800 stores READ MORE :

Once a Nectar card has been added, qualifying points will be credited to the shopper’s account within 28 days. A minimum spend of £1 applies.

‌



Several products are excluded, including gift vouchers, baby milk, lottery tickets, tobacco, vapes, nicotine products, proprietary medicines, spirits and liqueurs. Additional restrictions apply to alcohol purchases in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.

The launch expands the existing relationship between Nectar and Uber, which already allows members to exchange points for vouchers covering Uber journeys and Uber Eats orders.

Customers can therefore collect Nectar points when buying Sainsbury’s groceries through Uber Eats and later exchange their balance for an Uber voucher.

‌



To redeem points, members should open the Nectar app, visit the “Partners” section and select Uber. Katie Hunter, Uber Eats general manager for grocery and retail in the UK, said: “We know how much Uber Eats customers love Nectar, so bringing points directly to their Sainsbury’s orders was a no-brainer.

“Now, they can collect Nectar points on all their Sainsbury’s essentials as well as spending them across the entire Uber app. It’s all about delivering flexibility, convenience and value for customers right alongside their favourite groceries.”

Mark Given, Sainsbury’s chief technology, marketing and data officer, said the expansion would give Nectar members another way to receive value from the partnership.

Article continues below

He said: “Nectar members can already turn their points into Uber rides or Uber Eats treats – and now they can collect points when ordering Sainsbury’s groceries through Uber Eats too.

“It’s another way we’re helping customers get more from Nectar, whether they’re stocking up on essentials, planning dinner or making everyday life that little bit easier.”

Shoppers wishing to collect points must select groceries from a participating Sainsbury’s store through Uber Eats and provide their Nectar card number before completing the transaction.

News.title: More than half of England in drought, Environment Agency declares
News.content:
Drought has been declared across more than half of England as hot, dry weather takes its toll on the country's water supplies.

The Environment Agency (EA) announcement covers much of central, eastern and southern England, and is a public sign that further restrictions on water use might follow.

It added that the impacts are already being felt, including low river flows, early harvests and high risk of wildfires. More than 20 million people are already under hosepipe bans.

North Wales and the Upper Severn river basin entered drought conditions last week, Natural Resources Wales said.

Scotland does not declare drought but monitors "water scarcity". Some parts of eastern Scotland are in the most extreme category of "significant scarcity", according to the Scottish Environment Protection Agency.

Northern Ireland is not currently in drought.

News.title: Burnham doesn't rule out tax rises to fix social care
News.content:
In an emotional speech he praised those caring for his father, who has Alzheimer's, and said he wanted to deliver changes to help "my dad and the millions like him".

Speaking to reporters afterwards, he said he wanted to extract more from existing budgets to fund the reforms.

"I think we owe it to the public before we talk about tax rises.. you first have to look the public in the eye and say 'Are we doing everything we can do from within what we've got?'"

For example, he said his announcements on improving pay and training for the social care workforce "will be fully funded".

But he added that fuller reforms "will require difficult decisions" and these "would be put before the country at the right time, and we will hopefully proceed with people's consent".

Burnham said in "an ideal world" he would not want anyone to have to sell their home to pay for care, describing it as a "really awful process".

He added proposals he previously put forward, when he was health secretary in 2009, were intended to stop that, saying: "If everybody on the NHS principle contributed a little, it would mean everybody could protect the majority of what they'd worked for."

He later held talks with Lib Dem leader Sir Ed Davey and Conservative shadow health secretary Stuart Andrew as part of efforts to get cross-party backing for any changes. Tory leader Kemi Badenoch was unavailable.

The Conservatives have previously urged the prime minister to rule out tax rises or increased borrowing to pay for social care changes.

Speaking to the BBC's Radio 4 PM, Andrew said it had been important to set "red lines" around funding.

He acknowledged finding funding would be a "challenge" but added that there was "a significant amount of money in the system - it's just sometime it is not in the right place".

Burnham did not invite the leaders of Reform UK or the Green Party of England and Wales to the talks. Both parties have expressed disappointment at this.

The PM said there was a feeling at Westminster that social care was "too big a political risk" to deal with, adding he wants to take on the challenge as the "risks of failing to act are too great".

Burnham highlighted the financial impact of care costs on people and spoke of how fixing issues in social care could ease the pressure on the NHS and make savings.

The PM said Baroness Casey's review should consider how to pay for a national care service, adding there needs to a system that becomes "highly integrated" with the NHS.

Burnham said he wants to "immediately" focus on the social care workforce, noting a fair pay agreement is due to come into force from 2028/29 and described it as a "massive building block of a national care service".

News.title: Serial killer given whole life orders for murders of two men as police investigate four more deaths
News.content:
Serial killer James Desborough has been given two whole life prison sentences with no chance of parole - as police revealed they are looking into four unexplained deaths at the homeless shelter that housed him.

Desborough, already serving a minimum of 19 years for the murder of his prison cellmate, was given the whole life tariffs for killing 57-year-old Claudio Aquilino and Daniel Coleman, 43, in Cornwall.

Aquilino and Coleman met Desborough at Newquay's Sandy Lodge homeless shelter, where police are now reviewing the unexplained deaths of two other men and two women.

Sentencing, Mr Justice Pushpinder Saini described Desborough, 40, as "a highly dangerous individual who had no regard for the life of those you think are worthless".

Desborough befriended the two vulnerable men and used "extreme violence" on both of them, before dismembering and concealing their bodies, the judge said.

He said the former builder used their bank cards and made journeys to give the impression they were still alive.

News.title: Is World Cup sell-off plan a step too far by Infantino?
News.content:
Gianni Infantino is billing it as the democratisation of football.

But Fifa's announcement that it aims to sell off stakes in its football competitions - including the World Cup - to private investors via associates of US President Donald Trump has been met with incredulity and rage from fans, politicians and regional governing bodies.

The big selling point, according to Infantino, is $40m (Â£30m) in funding given to all Fifa countries to "develop the game" once the deal is finalised.

The Swiss has set a deadline of 19 September for football federations to accept his plans if they want to access an initial $20m (Â£15m).

This is the boldest move Infantino, an administrator who views himself as a world leader on par with presidents and prime ministers, has made in the decade since he became Fifa president.

If Fifa pushes the plan through, he will have consolidated his power for the long-term future and made investors wealthy along the way.

So why exactly does Infantino feel powerful enough to enact something so controversial, and what could the consequences be?

News.title: France fire crews face searing heat in battle to contain flames
News.content:
As the smoke eases, firefighters then move into the forest on foot to try and contain the latest flare-up.

They are the principal concern for the thousands of crews and volunteers combating the wildfires that have raged here for a week, forcing tens of thousands of residents and tourists to flee.

As temperatures peak at around 40C, fires restarting on their own are a constant threat.

After 20 minutes or so, the one we are watching is brought under control, only for another to suddenly emerge on the opposite side of the road.

"Leave now!" shouts an understandably irritable officer as he drives past. The smoke is becoming thicker and more aggressive. Indeed, time to leave.

Such is the vast scale of the infernos ravaging France's south-western Gironde region, that it is not always obvious what direction the smoke is coming from.

It simply descends as you travel west from Bordeaux along empty roads and through deserted villages.

The soil is powder-like and covered in endless pinecones and dried leaves. It explains how the wildfires have spread at the rate they have.

News.title: Some tech shares are plunging - what does that mean for the AI revolution?
News.content:
The euphoria for this technology has boosted the value of some world's biggest companies even as they spend hundreds of billions of dollars on the building blocks of the technology.

But over the last few weeks, the value of some of the companies that make those building blocks has plummeted - prompting some to question whether what some have dubbed "the AI bubble" is about to burst.

Some of the sharpest falls have been in Asia, with shares in Korean chip makers such as SK Hynix and Samsung down 46% and 35% respectively over the last month as investors worry the recent boom in demand for the chips that power AI is unsustainable.

Yet these shares still are up threefold and fivefold respectively over the last year, leading many to conclude that some caution and profit taking after such massive gains was inevitable â and indeed healthy.

The South Korean stock market is notoriously volatile, but concerns have spilled over into the big US companies.

Shares in Google and Tesla plunged briefly before recovering last week after both firms pledged to spend billions more on AI in the months and years to come despite so far it losing them money.

And with other big names such as Meta, Microsoft and Amazon reporting their latest financial results this week, investors have the opportunity to scrutinise just how much these companies are now betting on AI.

"There is still a healthy degree of scepticism about the ability of these investments to generate a commensurate level of return," Russ Mould, an investment director at AJ Bell, said.

But according to leading tech investor Eileen Burbidge despite the concerns there's not yet a serious reckoning.

"The AI bubble hasn't burst but it's letting out air," she told the BBC.

News.title: Funeral boss 'abandoned' bodies to 'let nature take its course'
News.content:
This story contains details some might find distressing.

Bodies found at a funeral home in varying states of decomposition had been "simply abandoned" and left "for nature to take its course", a court has heard.

Hull Crown Court has heard graphic descriptions of how 35 bodies and more than 100 sets of ashes were found at Legacy Independent Funeral Directors in March 2024.

Former undertaker Robert Bush has admitted 67 offences, including failing to bury and cremate people.

His sentencing hearing was told police found unidentified ashes in mouldy boxes at the Hessle Road premises, as well as family photographs on the "extremely dirty" floor, among other disturbing discoveries.

News.title: Cyber-attackers take 607,000 records from Department of Education
News.content:
Hackers have obtained about 607,000 records in a cyber-attack on the Department for Education (DfE) in England.

The data taken includes telephone numbers and email addresses relating to individuals and organisations but does not include bank details or other sensitive information.

The DfE confirmed the incident and said it is working closely with the National Cyber Security Centre and the National Crime Agency (NCA).

The department says the risk considered to individuals is not considered high and it is understood the attack was contained quickly.

The Turing Scheme portal - a programme providing funding for international education - and the DfE online help desk have both been affected, but are expected to be operating normally later this week.

The DfE has referred itself to the Information Commissioner's Office.

"We have robust processes in place to protect information and took swift action to contain this incident", a DfE spokesperson said.

"The information involved is limited to customer service contact details relating to individuals and organisations. No other data has been accessed".

It stressed the 607,000 figure relates to the total number of records affected, not individuals.

An NCA spokesperson said: "We are aware of an incident affecting the Department for Education and are working with partners to understand the circumstances and impact."

Cyber incidents within the education sector are becoming more frequent.

Around a quarter of further education institutions (24%) reported experiencing a breach or attack at least weekly according to the government's most recent Cyber Security Breaches Survey., external

And more than half of schools have reported an attack or breach in the last year.

News.title: Boy, 7, dies in hospital after beach tragedy
News.content:
A seven-year-old boy has died in hospital after a beach tragedy that also killed his teenage cousin and her mother, his family has said.

Musa Ahmed was on a day trip to West Mersea, Essex, on 22 July, when he and five relatives got into difficulty in the water.

While he was pulled from the water and airlifted to hospital, Shelina Rahman, 41, and 15-year-old Sameeha, died at the scene.

Musa's family said he died "in a state of ease and peace" at the Royal London Hospital on Tuesday evening.

The family had travelled to the island, near Colchester, from Barking in east London that morning.

Three others were also taken to hospital by ambulance after the incident, first reported to Essex Police at 17:35 BST, and were said by the force to be "recovering".

Musa's father, Shahin Ahmed, has said they were swept away by a "very strong" tide and police said they made "significant efforts to help each other".

Posting on Facebook earlier, Ahmed said of his son: "He made every person feel special and never failed to bring happiness."

News.title: Teenage Norwegian 'hitman' guilty of UK murder plot
News.content:
A teenager who travelled from Norway to the UK to carry out a "hit" for a Swedish organised crime group has been found guilty of conspiracy to murder.

An Old Bailey jury heard how Johannes Natland, 19, was arrested in a hotel room in Huddersfield with two working guns and 19 rounds of live ammunition in March 2025.

He pleaded guilty to possession of the firearms and ammunition but had denied the conspiracy charge.

Following a retrial, Natland showed no emotion as the jury brought in a unanimous guilty verdict after deliberating for just over 17 hours.

During the trial opening, prosecutor Alistair Richardson said the teen was "recruited" by the Foxtrot Network, which was described as a Swedish organised crime group backed by the Iranian regime.

Natland had claimed rather than carry out the attack, he had planned to shoot himself in the foot, telling jurors he had found himself in "a major pickle".

The court heard how the Foxtrot Network had been sanctioned by both the UK and the US for its close links to the Iranian government.

The group is infamous for pioneering the relatively new phenomenon of hiring teenage killers that Europol has called "violence-as-a-service" (VaaS).

Natland flew into Manchester Airport on an emergency passport on 17 March and was guided by videos on the messaging app Signal to Huddersfield, where the guns, a stolen car and a stash of cash were hidden.

News.title: Fix palliative care before assisted dying debate, says PM
News.content:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said that before assisted dying is considered in England and Wales, the funding of palliative and social care should be "fixed".

It is the first time Burnham has set out his position on the issue since becoming prime minister, as MPs prepare to debate it again when Parliament returns in September.

The government is likely to remain officially neutral, but Burnham's remarks suggest he personally will not back a bill being proposed by Labour MP Lauren Edwards.

The position is a shift from that of former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer, who voted in favour of the previous attempt to legalise assisted dying and gave time for the issue to be debated in Parliament.

Sir Keir's support was privately cited by some Labour MPs as a reason they backed the bill last time.

Burnham told reporters: "I take the view that that debate - and I don't say that there shouldn't be a debate at some point about those issues - personally, I think there's something that needs to happen first.

"That is the fixing of the funding of palliative care and social care.

"I think it is very challenging to introduce that wider debate in a context of people not receiving that care and having the peace of mind about that care."

In 2025, MPs voted in favour of a bill proposed by Labour MP Kim Leadbeater to legalise assisted dying.

But the bill was not passed by the House of Lords, after an unprecedented number of suggested amendments delayed its progress until it ran out of time in April this year.

Its opponents argued it had substantial flaws that risked vulnerable people being pressured into ending their lives early.

The proposed law - known as the Terminally Ill Adults (End of Life) Bill - would have allowed people over the age of 18 who were expected to die within six months to be given help to end their own life, subject to certain safeguards.

Labour MP Lauren Edwards plans to bring forward an identical bill in order to "finish the job" started by Leadbeater.

Following Burnham's comments, she said improving social care and legalising assisted dying was "not a case of either/or" and that the two things "can and must go hand in hand".

"The bill that has been before Parliament and thoroughly debated since October 2024 provides for a four-year implementation period - that means if my current bill becomes law next year, we would have until 2031 to fix the status quo that Andy Burnham rightly says is broken."

Jess Asato - a Labour MP and opponent of the bill - said MPs had "a responsibility to consider the safety of introducing such a flawed bill into a broken and failing care system".

"There can be no meaningful choice and no dignity at the end of life if we don't have a palliative care system that provides basic support for the vulnerable and an affordable social care system that gives everyone dignity at the end of their lives."

Burnham was asked about his views on assisted dying after he had announced plans to reform the social care system, with the view to create a national care service and to reach a political consensus on how to fund it.

In 2024, just before the first Commons vote on the Terminally Ill Adults (End of Life) Bill, Burnham told BBC Manchester he would "probably vote in favour of it" if he was in Parliament.

When he was previously an MP he abstained from a 2015 vote on another bill to legalise assisted dying because of concerns over safeguards and people feeling under pressure.

But he told the BBC in 2024 that he had had "family experience in the nine years since that has changed my view".

He said: "I think we do allow people to suffer and families to suffer too much."

He caveated his support as being for the principle of assisted dying and insisted he would want a requirement before any new law was implemented that hospices would be "properly funded and sorted out".

News.title: Man accused of Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor threat faces December trial
News.content:
A man charged with threatening Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor near his home on the Sandringham Estate in Norfolk will stand trial in December.

Alex Jenkinson, 39, is accused of causing the former Duke of York to "fear unlawful violence" during an encounter as he walked his dogs on 6 May.

The trial - which will begin on 21 December - is expected to include evidence from Mountbatten-Windsor via videolink.

Jenkinson is accused of using threatening, abusive or insulting words or behaviour and had been due to stand trial on Wednesday. At Westminster Magistrates' Court, chief magistrate Paul Goldspring postponed proceedings over concerns about the defendant's mental health.

News.title: Body of Scottish woman found inside suitcase in Greece
News.content:
The body of a Scottish woman has been found inside a suitcase in an abandoned building in Greece, prompting a multi-agency investigation.

Police Scotland confirmed they are liaising with authorities after the woman was reportedly discovered by a homeless man in the Kypseli district in Athens earlier this month.

Elisabeth-Jane Ross, 38, is thought to have travelled to Greece from Cyprus last month, state broadcaster ERT reports. She is believed to have died between five and seven days before she was found.

Greek police told BBC Scotland News the body of a British woman was found and fingerprint data from Interpol matched a woman born in 1988. Investigations are ongoing.

News.title: Chief constable resigns before misconduct tribunal
News.content:
The chief constable of Staffordshire Police has resigned, ahead of a gross misconduct hearing regarding his behaviour.

Chris Noble was suspended in August amid inquiries by the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC), with the watchdog confirming in March that it had opened two more investigations regarding his behaviour.

Noble resigned on Tuesday via a letter to the Police and Crime Commissioner for Staffordshire, Ben Adams.

The misconduct hearing began on Wednesday morning in Noble's absence and has since been adjourned.

He was chosen to lead Staffordshire Police after the retirement of the previous chief constable in 2021.

Prior to this, he was the assistant chief constable of Humberside Police.

In a statement, Staffordshire Commissioner for Police, Fire & Rescue and Crime, Ben Adams said: "I can confirm that yesterday [28 July], I received Chief Constable Chris Noble's resignation, which I have accepted with immediate effect.

"Becky Riggs will remain as Staffordshire Police's acting chief constable.

"The misconduct hearing will continue today as planned, under former officer provisions."

Staffordshire Police said that it would not be appropriate to comment due to ongoing misconduct proceedings.

In a recent statement, the IOPC said: "The chair of the panel has directed that no additional information relating to the detail of the allegations can be released at this time.

"We are continuing to investigate other allegations relating to Mr Noble. Given the sensitivity of those matters, for operational reasons, no further information can be provided at this time."

News.title: Pedestrian dies after being hit by several vehicles including police car
News.content:
A pedestrian has died after being hit by multiple vehicles including a police car.

Dyfed-Powys Police were called regarding concerns for the safety of a person seen on the A40 between the PC World roundabout and Abergwili roundabout, in Carmarthen, on Tuesday.

As officers reached the scene at about 21:50 BST, reports indicated several vehicles had crashed with the pedestrian, including a marked police car that was being used for a routine patrol.

The force described it as a "six-vehicle" crash.

No arrests have been made and the force has referred itself to the Independent Office for Police Conduct.

The force said inquiries to identify the pedestrian and next of kin were underway.

It added both carriageways of the road were likely to remain closed for a lengthy period of time while officers remained at the scene, and asked motorists to avoid the area.

Anyone with information is urged to contact Dyfed-Powys Police.

News.title: Woman accused of breaching Donaldson victims' anonymity
News.content:
A woman has been charged with breaching an anonymity order in relation to the victims of former DUP leader and convicted paedophile Jeffrey Donaldson.

Police said the 55-year-old was arrested in the Ballynahinch area on Tuesday.

She has been charged with a breach of a lifetime ban on reporting the identity of victims, and is due to appear before Downpatrick Magistrates' Court on 24 August.

Victims of sexual offences receive lifelong legal anonymity unless they waive their right to it.

Donaldson, who was an MP from 1997 until 2024, was convicted in June of 18 counts of sex abuse including one count of rape, which he committed against two women when they were children.

He was told by the judge that the sentence would be a lengthy one.

It has since been confirmed he is to appeal his convictions.

Former FBI Director James Comey has accused federal prosecutors of authorizing illegal surveillance and using the words of an infamous mobster to bring charges against him for allegedly threatening the life of President Donald Trump.

In a series of court filings late Tuesday, Comey's lawyers alleged that a top Justice Department official directed the Secret Service to conduct "unlawful" electronic tracking of his cellphone after he posted an online photo of seashells arranged to show the numbers "86 47" in May 2025.

Legal papers say the electronic surveillance included tracking Comey as he and his wife "stopped to visit the grave of their deceased son," according to The Associated Press.

The North Carolina federal court filings also show discussions among Secret Service personnel about "pinging" Comey's phone and a request to Verizon to provide his location over an "emergency" situation, CBS News said.

"At that time we did not believe that anyone's life was in immediate danger and legally it was a bad idea to ping the phone," an unidentified Secret Service official allegedly said in one message.

open image in gallery Former FBI Director James Comey is seeking to have charges against him dismissed over alleged prosecutorial misconduct ( Getty )

In a Wednesday statement to The Independent, a Justice Department spokesperson said: "On the specifics here, we decline to comment."

The Secret Service didn't immediately return an inquiry from The Independent.

Court papers also show that an FBI agent interviewed former Gambino crime family underboss-turned-informant Salvatore "Sammy the Bull" Gravano about the Mafia's use of the term "86."

Gravano said that gangsters used the term to refer to killing someone — as in having a person "86-ed" — and that Comey had to know what it meant, based on his law enforcement experience.

An FBI agent requested a review of the bureau's file for the case against infamous mobster John Gambino, which Comey worked on as a young prosecutor, but didn't find any reference to "86," the AP said.

open image in gallery Comey is charged with threatening President Donald Trump’s life by posting this photo of seashells arranged to show the numbers 86 and 47 on social media ( Department of Justice )

Gravano, who was a key cooperator in that case, also said he didn't recall discussing the term with Comey or hearing it in connection with the trial, according to the AP.

Comey, who Trump fired as FBI director in 2017, was charged with two felonies in April over his social media post on grounds that it amounted to a threat against Trump, who's serving as America's 47th president.

This week's court filings seek dismissal of the charges and a hearing on the evidence in the case, which Comey — an outspoken Trump critic — blames on the president’s hatred of him.

“Ample objective evidence — much of which comes directly from government officials’ own public statements and admissions — establishes that the President’s animus toward Mr. Comey led to this vindictive and selective prosecution,” Comey’s lawyers wrote in one of the filings, according to the AP.

The White House declined to comment and instead referred The Independent to the DOJ, which has previously said: "A North Carolina grand jury indicted Comey, and he'll have his day in court like any other defendant."

The case is the second brought against Comey since Trump returned to the White House in 2025 after repeatedly telling his supporters: "I am your retribution."

The first indictment, in which Comey was accused of lying to Congress, was dismissed in November by a judge who ruled that the interim U.S. attorney who obtained it, former Trump lawyer Lindsey Halligan, had been illegally appointed.

The judge cited the same grounds for also tossing out unrelated mortgage fraud charges against New York Attorney General Letitia James. She oversaw the successful 2023 civil prosecution of Trump, a former real estate developer, for exaggerating his wealth to obtain business loans.

A popular brewery that promised free beer to its patrons upon the death of President Donald Trump is having its alcohol permit revoked.

The Wisconsin Department of Revenue is planning to shut down the Minocqua Brewing Company by August 4, according to a newsletter published Sunday by brewery owner Kirk Bangstad, who described the business as “the state’s most progressive brewery.”

Bangstad, a liberal activist who often posts anti-Trump messages on the company’s social media accounts, said he plans to fight against the decision “tooth and nail” after receiving a letter from state officials dated July 15, and asked readers to donate to the brewery’s legal defense fund.

“We need all the money we can get to sue the Department of Revenue and stay in business,” Bangstad said in an email to The Independent.

“As you can imagine, I’m not taking this lying down,” he wrote in the Substack post. “We’re going to fight the state of Wisconsin tooth and nail, and once again, they’ll have to pry me out of my taprooms before I stop selling beer to thirsty progressives who come to visit us.”

open image in gallery Minocqua Brewing Company has until August 4 to appeal its alcohol permit being revoked ( Minocqua Brewing Company )

He went on to list each of the rules that the DOR’s Division of Alcoholic Beverages has claimed that the company had broken, and explained why he believes the minor violations do not warrant the shutdown.

The company, which has locations in Madison and Minocqua, has until August 4 to appeal the revocation.

As the agency carries out the investigation, Bangstad has shared his concerns that he might be getting pushed out of business due to his vocal political views.

“Everyone reading this, Democrat or Republican, should recoil at the thought of a small and thriving business being destroyed by their state government over such small violations—especially a brewery in the state of Wisconsin!” he said.

Wisconsin’s DOR did not immediately return The Independent’s request for comment on the allegations.

open image in gallery Donald Trump was at the White House Correspondents' Dinner in April when a shooting broke out, but he was unharmed ( Getty Images )

It comes after the brewery appeared to suggest on social media that it would give out free beer if Trump were to die, although the January 22 post did not include his name, as first reported by Fox News Digital.

“Free beer, all day long the day he dies,” the post said. “Show us this post when it happens in a few months and we’ll make good on that promise.” The post was later updated to clarify, “we meant the Madison Taproom because that’s open all year, if he dies in the summer, then it’s gonna be the Minocqua Taproom.”

After shots were fired while Trump was present at the White House Correspondents’ Dinner in April, the brewery’s Facebook said, “Well, we almost got #freebeerday.”

In a new Substack post shared Wednesday, Bangstad shared that he replied to Fox News Digital’s request for comment with a similar joke promising half-off beers in the name of Mitch McConnell, who was recently hospitalized.

Bangstad concluded his letter: “Together, we’ll get to the bottom of who’s trying to put us out of business and silence our voice in Wisconsin—one beer at a time.”

News.title: Driver fleeing cops in LA accidentally ends up with a dirt bike escort after almost running down scooter rider
News.content:
A driver who led officers in Los Angeles on an hour-long chase accidentally ended up with a dirt bike escort.

On Tuesday (28 July), the driver of a reportedly stolen Mercedes SUV sped and swerved across both freeways and city streets, with officers in hot pursuit.

At one point, as he entered the northbound 110 Freeway, the motorist encountered a large group of dirt bike riders, who performed wheelies alongside the car.

After exiting the freeway and entering a downtown LA parking structure, officers surrounded the area and launched a search for the suspect.

Multiple people inside the vehicle were detained, though officers are still searching for one additional person.

Anthony Mackie has recalled his first heartwarming on-set interaction with Avengers: Doomsday co-star Ian McKellen.

Both Mackie, 47, and McKellen, 87, will reprise their respective roles of Captain America and X-Men character Magneto in the fifth installment of the Avengers franchise, out in theaters this December.

While Mackie took over as Captain America from Chris Evans at the end of 2019’s Avengers: Endgame, before officially embracing the title in the 2021 limited series The Falcon and the Winter Soldier, his casting in Doomsday was not immediately clear to McKellen.

“I go to Ian McKellen, he goes, ‘Hello, son.’ I’m like, ‘Ian McKellen, sir. You’re amazing. It’s amazing to work with you,’” he recently recounted to IMDb on the red carpet at San Diego Comic-Con.

“He goes, ‘So what are you doing in the film?’ and I’m like, ‘I’m Captain America,’” Mackie continued, expressing confusion while gesturing an arc around his head in reference to his superhero’s iconic circular, star-spangled vibranium shield.

open image in gallery Anthony Mackie replaced Chris Evans as Captain America in 2019’s ‘Avengers: Endgame’ ( Disney )

open image in gallery ‘Avengers: Doomsday’ will feature an all-star cast of classic and new Marvel actors ( Andy Park/Marvel Studios )

“And he goes, ‘Wonderful... and you deserve that,’” he said, as the interviewer laughed. “Thank you, Sir Ian, thank you.”

Mackie has since portrayed the agile and strong superhuman in the latest Captain America iteration, Brave New World (2025).

Meanwhile, it’s been more than 10 years since McKellen’s latest appearance as mutant antihero Magneto in X-Men: Days of Future Past (2014). He originated the comic book villain in the 2000 film X-Men, later playing the character in X-Men: The Last Stand (2006), X-Men 2 (2006) and Days of Future Past. He additionally made a brief mid-credits cameo in The Wolverine (2013).

Avengers: Doomsday officially replaced Avengers: The Kang Dynasty, which was originally expected to star Jonathan Majors as Kang the Conqueror before he was convicted of assaulting his ex-girlfriend in 2023.

open image in gallery Ian McKellen and Mackie co-star in the forthcoming 'Avengers: Doomsday' ( Getty )

In the wake of the conviction, Marvel dropped Majors and rewrote and retitled the next Avengers film.

Premiering December 18, Doomsday will follow the Avengers as they team with the Fantastic Four, Thunderbolts and Earth’s other mightiest superheroes to save the multiverse from the evil Doctor Doom (Robert Downey Jr.).

Directed by brothers Joe and Anthony Russo, the film will welcome the return of several classic Marvel stars, including X-Men’s Rebecca Romijn and James Marsden and Thor’s Chris Hemsworth, alongside newer Marvel actors The Fantastic Four: First Step’s Vanessa Kirby and Pedro Pascal, Thunderbolts*’ Lewis Pullman and Florence Pugh, among others.

An extended trailer for the movie won over eager audiences at Comic-Con, following the release of an “underwhelming” first clip last week.

News.title: Tony review – Anthony Bourdain biopic didn’t need to linger on his tragic fate
News.content:

Anthony Bourdain made the necessary act of feeding ourselves feel like a rock ’n’ roll philosophy, a radical form of communication that could obliterate all boundaries of language, culture, and class. His suicide in 2018 was, therefore, particularly hard. For many, he’d become an emblem of what it means to live with an open heart and an open mind.

Matt Johnson’s Bourdain biopic film Tony – which casts The Holdovers breakout Dominic Sessa as the chef, author, and documentarian in early adulthood, on the cusp of brilliance – uses the coming-of-age narrative to capture that recognisably Bourdain-esque sense of culinary revelation. As a film about what it means to embrace what’s in front of you and not what’s in your mind, it’s a lovely and deeply likeable work.

Yet Johnson and his co-writers Matthew Miller, Todd Bartels, and Lou Howe seem pressured to address Bourdain’s death in some way, as if the film would be neglectful not to. There’s some jarring foreshadowing where you can almost feel the film pause to turn solemnly to its audience and disclose, “and, of course, you know the rest of the story…”.

open image in gallery Dominic Sessa in 'Tony' ( Bob Gruen )

The Bourdain in Tony is as much a reflection of the real person as he is a literary creation, carved out from two brief chapters in his 2000 memoir Kitchen Confidential in which he describes the summers he spent washing dishes in Provincetown, Massachusetts. He considered himself, at that time, to be “a spoiled, miserable, narcissistic, self-destructive and thoughtless young lout, badly in need of a good ass-kicking”.

Johnson opens with Bourdain, calling himself Tony, pitching his “idea for an idea” of a book in the hopes of securing a writing fellowship at Vassar College in 1975. He mentions a JD Salinger slant, without realising that he is, in fact, carrying around all shades of The Catcher in the Rye’s Holden Caulfield, as “spoiled, miserable, narcissistic, self-destructive and thoughtless” in nature.

He can barely initiate a conversation without mentioning he’s a writer, including with the girl he’s infatuated by (Emilia Jones’s Nancy, a relatively thankless love interest role), and follows her to Provincetown when he fails to land the fellowship and can’t bear to tell his judgemental mother (Dagmara Domińczyk). There, he stumbles into a local seafood joint named The Flagship, unremarkable in its wood-clad walls and sparse menu, yet oddly serene when blessed by the presence of its chef, largely because he’s played by the ever-soulful Antonio Banderas. He hints at something poetic beyond the testosterone fumes emitted by the rest of the staff, Sal (Leo Woodall), Stavros (comedian and podcaster Stavros Halkias, playing up his own abrasive persona), and Tyrone (Michael Jibrin). Johnson – who also directed this year’s funniest film, Nirvanna the Band the Show the Movie – makes these kitchen scenes a boisterous breeze.

This version of Bourdain isn’t so different to the “spoiled, miserable, narcissistic, self-destructive and thoughtless” teen Sessa played across from Paul Giamatti in The Holdovers, but it’s such a tricky character type to get right and the actor does it so effortlessly that I’d happily watch him do it a hundred more times. He talks to everybody from beneath a furrowed brow, a dead-eyed stare, and the occasional twitch of a smirk, delivering an arrogant semi-creep who’s just translucent enough for us to see and feel for the broken, lonely child beneath.

open image in gallery Sessa and Antonio Banderas in ‘Tony’ ( A24 )

In fact, Sessa adds such depth and texture to his Caulfield riff that it feels ultimately unnecessary for Johnson to add any explicit reference to the darker, sadder shades of Bourdain’s psyche. It’s already there. In quiet moments, a sense of defeat will crawl across his features. Yet Tony makes a concerted effort to transform Sal, a heavy drug user with a conquering disdain for women, into the metaphorical path of temptation, leading to a few clumsy lines about “sin eaters” and the idea some people carry darkness with them so others can live in the light. You can feel, in these moments, the film grasping at the threads in some effort to present a greater thesis about Bourdain’s life. It feels unnecessary. The audience knows who Bourdain was and part of that was what a wonderful storyteller he was. And this is a wonderful story to tell.

Dir: Matt Johnson. Starring: Dominic Sessa, Emilia Jones, Dagmara Domińczyk, Rich Sommer, Stavros Halkias, Leo Woodall, Antonio Banderas. Cert 15, 106 minutes.

‘Tony’ is in cinemas from 14 August

If you are experiencing feelings of distress, or are struggling to cope, you can speak to the Samaritans, in confidence, on 116 123 (UK and ROI), email jo@samaritans.org, or visit the Samaritans website to find details of your nearest branch.

If you are based in the USA, and you or someone you know needs mental health assistance right now, call the National Suicide Prevention Helpline on 1-800-273-TALK (8255). This is a free, confidential crisis hotline that is available to everyone 24 hours a day, seven days a week.

If you are in another country, you can go to www.befrienders.org to find a helpline near you.

News.title: The surprising costs of the Iran war: More expensive Lysol wipes and Durex condoms
News.content:

Household goods giant Reckitt Benckiser, known for producing health and hygiene products including brands such as Lysol, Mucinex and Durex condoms, says it will raise prices to offset higher costs caused by the Iran war, according to a report.

Reckitt plans to raise prices in North America and Europe, following similar increases in emerging markets, which have helped cushion the impact of higher costs stemming from the conflict, namely volatile oil prices that surged past $100 a barrel earlier this year.

Kris Licht, the chief executive of the U.K.-based company, told The Wall Street Journal that price increases will only affect some products.

The company also plans to take other productivity measures to help offset the cost of inflation, Licht said.

Reckitt raised prices in emerging markets earlier this year, which Licht said was effective. However, the full effects of cost inflation are yet to be seen, he said.

open image in gallery Reckitt Benckiser, known for brands including Durex, will raise prices of some of its goods to offset the costs of the Iran war ( PA Archive )

“There’s somewhat of a delay in some of these supply chains as the cost increases roll through,” he told the outlet. “We should see it in the next three months.”

Reckitt reported its second-quarter results Wednesday, indicating price increases in emerging markets.

Like-for-like sales in emerging markets rose 9.4 percent, 6.2 percent from price increases, according to the report. Like-for-like sales measure a company’s revenue growth by comparing sales from the same stores or products over two different periods.

open image in gallery Reckitt, which makes Mucinex, will also take other measures to try and offset the costs of inflation, according to the report ( Reuters )

Reckitt has kept its portfolio of health brands mostly protected from price increases, according to Licht, who said volumes in the segment are not as impacted by price increases.

“We oftentimes are seeing very little response, if any, on volume when we take some pricing on the health side — which is a little bit different than the hygiene business,” Licht told the newspaper.

The CEO told Reuters its operations and supply in the Middle East improved during the second quarter after the initial ceasefire between the U.S. and Iran.

“There is a headwind on cost when oil prices are up but as you’ve seen they also come down quite quickly. So it’s a manageable impact for us,” Licht told Reuters. He said that since oil prices have decreased, the company is anticipating a reduced hit from higher input costs this year.

Along with its second-quarter results, Reckitt on Wednesday launched a share buyback worth up to 500 million pounds, or $665 million in U.S. dollars.

News.title: Jet-ski, Rolex watches and Mercedes-Benz truck seized by police in Liverpool after drug raid
News.content:

Read our Privacy notice

A jet-ski, two Rolex watches, and a fleet of vehicles were among a haul of high-value items seized by police during a drug raid on a home in Liverpool.

Officers from Merseyside Police executed a warrant at a property in Speke on Tuesday as part of an ongoing investigation into drug supply.

The force stated that the seized assets are suspected to have been purchased with the proceeds of criminal activity.

Beyond the luxury goods, police also confiscated an e-bike, a quantity of cash, a PS5 game console, gaming equipment, and two iPhones.

open image in gallery An e-bike was also seized at the property ( PA )

The four vehicles taken included a white Mercedes X250 pick-up truck and a Peugeot Boxer van.

A 37-year-old man and a 29-year-old woman, both from Speke, were arrested on suspicion of acquiring, using, or possessing criminal property and possession with intent to supply cannabis.

They have since been released on conditional bail.

Chief Inspector Kev Chatterton said: “Offenders involved in the supply of drugs bring fear, violence and intimidation into the heart of our communities.

“They do so to line their own pockets while others go out and earn an honest living.

“We simply will not tolerate this and conduct warrants, stop searches, land searches and targeted operations all year round in order to disrupt their activities so that they realise crime does not pay.

“I want to reassure those communities affected that we will continue putting offenders before the courts and seizing their ill-gotten gains.”
