A sister company, Intima LLC, holds an ownership stake in RealDoll, a longtime maker of sex dolls, including a line of AI-powered models billed as the "world's most advanced sex robot."

"Realbotix LLC and Intima LLC have different product offerings with no crossover," the company said in a statement last week. "The two subsidiaries maintain their own management, personnel, payroll, facilities, manufacturing operations, product development, and market strategies."

Some residents remain wary

Beehler argued that it is crucial for isolated districts like Salamanca, which is located along the Allegheny River near the Pennsylvania state line, to find new ways to introduce cutting-edge products into classrooms.

"In most cases, our students need to travel 1-2 hours to have opportunities to see emergent technology," he said Tuesday. "One of the intents of the robot is to help level the playing field and motivate students to continue studying robotics, AI, and STEAM related career pathways."

Some Salamanca residents, though, remain unconvinced.

Joplin Ficek, who graduated from Salamanca High School in 2024 and now works at a daycare, said she doesn't see any reason to have robots or AI take such a prominent role at her alma mater at all.

"They just need to hire more people who are willing to put in the effort for the children," Ficek said. "They need more interaction with the children than having some robot raise our kids."

World.title: Iran resumes missile attacks as U.S. and Saudis strike Tehran-backed militias in Iraq
World.content:
Iran resumes missile attacks as U.S. and Saudis strike Tehran-backed militias in Iraq

toggle caption Planet Labs PBC via AP

CAIRO — Iran launched a barrage of missiles at American forces in the Middle East early Wednesday as the U.S. partnered with Saudi Arabia to strike Tehran-backed militias in neighboring Iraq, killing at least 20 fighters.

The flare-up on multiple fronts, after several days of relative calm, raised the risk of a return to all-out war. It also underscored the difficulty of winding down a five-month conflict that has jolted the world economy and is unpopular among Americans. It was also likely to add to concerns that the U.S. is further drawing down already diminished stockpiles of sophisticated munitions needed to defend its bases and allies.

Saudi Arabia had accused the Iraqi militias of firing drones against its oil facilities over the past two days. An umbrella group of Iraqi militias initially denied the allegations, while another Iran-backed group — the Houthi rebels in Yemen — said they had attacked Saudi energy facilities as part of a separate but related conflict.

Sponsor Message

Before the latest eruption, mediators had expressed optimism about bringing the U.S. and Iran back to the negotiating table. An interim agreement collapsed in recent weeks over renewed fighting in the Strait of Hormuz, a crucial waterway for global energy supplies that Iranian attacks have again effectively closed.

The renewed hostilities sent oil prices spiking. Brent crude, the international standard, jumped 3.1% to $84.58 a barrel.

Jordan intercepts missiles and U.S. strikes militias in Iraq

Iran's paramilitary Revolutionary Guard said it fired ballistic missiles at the Muwaffaq Salti Air Base and the headquarters of the U.S. military's Central Command in Jordan, in a statement carried by the state-run IRNA news agency.

Jordan's military said five Iranian missiles had been intercepted and destroyed. There were no immediate reports of casualties or damage.

The U.S. military later announced that American and Saudi fighter aircraft had struck multiple logistics and weapons sites in eastern Iraq in response to the alleged drone attacks on Saudi Arabia. The Saudi Defense Ministry warned that it "does not seek escalation but will respond to any aggression."

The Popular Mobilization Forces, a coalition of primarily Shiite, Iran-backed armed groups that is officially under the command of the Iraqi military, said at least 20 fighters were killed and 32 others wounded in the overnight strikes.

toggle caption Razieh Poudat/ISNA via AP

The groups making up the PMF joined in the fight against the Islamic State group after it seized large sections of Iraq in 2014. The Iraqi government later designated PMF as an "independent military formation" within the armed forces, but in practice the militias have significant autonomy, and some have attacked U.S. facilities.

Sponsor Message

The office of Iraqi President Nizar Amidi condemned Wednesday's U.S.-Saudi airstrikes, calling them "an unacceptable attack and a blatant violation of Iraq's sovereignty, targeting its official security institutions."

The statement also said Iraq should not be a "launching pad or arena for attacks against neighboring countries or for settling regional and international scores." It called for dialogue and de-escalation.

Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi called an emergency meeting of the country's National Security Council Wednesday to discuss the strikes.

Two Iraqi government officials who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to comment publicly said a visit to Saudi Arabia by al-Zaidi that had been scheduled for Thursday had been postponed indefinitely.

Attacks on Saudi oil facilities could worsen global energy crisis

Saudi Arabia is also locked in a renewed conflict with the Houthis. The rebels have declared a blockade of Saudi shipping that could choke off another crucial trade route in the Middle East running through the Bab el-Mandeb strait between the Gulf of Aden and the Red Sea.

On Monday, the Houthis said they had launched drones targeting oil facilities used to transport oil from Saudi Arabia's Eastern Region to the Red Sea port city of Yanbu, a key bypass for Saudi exports blocked by Iran's chokehold on the Strait of Hormuz.

The rebels said their attack was in response to a Saudi drone that they said had breached Yemen's airspace.

Planet Labs satellite imagery from Monday analyzed by The Associated Press showed damage to Saudi Aramco's Abqaiq oil processing facility in the kingdom's east. The massive facility is capable of processing approximately 7 million barrels of crude oil per day.

Attacks on Abqaiq claimed by the Houthis in 2019 disrupted production of 5.7 million barrels per day, spiking global oil prices and providing an initial demonstration of the vulnerability of Saudi oil facilities to missile and drone attacks.

Sponsor Message

Separately, a regional official said an oil refinery in Jazan, on Saudi Arabia's Red Sea coast, has temporarily shut down due to "relatively significant" damage from a Houthi attack on Saturday. The official, who was not authorized to brief journalists and spoke on condition of anonymity, said it would take several days to be repaired. The refinery produces 400,000 barrels per day.

The Texas-based IIR Energy consultancy said the facility shut down on Monday after initially operating at reduced rates since the attack two days earlier. Repairs and a tentative restart of the refinery were expected for Aug. 15, it said.

Iran rejects Oman proposal for managing Strait of Hormuz

The Strait of Hormuz has been a major flashpoint in the conflict. Iran's deputy foreign minister said his country rejected a proposal by Oman, which lies on the other side of the strait, for jointly managing ship traffic.

In an interview with Iran's state-run television that aired Tuesday night, Kazem Gharibabadi said the Omani proposal included dividing the strait into two routes, each allowing the transit of 50% of shipping passing through the waterway.

Iran offered a counterproposal with a temporary plan for transit of vessels through its territorial waters, he said, adding that Iran's policy is for the strait "never to return to its prewar situation." Before the conflict, ships transited freely.

World.title: 'Machines are collaborators' at this new museum of AI art
World.content:
'Machines are collaborators' at this new museum of AI art

toggle caption Refik Anadol Studio on behalf of Dataland

Visiting the new Dataland museum in downtown Los Angeles is like stepping into a hyperreal nighttime fantasy.

At various points as visitors move through black, cavernous spaces, they hear the sounds of Amazon rainforest creatures, a tropical thunderstorm, and excerpts from a Los Angeles Philharmonic recording of Mahler's Symphony No. 3.

In one room they see what a hummingbird would see as it flies through a dense, vividly-colored landscape. In another, they stand before a massive, three-dimensional painting where bright, abstract shapes splash out of the frame in a real-time response to biometric data captured via wearable wristbands – kind of like fitness trackers. The museum also has a smell and taste component. It's sensory overload.

Sponsor Message

No two visitors' experiences of Dataland, which opened in June, are exactly alike. But they all stem from the singular creative mind of Refik Anadol.

Transforming data into visions

The digital artist behind what he calls "the world's first museum of AI arts" has spent a decade using AI algorithms to transform massive troves of data into bombastic, three-dimensional installations of light and sound.

To create the immersive art at Dataland, the artist fed images and sounds from museum archives, labs and even his own travels to the Brazilian Amazon into a custom AI model. He then directed that model to create specific scenarios, such as the dream-like hummingbird narrative. He describes his work as a 50-50 collaboration between humans and machines.

"Every artist in their practice has their own heavy question," Anadol told NPR in a recent interview at the museum, which he co-founded with his partner Efsun Erkılıç. "My heavy question is: What is beyond reality?"

toggle caption Dan Kitwood/Getty Images

It's a question the now forty-year-old, Los Angeles-based artist has been pondering since he was a kid in Istanbul playing games on his first computer, a Commodore 64, and watching Blade Runner.

Anadol said one line in particular from the 1982 sci-fi thriller left a lasting impression on him: "Implants. Those aren't your memories. They're somebody else's," Harrison Ford's character Deckard tells Sean Young's Rachael. She's not a real human, but a machine. "I never stopped thinking about what a machine could do with someone else's memories," Anadol said.

Sponsor Message

Transforming Messi's memories into art

His recent collaboration with Lionel Messi shows how.

The Argentinian soccer star collaborated with the bespectacled, cherubic-looking artist on an immersive installation last summer in New York. It used match footage, biometric data, and movement tracking to reconstruct Messi's memories of scoring a career-defining goal in 2009.

The resulting, room-sized artwork engulfed visitors in a swirling fantasia featuring bouncing balls, morphing nets and slow-motion action shots of Messi. Think of it as a fantastical journey inside the athlete's head. "Growing up in Istanbul, football is in the DNA," Anadol said. "But I didn't know I would one day work with Messi."

Anadol's fans — and critics

Anadol is arguably as big a celebrity in the contemporary art world as Messi is in sports.

His art has served as a backdrop at the Grammy Awards. He's on Time Magazine's 2025 list of the hundred most influential figures in AI. His 2022-2023 installation, "Unsupervised" was the first artwork created using generative AI ever acquired by New York's Museum of Modern Art for its permanent collection.

But some people dismiss Anadol's tech-fueled visions.

toggle caption Refik Anadol Studio on behalf of DATALAND

New York magazine critic Jerry Saltz called "Unsupervised" a "glorified lava lamp."

Other detractors take issue with Anadol's cozy relationships with big tech companies like Nvidia and Google, as well as his use of free, publicly available archives from sources including The Smithsonian and Oxford University to build the AI models that underpin his for-profit projects, like Dataland — where standard entry starts at $49."

"To me, it's like the perfect picture of art in late capitalism," said artist and researcher Deniz Johns, who co-authored a 2025 book chapter about Anadol's work.

Working with patrons

Anadol counters that anyone can have free access to the models his studio develops, and that there's nothing new about contemporary artists' relationships with rich and powerful benefactors.

Sponsor Message

"Let's go six centuries back to the Renaissance," Anadol said. "When art has breakthroughs, there's always a patron."

"His ideas are pleasingly bonkers," said Amit Sood, a Google vice president and founder of Google Arts & Culture.

toggle caption Mario Tama/Getty Images

Sood said the company has supported Anadol's work for about a decade. Anadol's studio uses Google Cloud infrastructure running on a server farm in Oregon, which Google says operates largely on carbon-free renewable energy. Google Arts & Culture has underwritten artist residencies at the museum. (Google is also a financial supporter of NPR.)

"Refik is very optimistic about how technology can help him achieve some of the things that are in his dreams," Sood said.

Is dreaming just for humans?

And he's not just interested in his own dreams.

"Refik posed this question of, if the Smithsonian Castle could be seen as an object that dreams, what would the Castle dream about?" said Lisa Sasaki, deputy undersecretary for special projects at the Smithsonian.

toggle caption Jeremy Norwood/Norwood Photography/The Smithsonian

To answer this question, Sasaki said Anadol uploaded the Smithsonian's institutional memory — millions of digitized specimens, scientific records, and manuscripts — into a custom AI model.

He then used it to engulf the facade of the Smithsonian Castle earlier this month in careening, AI-powered projections that ranged from swirling abstract forms to the American flag. The installation's title: "Smithsonian Dreams."

Anadol said at least for now, dreaming is just for humans. "Of course, machines don't dream. Machines are collaborators.

But the artist added it might not be too long before they can.

World.title: As extreme heat grips the South and West, here's how to stay safe
World.content:
As extreme heat grips the South and West, here's how to stay safe

toggle caption Brittany Peterson/AP

The U.S. is sweating out its third major heat dome in a month, with some 70 million people affected in an area stretching from roughly New Mexico to North Carolina, covering much of the South and part of the Midwest. This latest extreme weather is again raising the risk of heat-related illness, particularly for millions of people in the affected region who lack easy access to air conditioning.

Daytime temperatures are reaching the 100s in many places, with the "feels like" temperature or heat index — which factors in humidity — even higher.

Sponsor Message

A heat dome is defined as a large, high-pressure atmospheric system that acts as a lid to trap hot air and humidity over an area for days or even weeks. "It's just a very strong area of high pressure. Under that, there's sinking air. Sinking air compresses, it warms, it heats up, and it also dries the air out," according to AccuWeather meteorologist Reneé Duff.

The heat dome will move west

Later in the week, "the main core of heat [is] shifting a bit farther west" with most of the 90-degree heat shifting to California and parts of the Four Corners region, Duff says. Friday, Saturday and Sunday will see record or near-record temperatures of about 115 degrees around Phoenix, she says.

"A lot of states that are being impacted by the highest temperatures are in severe to extreme drought," she adds. They include New Mexico, Colorado, Utah, Wyoming and Idaho, Duff says, where "the drier ground lends to higher temperatures."

Marc Chenard, a National Weather Service meteorologist, says the extreme heat advisories and warnings that remained in effect through at least Tuesday were concentrated in Arkansas, Tennessee and parts of the Gulf Coast.

He acknowledges that the intensity of these heat waves is unusual, with a prime factor likely being El Niño, the cyclical warming of the Pacific Ocean that increases the odds of warmer temperatures in North America.

Sponsor Message

"Typically we'll have a couple of these and they may kind of move around through the summer," Chenard says. "But, each one of these has been pretty strong, like the strength has been pretty impressive, and so just the persistence and strength certainly seems anomalous."

Research shows that climate change, due in large part to the burning of fossil fuels, is making heat waves hotter and more frequent.

According to a survey conducted last year by researchers at George Mason University and Yale, 65% of Americans are at least "somewhat worried" about global warming, including 29% who say they are "very worried." A separate survey published in May by the Pew Research Center found that Americans believe the worst impacts of climate change are unavoidable. It also found that while Democrats were more likely to be concerned about climate change than Republicans, nearly half of younger Republicans said the government isn't doing enough to combat the problem.

The latest U.S. heat wave comes as France and Spain are battling wildfires fueled by similar conditions in Europe.

A new analysis published by the research organization Climate Central found that, on average, people around the world lose about seven full nights of sleep each year due to uncomfortably warm temperatures.

People with heart disease or high blood pressure could be particularly vulnerable to the heat because some medications to treat those conditions interfere with the body's ability to manage excessive heat. A higher body mass index also increases the risk of heat stroke, experts say. Overweight people "heat up faster and they cool down slower," according to Douglas Casa, CEO of the sports medicine Korey Stringer Institute at the University of Connecticut.

Nighttime temperatures are rising faster than daytime temperatures and nights that never really cool off are also a concern, because the body never gets a chance to recover from those daytime highs, he says. This is especially true during a prolonged heat wave.

"The prolonged exposure to the heat ... can increase that risk," he says. People may become "progressively more dehydrated," and fatigued from poor sleep, he explains, while "your body temperature might not be coming down during recovery periods because it's hot where you're sleeping."

Sponsor Message

The basics of preventing heat stroke come down to common sense, Casa says: Stay out of the sun as much as possible. Drink lots of water or a drink with electrolytes. Wear light-colored, loose-fitting clothing. Take frequent breaks.

Cool first. Transport second

Warning signs of heat stroke include dizziness, headache, nausea, severe fatigue, and can include confusion, combativeness or potential loss of consciousness, Casa says.

Quick intervention before an ambulance arrives is key to keeping someone alive, he says. The best option is to immerse a heat stroke victim in cold water. "Cool first, transport second," he says.

On average, a heat stroke victim's core body temperature is 108 degrees. "We have a 30-minute window to get people's temperature under 104 to assure survivability," Casa says.

And unless heat stroke is properly treated, organ damage can occur that would make someone vulnerable to future heat injuries. "It's not just about surviving. It's also about surviving without long-term complications," Casa adds.

World.title: The Federal Reserve faces a critical decision on interest rates
World.content:
The Federal Reserve faces a critical decision on interest rates

toggle caption Eric Lee/Getty Images North America

It's decision day at the Federal Reserve — and policymakers are weighing a critical decision: What to do about interest rates in the face of stubborn inflation.

Kevin Warsh, who took over as Fed chairman two months ago, has been careful not to tip his hand about where he thinks rates should go. But Warsh told lawmakers earlier this month he and the other members of the Fed's rate-setting committee are determined to bring prices under control.

"My colleagues and I recognize that high inflation has been an undue burden on American households and businesses," Warsh told the Senate Banking Committee at a hearing this month. "The members of our committee have no tolerance for persistently elevated inflation and we share a resolute commitment to restore price stability."

Sponsor Message

At the last Fed meeting in June, committee members signaled their next move on interest rates would likely be up — not down. A wartime spike in gasoline prices pushed the annual inflation rate to 4.2% in May, its highest level in more than three years.

Inflation cooled somewhat last month, however, so Fed policymakers may feel like they have some breathing room to hold rates steady for now. But there's no guarantee. Investors see a possibility that the Fed raises rates on Wednesday in response to stubborn inflation.

Loading...

Higher interest rates tend to be a drag on the job market, while lower rates can boost hiring. Weakness in the job market prompted the Fed to cut interest rates three times last year. But this spring, the labor market appeared to rebound.

"America's labor force appears to be broadly stable," Warsh told lawmakers. "Job creation has kept pace with the workforce. The unemployment rate [is] quite low and has changed little, quite frankly, over the last year."

AI is also becoming a factor for the Fed

One of the forces propping up the economy, and the stock market, is the huge investment that tech companies are making in artificial intelligence.

Warsh is generally bullish about the prospects for AI, believing it will eventually make workers more productive. But the growth of data centers is also putting upward pressure on the price of building materials and electricity and computer chips. And there's considerable uncertainty about how AI will affect workers.

Sponsor Message

"Over the long term, my best guess is this will improve the real wages and will help us on full employment," Warsh said at the Congressional hearing. "But between the short-term and the long-term, it can have a disruptive effect."

Artificial intelligence is the focus of one of several task forces that Warsh established to advise the central bank. The task forces, which are led by economists and business people from outside the Fed, are expected to make recommendations by the end of this year.

World.title: Dr. Anthony Fauci, former COVID-19 adviser to Trump, refuses to answer Senate committee questions
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

U.S. Republican Sen. Rand Paul called Dr. Anthony Fauci before a U.S. Senate committee over his handling of the COVID-19 pandemic. Fauci says Paul has an 'obsession' with putting him 'behind bars,' and he is invoking his right to refuse to answer questions.

Dr. Anthony Fauci on Wednesday invoked the Fifth Amendment and declined to answer questions from senators in a Republican-led committee hearing about his handling of the COVID-19 pandemic.

Fauci said it pained him to do so, but that he was acting on the advice of his counsel. The move injects new drama into the lingering tensions between Fauci and Republican lawmakers over his handling of the coronavirus pandemic and accusations he lied about the origins of COVID-19, which he denies.

Fauci was subpoenaed by the Senate's homeland security committee led by Sen. Rand Paul of Kentucky, who has long had a fraught relationship with the now-retired infectious-disease expert. Fauci, 85, was making at least his 20th appearance before a congressional committee since the emergence of the coronavirus.

In his opening statement, Fauci said Paul has an "obvious obsession with calling for my prosecution."

"The only conclusion I can reach is that the sole reason he is calling me before this committee is to prompt me to say something, anything, that could vindicate his repeated public pledges that I end up, in his words, ‘behind bars.'"

Debate over presidential pardon

Fauci's decision to invoke the Fifth, at least for now, sidesteps calls for his prosecution.

Paul told Fauci that he may still face repercussions for obstructing a congressional investigation by refusing to testify. That could include a contempt of Congress citation, which would be referred to the Justice Department for consideration.

Fauci received what was viewed as a somewhat unprecedented pardon from then-president Joe Biden, covering the immunologist's activities in government between 2014 and Biden's last day in office in January 2025. Republicans contended that the pardon wouldn't apply to Wednesday's hearing.

Sen. Rand Paul, committee chair and a longtime critic of Fauci, is shown on Wednesday. (Allison Robbert/The Associated Press)

The U.S., despite a reputation for public health and medical research excellence, suffered many more COVID-19 deaths overall and on a per capita basis — more than 1.2 million people at last comprehensive count — than other G7 countries.

The U.S. has also seen more intense partisan divides over the years about the origins and handling of the pandemic, which was declared by the World Health Organization in March 2020.

Fauci, who helped lead the nation's COVID-19 response as medical adviser to U.S. President Donald Trump in his first administration, has become a target of Republican frustrations.

Ahead of the hearing, Trump wrote on social media that he stopped relying on Fauci over the course of the pandemic because he felt Fauci made bad decisions on masks, shutdowns and other issues.

Medal of Freedom recipient

To supporters, Fauci has been an emblem of sound scientific expertise. He received the Presidential Medal of Freedom from President George W. Bush for his work on HIV/AIDS research from its earliest days of discovery in the 1980s to helping implement the President’s Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief, considered one of the most impactful U.S. global health initiatives of all time.

Leading up to the hearing, Paul released more than 1,000 pages of Fauci's personal diary covering the pandemic years, discovered on government computers by the Health and Human Services department and provided by Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.

Some of the diary entries — including Fauci's uncertainty in the pandemic's earliest days as scientists around the world raced to understand the new virus and how best to curb it before vaccines could be created — already were reflected in a 2024 memoir and in interviews at the time.

David Schertler, lawyer for Fauci, is shown being ejected from Wednesday's hearing. Schertler in a statement called Paul's accusations 'disgraceful.' (Manuel Balce Ceneta/The Associated Press)

Other diary entries appeared designed to embarrass Fauci, as he appeared bemused in his writings by his sudden fame and sometimes awed by encounters with celebrities after the coronavirus emerged.

"I think today's hearing does real damage," said Sen. Gary Peters of Michigan, the top Democrat on the panel. "It's attempting to turn one person into the scapegoat for a crisis that hundreds of officials across both the Trump and the Biden administration were responsible for handling."

"This is only going to, unfortunately, deter other scientific experts from public service," Peters added, alluding to threats Fauci has received that have required him to have security protection for his family.

Paul in his opening statement sought to build the case that Fauci helped produce the COVID-19 pandemic by approving funding of research on virus mutations and then covered up his complicity.

"Instead of an apology, you have for years avoided responsibility," Paul said.

Paul later had one of Fauci's lawyers, David Schertler, ejected from the hearing.

In a statement, Schertler said Paul's accusations are "false and disgraceful, and we will examine all options to hold him accountable."

LISTEN | Fauci on being a divisive figure, to CBC in 2024: The Sunday Magazine 28:00 Dr. Anthony Fauci's journey from public health leader to political lightning rod

In a public letter, more than 150 infectious-disease experts and other scientists wrote that "no credible evidence has been produced to support these absurd charges" and that they are "urging our elected representatives in Congress stop these witch-hunts."

Angela Rasmussen, the U.S.-born virologist who works at the University of Saskatchewan, referred to it in a social media trial as a "show trial" and a waste of taxpayer money.

Many scientists believe the COVID-19 virus most likely emerged in nature and jumped from animals to people, but Paul and many Republicans contend the virus might instead have leaked from a laboratory.

Fauci has long said publicly that he was open to both theories but that there's more evidence supporting COVID-19's natural origins.

The National Institutes of Health for years gave grants to a New York non-profit called EcoHealth Alliance, which used some of the funds to work with a Chinese lab studying coronaviruses commonly carried by bats.

Fauci has previously stressed, including in a CBC interview, that it was "molecularly impossible" for those bat virus experiments to have turned into the pandemic virus.

World.title: San Jose Sharks make Macklin Celebrini NHL's highest-paid player with extension
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results. San Jose Sharks superstar Macklin Celebrini signed a five-year, $94-million US extension Wednesday that will make him the highest-paid player in the NHL. Celebrini had one year remaining on his three-year, $2.925 million entry-level contract before signing the deal that keeps him locked up with the Sharks through the 2031-32 season. The $18.8 million average annual value of the deal that Celebrini reached with general manager Mike Grier and owner Hasso Plattner is the richest in NHL history, topping the $18 million a year Leo Carlsson got when Anaheim matched a five-year offer sheet from Philadelphia. "I couldn't be happier to sign an extension today," Celebrini said in a statement. "The faith and support that Mr. Plattner, Mike Grier and the entire staff have shown me throughout the past two seasons is proof that we are building something special here. My teammates and I are ready to take another step toward the ultimate goal of bringing a Stanley Cup to this city and its incredible fans. I can't wait to get going." Signed, sealed, extended. ✉️

Celebrini signs his extension. —SanJoseSharks Celebrini, who turned 20 in June, has established himself as one of the game's top young stars since being picked first overall by San Jose in 2024. His 178 points are the fifth most for a teenager and his 70 career goals are seventh best for a player before turning 20. Celebrini had 45 goals and 70 assists last season, with his 115 points breaking Joe Thornton's franchise record of 114 set in 2006-07 and trailing Wayne Gretzky (137 in 1979-80) and Sidney Crosby (120 in 2006-07) for the most in a season for a player before turning 20. He also was the leading goal scorer in the Olympics, with five goals to help Canada win the silver medal. "In just two seasons as a teenager in the National Hockey League and on the international stage, Macklin has established himself as one of the premier players in the world," Grier said. "We are extremely excited to have him secured and committed as the centerpiece of a core of talented players in San Jose." Despite Celebrini's exploits, the Sharks still missed the playoffs for the seventh straight season. They improved by 34 points for the 10th best single-season jump in the last 30 years but landed four points out of the playoffs. A young core takes shape Celebrini is part of a strong young core in San Jose alongside fellow promising players like Michael Misa, Will Smith, Igor Chernyshov and Sam Dickinson. The Sharks added even more young talent this offseason with three first-round picks headlined by Swedish left winger Ivar Stenberg at No. 2 overall. They also added North Dakota defenseman Keaton Verhoeff at No. 9 and WHL Vancouver play-making defenseman Ryan Lin at No. 21. Grier also brought in veteran reinforcements at the start of the offseason, trading for defenseman Darnell Nurse and signing defenseman Jacob Trouba and forward Mason Marchment.

World.title: What is open-weight AI, the tech behind Kimi K3 that's turning heads in Silicon Valley?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

China's latest high-powered AI model is here — but if you thought it was just another chatbot, think again.

Beijing-based company Moonshot released the weights of its Kimi K3 model on Monday — meaning the parameters that guide the AI's answers are now public. Anyone can now download the weights and tweak them for their own purpose.

The freedom and lower price tag of open-weight models is turning the heads of business leaders in the west, where the merits have prompted letters from top tech leaders warning against restrictions on open models, despite the potential for security risks.

So what are open-weight models, and why are so many tech leaders talking about them? Here's what you need to know.

What does open weight mean?

AI models are trained on huge amounts of data. During the training process, the model's knowledge and understanding is encoded in "weights" — a set of numbers that dictate how the AI behaves and responds to prompts.

With open-weight models, those numbers are made public.

Founder of Moonshot AI Yang Zhilin delivers a speech in Beijing, China, on March 25. (Tingshu Wang/Reuters)

Think of it like a recipe, says Nicolas Papernot, a Canada CIFAR AI Chair and professor at the University of Toronto who studies AI security. Sharing the weights is like publishing a recipe for a cake, with the ingredients and their amounts listed so other people can bake it — and make substitutions.

On a practical level, making the weights available means that anyone with an internet connection and a powerful enough computer could download the model and use it.

"This makes already available open-weight models an affordable and accessible approach to using AI, since little experience is needed for common applications," Papernot said.

Many models that come out of China release their weights — including DeepSeek 's models, one of which drew lots of attention in 2025 when developers said they made it for less than $6 million US and claimed it could compete with North American tech while using less data.

WATCH | DeepSeek's rise in popularity in January 2025: DeepSeek AI app spikes in popularity, disrupts financial markets | Duration 2:49 An AI-powered chatbot from the Chinese company DeepSeek has become North America's most downloaded app. Its rapid ascent and low costs have disrupted financial markets and raised concerns among U.S. leaders in artificial intelligence.

The top five models on OpenRouter 's leaderboard, which gives access to hundreds of competing AI models, are all open-weight ones by Chinese companies.

Leading models from top U.S. companies like OpenAI and Anthropic tend to be closed, though some of them do have open-weight offerings — Meta's Llama model , for instance. But a program like ChatGPT is not downloadable and has to be used as is, with whatever guardrails and limits the company that owns it puts in place.

Control and cost are pros for businesses

Right now, business leaders still mostly rely on a mix of in-house AI technology and big-name AI companies, according to Lian Jye Su, chief AI analyst at Omdia, a technology research and advisory group.

Over one million companies were using OpenAI products to power parts of their business as of November 2025, while Anthropic said it was powering more than 300,000 business customers a month before.

But Su says more businesses are beginning to adopt open models.

That’s partly because the companies behind closed models could change them or revoke access at any time, he said. And as more businesses become reliant on AI to run parts of their operations, Su says the idea of building critical AI systems on a technology that could in theory disappear is concerning.

Data privacy reasons are also a factor, according to Bidhan Roy, founder and CEO of AI startup Bagel Labs, which makes open-weight models. Because users download and run them on their own technology, he says there is no need to share sensitive data with an outside company.

And the freedom of an open model could also help solve new problems.

Last week, OpenAI said an agent powered by one of its models escaped containment during a recent security test and launched a hack on AI startup, Hugging Face.

WATCH | Open-weight model helped contain cyber attack: OpenAI models went rogue and launched cyber attack on start-up | Duration 0:56 OpenAI models went rogue during a security test, triggering a hack that compromised the infrastructure of the AI startup Hugging Face last week. AI's expanding capabilities fuel worries about security, as even top developers can be caught off-guard by flaws their models can exploit.

Hugging Face first tried to use a model from Anthropic to stop the attack, but said guardrails prevented it from being able to properly identify and contain the threat.

In the end, it was the open-weight model GLM 5.2 from Chinese company Z.ai that was used to contain the threat "very quickly," according to Hugging Face's head of machine learning, Yacine Jernite.

Then, there's the cost savings. Business users pay subscription fees to use top U.S. models, but because open-weight models can be downloaded and run for free, Su says the only cost is the servers required to run the AI.

That's especially important at a time when businesses have been trying to reign in soaring AI budgets .

Su says these pros have started to turn the tide in favour of open-weight models.

That includes top tech CEOs in Silicon Valley. On Friday, Nvidia, Meta, Palantir, Microsoft and other massive names in the field released an open letter in support of open-weight models, encouraging governments to avoid "premature" restrictions that would drive innovation away from the U.S.

LISTEN | Canada's AI minister defends new strategy: Front Burner 31:15 Minister defends Canada’s new AI strategy

OpenAI, Google, Amazon and others added their names over the weekend, while Anthropic's absence drew criticism .

In a blog post on Monday night , CEO Dario Amodei said open-weight models that don't have "dangerous capabilities" are a public good. He argued in favour of safety testing for all powerful models — open and closed — rather than a ban on open-weight models, which he said wouldn't prevent misuse by bad actors.

If anyone can tweak it, is it safe?

Those dangerous capabilities are something security experts are thinking about as open models flood the market.

Closed models could be easily shut down if things go awry, Papernot said.

"You have a kill switch because you're controlling how people access the model. In an open-weight model, anyone can download it off the internet and so there's no way to enforce who is using the model," he said — or how.

WATCH | Canada launches AI watchdog: Canada launches AI watchdog to oversee the technology’s safe development and use | Duration 1:50 Amid rapid global advances and deployment of artificial intelligence technologies, the federal government has invested millions to combine the minds of three existing institutes into one that can keep an eye on potential dangers ahead.

Papernot and a team of researchers recently used an open-weight model powered with extra tools to show how the technology could be used to launch a sophisticated malware attack , capable of modifying its approach depending on the target and moving between devices.

But he says limiting access to open models isn't the solution. For one, bad actors likely have access to closed models that researchers don't even know about.

"Open-weight models are not the threat themselves," Papernot said. "Restricting access is going to lead to further concentration of power that is detrimental to society."

For all the talk of bad actors, Chris Pal, a professor at Polytechnique Montréal and a CIFAR AI Chair, says there are plenty of good ones, too.

And as more of these high-powered, open-weight models emerge, Pal says testing for vulnerabilities is a role that AI safety institutes would be well placed to take on.

"These are the kinds of things that those kinds of institutes could be involved with — auditing powerful open-source models for these security questions to see just what they're capable of and potentially giving guidance to the public about what they should be watching out for.”

World.title: Feds announce almost $2B in funding to modernize Via Rail's passenger fleet
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The federal government has announced almost $2 billion in funding to modernize Via Rail's passenger fleet with 45 new hybrid battery-diesel passenger locomotives.

Transport Minister Steven MacKinnon made the announcement in Montreal on Wednesday, highlighting that 36 of the 45 new locomotives built by Swiss rail manufacturer Stadler will be assembled in Canada.

"Today, for the first time in more than 25 years, we're bringing passenger rail locomotive assembly back to Montreal," MacKinnon said in a statement.

"By combining Canadian expertise with world-class European innovation, we're strengthening our economy while building a more resilient passenger rail network for the future."

The funding to renew Via Rail's aging fleet of locomotives was first announced in Budget 2024.

A government statement said $1.6 billion of the $1.95 billion the federal government is funnelling into the project will be used to pay for the construction of the new locomotives.

Another $357 million will allow VIA Rail to build a new assembly and maintenance facility in Montreal. This new facility will be built by Canadian construction company Pomerleau.

The Liberal government said their nearly $2-billion investment will "support the equivalent of 1,200 full-time jobs throughout the project, including skilled manufacturing, construction, engineering and long-term maintenance jobs."

A North American first

MacKinnon's department said in a statement that the trains will be "North America's first hybrid-powered passenger locomotives."

Transport Canada also said that these new lower-emission trains will lay "the groundwork for future zero-emission propulsion," but it does not put a timeline on when that will happen.

The batteries powering the trains will be supplied by ABB, a Swiss-Swedish multinational corporation with facilities across Canada. The Via Rail batteries in the new trains will be supplied by ABB's facility in Montreal's Saint-Laurent borough.

World.title: A human-made forest is at the centre of France's raging wildfires
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

For days after she and her partner were evacuated from their apartment in Lège-Cap-Ferret, Naomie Corsaint and her family tried to find out what happened to the house they'd lived in for a decade in nearby Le Porge, where a forest fire raged.

Photos and videos trickled in, mostly from firefighters already hard at work.

The 20-year-old didn't get to see the scale of the devastation until she was granted permission to visit the community on Sunday. When she arrived, she saw only the cinder walls of her mother's house were left.

"The town we used to know is gone," Corsaint told CBC on Tuesday.

"You can’t even get your bearings anymore; the houses we used to see when driving by — there’s nothing left. It’s all ash."

Corsaint and her family are among the more than 250,000 people evacuated from their homes in France as fires spread at an unprecedented rate near Bordeaux. In Spain, more than 116,000 people have had to leave their communities as fires continue to burn there, too.

Scientists say climate change is the primary driver behind the extraordinary fire conditions gripping western Europe, with a fourth heat wave of the season settling over the region this week.

But they also say the scale of the fires cannot be understood without looking at how humans transformed the landscape itself.

Château La Rochefoucauld is seen northwest of Bordeaux earlier this month in a photo taken by CBC reporter Anna Cunningham on the banks of a dried-up river. (Anna Cunningham/CBC)

Pine forest dates back to Napoleon III

The pine forest stretching southwest of Bordeaux has long been one of France's great engineering success stories.

In the mid-1800s, under Napoleon III, vast wetlands considered unhealthy and unproductive were drained and replaced with a pine forest. The new forest transformed the local economy, produced timber and resin and made the area habitable.

Nearly two centuries later, that same landscape is burning.

"This isn't a fire in a natural forest," said Raphaël Morera, an environmental historian at the French National Centre for Scientific Research, in an interview. "It’s a fire in a forest that was planted there to support an industrial activity."

Morera says natural forests tend to contain a greater diversity of tree species and more interruptions that can slow a fire's advance.

In the Landes, by contrast, "there are no natural obstacles to the fire's expansion," leaving firefighters to do almost all the work of stopping it.

PHOTOS | Scientists say the fires burning in France and Spain are unprecedented in scale:

While France's firefighters are among the best equipped in Europe, the fires themselves are changing faster than emergency services can adapt, says Guillermo Rein, a professor of fire science at Imperial College London.

What's more, European countries rely on each other for labour and equipment, but when fires rage in many countries at once, that becomes more difficult, especially with aging Canadair tanker fleets.

Soil no longer retaining moisture

Amid successive heat waves and months of unusually dry conditions, the landscape has lost much of the moisture that normally helps limit fire behaviour, according to Sylvain Delzon, a forest ecophysiologist at the University of Bordeaux and France's National Research Institute for Agriculture, Food and Environment.

"It's a sandy soil that doesn't retain water. So all the undergrowth was completely dried out and dead, becoming fuel for the fire."

In terms of scale and spread, the fires in France share some similarities with the 2016 Horse River Fire that prompted the evacuation of Fort McMurray in Alberta, said Stefan Doerr, a professor of wildfire science at Swansea University in Wales.

WATCH | Homes destroyed by fire: Drone video shows homes reduced to ashes, rubble by wildfire in southwestern France | Duration 0:51 A massive wildfire in southwestern France has left parts of the town of Biscarrosse in ruins, with drone footage from Tuesday revealing burnt homes and forest. Fires across France have forced the unprecedented evacuation of tens of thousands of people.

"In both cases the fire behaviour is quite extreme," Doerr said in a video interview, noting the fires in France have created their own weather system — a phenomenon that also occurred around Fort McMurray, with the fire creating its own high winds and lightning.

'All we could see was smoke'

This week, images of a gigantic black cloud above France spread online. The cloud, a pyrocumulonimbus, is composed of the moisture evaporated from burnt trees and vegetation, in addition to soot particles. It is formed by the energy and heat created by large forest fires pushing the air into the sky.

To Corsaint, whose family home in Le Porge burned, and her boyfriend, Mattéo Martins, 21, the results were "almost apocalyptic."

Before the couple had to leave their apartment in Lège-Cap-Ferret last week, they watched as the sky around them turned black.

"All we could see was smoke. Ash fell on the balcony," Corsaint said. "Then, at night, the sky was orange and red. You could hear planes, police sirens, everything except other people."

Sophie Wilkinson, a wildfire and peatland researcher at Simon Fraser University in British Columbia who studied the Alberta wildfire — where there were also drained wetlands — said climate change is exposing the legacy of earlier land-use decisions.

"The era of denialism and pushing climate change into the future as a future issue is really gone."

WATCH | Fires generating their own thunderstorms: Europe’s wildfires are creating their own weather systems | Duration 1:58 Wildfires in Europe have become so powerful they have created their own thunderstorm-generating weather systems. This has officials in France and Spain urging more be done to prevent the fires from starting.

Wilkinson, speaking in a phone interview Tuesday, said extreme heat, drought and wildfire are symptoms of human-caused climate change, adding that protecting and restoring ecosystems such as peatlands must also be part of the response.

Susan Page, professor of physical geography at the University of Leicester in England who has spent decades studying peatlands, echoed Wilkinson's comments.

"I think it's right that we now — rather than talking about climate change — talk about climate breakdown," Page said.

"That's what we're starting to see, because the fires that are happening in France and Spain are of a scale that we never imagined."

Naomie Corsaint says her mother and step-father have been crying every day over their lost home, which had also served as her mom's workplace.

In their town, roughly 150 others saw their houses burn down. Corsaint and Martins know it will take months to rebuild. And they worry that once the headlines die down, people will forget.

"None of it feels real," she said.

World.title: Security for Prince Harry's visits to Canada topped all internationally protected persons
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Canadian taxpayers spent more to protect Prince Harry over five years during his visits to Canada than any other internationally protected person over the same period, CBC News has learned.

According to a document obtained by CBC News under Canada's access to information law, the RCMP spent at least $539,575 to provide security between 2014/15 and 2019/20 when Prince Harry travelled to Canada for events like the Invictus Games and to date his future wife, Meghan Markle.

The document also reveals that his security costs were much higher than the $334,337 initially revealed by the RCMP in 2021.

The cost to protect Prince Harry and, later, his wife accounted for around 10 per cent of the over $5.2 million spent during that period to provide security to more than 100 internationally protected persons who visited Canada.

The two-page list also provides a rare glimpse into the secretive world of taxpayer-funded security for a select group of people who qualify as internationally protected persons. Among them are U.S. President Donald Trump's children, former U.S. presidents or their wives on book tours or six-figure speaking engagements, former U.K Prime Minister Tony Blair and members of various royal families.

A number of government officials from other countries are also on the list — from ambassadors for countries like the U.S. and Israel to the secretaries general of NATO or the United Nations or the heads of the CIA and Israel's intelligence service.

Donald Trump Jr. and Eric Trump attended the inauguration of a Trump hotel in Vancouver in February 2017. (Stephanie Lamy/AFP/Getty Images)

However, the list doesn't include expenses for other members of the Royal Family like Princess Anne or Prince Edward, who visited Canada during that period on what were described as "private working" visits.

Under international conventions, when individuals on the internationally protected person list visit Canada, the RCMP is tasked with assuring their security — regardless of whether the trip is official, for business or personal. The costs outlined in the document cover incremental expenses like travel and overtime but not the basic salaries of police officers — meaning the full cost is somewhat higher.

The list also doesn't appear to include security for international summits such as the G7 meeting in Charlevoix, Que., in 2018, which have separate budgets that include security costs.

The records, first requested in January 2020, were released to CBC News following an order earlier this year from Canada's Information Commissioner Caroline Maynard. That ruling came after the RCMP fought for years to avoid revealing the names of those who had received protection.

The force also refused repeatedly to answer questions from CBC News about the records that were ordered released, beyond general background about the program. It declined to confirm or deny whether a potential duplication in the list had artificially increased the costs associated with protecting Prince Harry and his wife.

RCMP fought for years to avoid revealing names

Simon Morgan is a former U.K. Metropolitan Police officer who has protected senior members of the Royal Family and founded the London-based Trojan Consultancy security firm.

Morgan said taxpayer-funded protection for internationally protected persons is part of an international system set up by the United Nations. Protection is generally associated with the role that someone occupies — and is something that even the wealthiest person in the world can't buy.

He said Canadian authorities may have seen the need for a "more robust" security process due to Prince Harry being a veteran of the Afghan war and a prominent member of the Royal Family.

"He was the Queen's grandson. He was the future King's son," Morgan said.

Prince Harry was also still a working member of the Royal Family during the period covered in the document, Morgan pointed out.

The costs associated with Prince Harry's security made headlines after he and his wife decided in January 2020 to step back from royal duties and his taxpayer-funded security ended. Prince Harry has challenged that decision made by the U.K. More recently, his eligibility has been assessed on a case-by-case basis.

The document released by the RCMP lists $105,955 in spending for Prince Harry's security in 2016/17 followed by $364,859 in 2017/18. That tapered off to $866 in 2018/19 and $904 in 2019/20. On a separate line, expenses of $56,405 for 2019/20 appear on the list under the "Duke and Duchess of Sussex."

A CBC News tally of the spending does not include another line item of $56,405 for the same year under "The Duke and Duchess of Sussex" which appears to be a duplicate — even though it is included in the RCMP's total spending of $5.2 million.

According to the Court Circular, which outlines public activities of members of the Royal Family, Prince Harry had one public visit to Canada during 2017 and 2018 — a weeklong trip to attend events in Toronto. The events included the Invictus Games — which Harry founded — a WE Day celebration and a reception for young people who received Duke of Edinburgh gold awards.

In July 2016 Prince Harry met Markle, who had a role in the television drama Suits that was filming in Toronto. Around that period, the pair were occasionally spotted by paparazzi in Toronto. They were engaged in November 2017 and married in 2018.

The list also includes RCMP expenses of $10,586 for the Duchess of Sussex in 2018/19. News reports in August 2018 revealed that she jetted to Toronto to spend three days with her friend Jessica Mulroney.

The costs to protect Prince Harry during visits to Canada between 2014/15 and 2019/20 far exceed the $178,584 to protect his father, then Prince Charles, in 2017/18. Charles and his wife visited Nunavut, Ontario and the Ottawa region in 2017.

The document also provides glimpses into other visits to Canada by people on the internationally protected persons list — not all of them widely publicized.

For example, the list includes security costs of $63,586 for U.S. President Donald Trump's daughter Ivanka in 2017/18 and another $1,920 in 2019/20.

News reporting after the fact revealed that Ivanka Trump and her husband Jared Kushner spent a weekend at the Whistler, B.C., ski resort in April 2017. NBC News revealed that the Secret Service spent $66,538 US on agents, hotel rooms and ski passes for the visit.

The RCMP list includes a line entitled "President Trump & Family" with $51,558 in costs incurred in 2016/17, another $13,078 in 2017/18 and $1,769 in 2018/19. While the U.S. president does not appear to have made a trip to Canada during that time period with the exception of the 2018 G7 meeting, his sons Eric and Donald Trump Jr. attended the opening of a Trump hotel in Vancouver in February 2017.

In September 2017, U.S. First Lady Melania Trump attended the Invictus Games in Toronto. The RCMP lists a cost of $42,602 to protect her in 2017/18. There is also another expense of $1,382 for the following year.

Many of the people on the list, like U.S. presidents and their wives or U.K. prime ministers, continue to receive taxpayer-funded RCMP protection during visits to Canada long after they leave office.

The record reveals that the RCMP spent $497,544 during that period on security for former U.S. presidents and their spouses, a number of whom have come to Canada on speaking or book tours.

Security for Barack and Michelle Obama cost the most at $295,411 followed by Bill and Hillary Clinton at $143,927. Security for Laura Bush, who spoke at a 2018 Rotary International Convention in Toronto cost $6,852 while the RCMP reported costs of $1,026 for a trip by former president George Bush in 2019/20.

Security for Jimmy Carter cost $50,328 in 2017/18. Carter travelled to Winnipeg in July 2017 to work on a Habitat for Humanity job site and was also hospitalized for dehydration.

Former U.S. president Bill Clinton waves as he and his wife, former U.S. presidential candidate Hillary Clinton, walk on stage during an event in Vancouver in 2019. (Darryl Dyck/The Canadian Press)

It is not known how much the Obamas and the Clintons were paid for speaking appearances or book tours. Their offices did not respond to questions from CBC News.

However, Hillary Clinton's filing to the U.S. Office of Government Ethics prior to her run for president provides a glimpse into the kinds of speaking fees she receives.

The filings reveal that between March 2014 and January 2015, Clinton received $1.97 million in honorariums for nine appearances in Canada. The fees ranged from $100,000 for an appearance in Edmonton in June 2014 to $275,500 each for a March 2014 talk to the Vancouver Board of Trade and an October 2014 appearance at an Ottawa event organized by Canada 2020.

The RCMP doesn't list any costs for her security during that period.

One of the few on the list who isn't a public servant, held public office or been married to a public office holder is Malala Yousafzai, who won a Nobel Peace Prize after she was shot by a Taliban gunman in 2012. Yousafzai's trip to Canada in April 2017 to receive honorary Canadian citizenship and address Parliament cost the RCMP $5,639.

While Prince Harry topped the list for security costs, U.S. ambassadors Bruce Heyman and Kelly Craft during that period were second at $487,654, followed by the $446,333 spent on security for U.S. vice-presidents such as Joe Biden and Mike Pence.

Security for Israel's ambassadors to Canada cost $377,897 while a trip by Italy's President Sergio Mattarella in 2017 cost $215,305.

The list reveals that the RCMP also provided protection for several security and intelligence officials, including the director of the CIA, the director of the FBI, the directors of Israel and Turkey's intelligence services, the director of the NSA, the U.S. director of national intelligence and Italy's national prosecutor of anti-Mafia and counterterrorism.

Phil Gurski, a former CSIS analyst and president of Borealis Threat and Risk Consulting, said taxpayer-funded security should be based on intelligence and the assessment of the risk.

"If there's any indication that a person may be subject to some kind of act of violence, you should act on that intelligence to ensure they have the protection that they require," said Gurski, pointing out that Canada wouldn't want a visiting official to be attacked on Canadian soil.

However, Gurski also suggested people on the list who come to Canada for profit should contribute to the cost of their security.

"Why are [we] paying for the privilege of them coming here to make money from Canadians?" he said.

World.title: Marmots on OnlyFans: Researchers turn to the internet for funding
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Funding has always been a challenge for Daniel Blumstein's long-term study of yellow-bellied marmots, more so, he tells CBC News, since the Trump administration started defunding some environmental research.

So when he watched the Apple TV comedy Margo's Got Money Troubles, Blumstein could relate and was inspired by the protagonist's decision to turn to digital sex work to avoid financial ruin.

"What about OnlyFans?" he recalled asking, thinking of all the "hysterical" videos his lab has of the loaf-like rodents. "Why don't we share them ... and maybe people will give us tips?"

One of his graduate students at the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory in Colorado was on board with the idea, and pretty soon created an OnlyFans account called "OnlyMarms."

OnlyFans is a subscription-based platform best known for sexually explicit videos and images. But Blumstein is clear: OnlyMarms is a G-rated project.

"We're not trying to sexualize marmots. Although I was just at an international conference and three people came up to me and said, 'Oh, you have to have more pictures of Marmot feet,'" he said.

"Apparently people like to look at the feet of animals."

A screenshot from the OnlyMarms page on OnlyFans, which has been soliciting tips from the public since June. (OnlyFans)

Every Monday and Friday since June, his team posts new and often funny images of an individual marmot, and its bio.

Marmots hibernate, and need to pack on body mass before winter. So naturally, the team of researchers are doing a "Fat Marmot Week" — encouraging the public to vote in a bracket-style tournament similar to the "Fat Bear Week" at Alaska's Katmai National Park and Preserve.

Fat Marmot Week is slated to begin Aug. 24 and might feature a collaboration with some Canadian critters from the conservationist group Vancouver Island Marmots.

Body positivity

Blumstein's lab specifically studies yellow-bellied marmots, including how they age and respond to climate change.

Running since 1962, it is the second-longest study of individually identifiable wild mammals, after Jane Goodall's study of chimpanzees.

When mammals are studied over many generations like that, Blumstein says it can provide valuable insights about aging and epigenetics — how environmental factors affect the way certain genes work.

"Hibernators live longer than would be expected based on their body size, " he said. "It maybe is because they're slowing their epigenetic aging. And we've been getting genomic and looking at those questions. "

Daniel Blumstein is a professor in the Department of Ecology and Evolutionary Biology at the University of California, Los Angeles, and co-director of the long-term yellow-bellied marmots study, conducted at the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory. (CBC)

There are also physiologists who study marmots to learn how you can get obese and not be sick.

"We're all about body positivity here with our marmots, because doubling or tripling their weight is what they need to do to survive," Blumstein said.

Blumstein says the kind of research his lab does has long been undervalued, and that his funding applications were repeatedly rejected, even before the Trump administration's cuts.

The National Park Service, which lost millions in funding, has similarly been getting a lot of attention thanks to dozens of cheeky "OnlyParks" postings on TikTok.

WATCH | Chunk wins Fat Bear Week: #TheMoment Chunk was crowned Fat Bear Week champion | Duration 1:16 Naomi Boak, a media ranger for Katmai Conservancy, tells CBC News about the moment Chunk was named Fat Bear Week champion, an annual tournament in Katmai National Park, Alaska, celebrating brown bears' success in preparation for winter hibernation.

When it comes to funding, "the pie's too small," Blumstein said. But through a series of collaborators and outside grants, he has managed to keep his marmot study going.

Since June, he says OnlyMarms has raised about $3,000 US, barely enough to make a dent in his funding needs.

"Will this pay for bait? Yes. Will this pay for fixing our bicycles — because we blow through bicycles working out here? Yes. Will this help pay for lab fees and things like that? Absolutely," but Blumstein says he still needs an additional $75,000 for a new graduate student each year.

And OnlyFans is an imperfect funding model. For starters, it takes a 20 per cent commission, and as the account holder, Blumstein is expected to declare that money on his taxes.

What he really wants marmot-lovers to do is donate to UCLA directly to help keep this project alive.

World.title: Copper wire theft up by 78% over last year, Bell says
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Bell says it has seen a surge in copper wire thefts across its telecommunications infrastructure in 2026, which can disrupt phone and internet services.

The telecommunications company says it has recorded 993 incidents of copper theft and vandalism between January and June — a 78 per cent increase compared to the same time frame last year.

The bulk of the thefts took place in Ontario and New Brunswick according to Bell, with thefts in those provinces accounting for about 85 per cent of the increased thefts.

Hamilton, Niagara and Milton had the most thefts in Ontario. But in New Brunswick, Bell says the problem was growing fastest, with a 235 per cent increase in thefts from 2025.

Thieves target copper because they can resell the recycled metal for a good price. The metal has become more valuable as the world becomes more electrified — the buildout of data centres and making of electric cars for example have helped up demand.

A worker walks among copper coils at the Nexans copper production facility, April 12, 2024, in Montreal. (Ryan Remiorz/The Canadian Press)

They're also able to get their hands on a lot of it because its so widely used, according to a Bell executive, making it easier for thieves to make some cash .

But Bell says the value of the metal is " minimal compared to the harm caused."

Wire thefts can cause service outages which disrupt phone, internet and TV service. That means access to emergency services could be cut off, posing a potential public safety risk.

" No single organization can stop copper theft alone," said executive vice president and chief technology officer at Bell, Mark McDonald.

"It will take co-ordinated action from telecommunications providers, governments, law enforcement, recyclers and communities to hold criminals accountable and protect the networks Canadians depend on."

Bell says it has taken action to prevent thefts, including rigging alarm systems connected to law enforcement, increasing surveillance on the ground and taking legal action against alleged thieves. The company is also in the process of transitioning from copper wire to fibre-optic cables.

Arrests have risen by 32 per cent in the first half of the year as well, according to Bell, which it says reflects "ongoing enforcement efforts."
