The exchange comes ten days before the handover of power to president-elect Abelardo de la Espriella.

Rodríguez, once one of the president's closest officials, said he began to distrust her during her tenure at DAPRE and pressured her to resign. She said he accused her of being allied with paramilitary sectors and of other offenses, and said she interpreted as threats certain remarks about the president's past in the guerrilla movement. “I think he is my greatest victimizer,” she said, adding that she fears for her safety. None of those claims has any judicial backing.

The president rejected the accusations and made his own. He said he removed her from DAPRE over what he described as “a subordinate relationship to political sectors that are heirs to paramilitarism,” and attributed her recent dismissal to “her disloyalty to the government program and the use of public office for private ends.” He said he had kept her at the Adaptation Fund despite having lost confidence in her. Those allegations have likewise not been brought before the courts.

Rodríguez also repeated corruption allegations she had made over the weekend. She said she had blocked a maneuver to divert more than 1.2 trillion pesos, some $380 million, from the Adaptation Fund to the National Disaster Risk Management Unit. She argued those funds should go to flood-control works in the La Mojana region, scheduled through 2029, rather than to the response to the El Niño phenomenon. The accusation has not been independently corroborated.

The president had said on Monday that the official is on medical leave for psychiatric reasons. Rodríguez responded that she is experiencing depression and anxiety stemming from the situations she faced in government, called those remarks “unfortunate and stigmatizing,” and said her diagnosis does not affect her professional capacity. Petro said the decision to remove her is unrelated to that diagnosis.

The official requested protection from the incoming government. De la Espriella said on social media that he had instructed his future interior minister, Rodrigo Lara, and the designated head of the National Protection Unit to guarantee her security. Lara later said he gives “very high credibility” to the allegations given how close the official had been to the outgoing president. Rodríguez was the fifth of six directors to pass through DAPRE during this administration.

World.title: “Who is that guy?”: Lula's response to Milei's remarks in São Paulo
World.content:
“Who is that guy?”: Lula's response to Milei's remarks in São Paulo

28th Tuesday, July 2026 - 10:55 UTC Full article

The remarks led to the sharpest diplomatic response between the two countries in years

Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva addressed for the first time the remarks made against him by Argentine President Javier Milei, with a brief and ironic response that avoided escalating the controversy. Asked by reporters while preparing to receive South Korean President Lee Jae-myung, he replied: “Who is that guy?”

The reaction contrasts with that of the rest of the Brazilian government, which took a firmer stance. Foreign Minister Mauro Vieira described the Argentine president's remarks as “serious and unacceptable” and said they “constituted interference in internal affairs, in national affairs.” Speaking to TV Globo, he nonetheless defended the diplomatic route: “We must work to achieve understanding between nations, and diplomacy is based on that, on dialogue,” he said.

Finance Minister Dario Durigan questioned the Argentine leader's economic argument and compared the two countries' situations. In a radio interview, he said Milei had spoken about Brazil's situation despite Argentina posting a higher country risk, a larger public debt, and higher inflation. “One cannot fall for the narrative of those who claim the situation will become apocalyptic,” he said.

The episode began on Saturday, when Milei took part in São Paulo in the event formalizing Senator Flávio Bolsonaro's presidential candidacy for the October 4 elections. In a speech of about 25 minutes, the Argentine president avoided naming Lula and referred to him with terms such as “thief” and “convict,” while also using crude language about the region's left-wing governments. He argued that Brazil could face an adverse economic scenario if it does not change its political course.

The remarks led to the sharpest diplomatic response between the two countries in years. On Sunday, the Brazilian government recalled its ambassador in Buenos Aires, Julio Bitelli, whose return has no set date, and summoned Argentina's ambassador in Brasília, Daniel Raimondi, for explanations at Itamaraty. The president of the Supreme Federal Court, Luiz Edson Fachin, also issued an institutional note after Milei disparaged one of the court's justices.

In Argentina, a group of lawmakers filed a motion of censure over the remarks in the Chamber of Deputies. Argentina's foreign ministry had not issued an official response to the Brazilian statements as of this writing. Brazil and Argentina are Mercosur's two largest members and each other's main trading partners.

World.title: Fujimori's inauguration brings Southern Cone and Andean presidents together in Lima
World.content:
Fujimori's inauguration brings Southern Cone and Andean presidents together in Lima

28th Tuesday, July 2026 - 10:30 UTC Full article

Fujimori will become the first woman to reach Peru's presidency through the ballot box

The presidents of Bolivia, Paraguay, Chile, and Honduras arrived in Lima on Monday to attend the handover ceremony at which Keiko Fujimori will assume Peru's presidency for the 2026-2031 term. The leaders of Argentina, Javier Milei; Uruguay, Yamandú Orsi; Panama, José Raúl Mulino; and Ecuador, Daniel Noboa, are also expected to take part.

Interim President José María Balcázar hosted an official dinner for the delegations on Monday night at the Government Palace in the capital's historic center, and on Tuesday will hand the presidential sash to Fujimori on the anniversary of Peru's independence.

Several delegations arrived with defined bilateral agendas. Bolivia's Rodrigo Paz, on his first visit to the neighboring country, will hold a meeting with Fujimori with the stated aim of “restoring diplomatic dialogue between the two countries,” according to Foreign Minister Fernando Aramayo. La Paz's priorities include setting up a binational cabinet in the short term and advancing the use of the Peruvian port of Ilo, which for landlocked Bolivia holds “commercial, tourism and energy” significance.

Chile's José Antonio Kast had already held a video call with the president-elect on July 10, in which they discussed migration and coordination against transnational organized crime. The two also agreed on the need to revitalize the Pacific Alliance, a bloc in which both countries are full members and which they see as a key mechanism for commercial projection toward Asia-Pacific markets.

Paraguay's Santiago Peña, who arrived with his wife, has bilateral and business meetings scheduled, while Honduras's Nasry Asfura will meet with business leaders and officials to promote cooperation opportunities, according to their respective governments.

Fujimori will become the first woman to reach Peru's presidency through the ballot box, after winning by a narrow margin of 49,641 votes over left-wing candidate Roberto Sánchez in the June 7 runoff. She takes office on her fourth attempt, following three consecutive runoff defeats.

The incoming president assumes office facing two main challenges: citizen security, the population's foremost concern, and political stability in a country where no president has completed a five-year term over the past decade. Her electoral rival turned to the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights alleging irregularities, a request the National Elections Board dismissed before proclaiming the results.

World.title: Trump asks the Supreme Court to allow his mail-voting restrictions before the midterms
World.content:
Trump asks the Supreme Court to allow his mail-voting restrictions before the midterms

27th Monday, July 2026 - 22:26 UTC Full article

Trump has repeatedly maintained that mail-in voting facilitates electoral fraud

The US government on Monday filed an emergency request with the Supreme Court seeking authorization to implement President Donald Trump's executive order restricting mail-in voting, which lower courts have blocked. The request comes 99 days before November's midterm elections, which will determine control of Congress.

The filing followed by two days a decision by the First Circuit Court of Appeals, based in Boston, which refused by a two-to-one vote to stay the injunction issued on June 25 by a district judge. That ruling keeps the order blocked in twenty-three Democratic-led states and the District of Columbia, which sued the administration.

The order, signed in March, tasks the director of Citizenship and Immigration Services and the commissioner of the Social Security Administration with drawing up a list of eligible voters, and bars the Postal Service from sending ballots to anyone not on it. The plaintiff states argue that the Constitution reserves the conduct of elections to the states and Congress, not the executive branch, an argument accepted in the earlier rulings.

In its filing before the high court, the administration framed the order as “general policy guidance” and stressed that the Postal Service has not finalized any regulations. The appeals judges had noted, by contrast, that the measure sets rapidly approaching deadlines requiring states to reorganize their procedures immediately, while also ensuring that officials and the public understand the rules governing the September and November votes. A White House spokesperson said the lower courts' decision “is not the final say” and that the administration expects a favorable outcome.

Trump has repeatedly maintained that mail-in voting facilitates electoral fraud. Election officials, courts, and federal agencies concluded that there was no evidence of widespread fraud in the 2020 elections, when that method saw unprecedented use during the pandemic, and noted that the system includes multiple verification and audit mechanisms.

The initiative is part of a broader set of government actions on electoral matters. The administration is pressing Congress to pass the SAVE America Act, which would require documentary proof of citizenship to register on the federal roll and remains stalled in the Senate, and has sued twenty-nine states to obtain copies of their voter registries, which include dates of birth, driver's license numbers, and portions of social security numbers. Courts have blocked access in three states and have yet to rule in the rest.

World.title: At the Central American and Caribbean Games, powerhouse Mexico builds for the 2028 Olympics
World.content:
Mexico is off to a commanding start at the 2026 Central American and Caribbean Games in the Dominican Republic, reinforcing its status as the region’s powerhouse as the century‑old competition enters its second week.

The Games opened Friday with a music‑ and fireworks-filled ceremony at Félix Sánchez Olympic Stadium in the nation’s capital, Santo Domingo.

Las grandes celebraciones deportivas también son una oportunidad para unir a todo un país. Así vivimos la inauguración de los XXV Juegos Centroamericanos y del Caribe Santo Domingo 2026, una edición histórica que marca el centenario de esta competencia y reúne a los mejores… pic.twitter.com/qbT12Gdozl — Barrick Pueblo Viejo (@BarrickRD) July 28, 2026

They are the oldest regional multiple-sports competition in the world recognized by the International Olympic Committee.

Running through Aug. 8, this year’s edition marks the centennial of the Games, first held in Mexico City in 1926. More than 6,000 athletes from 37 countries and territories are competing in 40 sports.

Mexico is the only nation to have appeared in all 25 editions and is the two-time defending champion, with 13 championships overall.

At the 2018 Games in Barranquilla, Colombia, Mexico won 132 golds among 341 total medals, then raised the bar in 2023 in San Salvador, El Salvador, with 145 golds and 353 medals overall.

Mexico’s best haul all-time was winning 375 medals in the 2010 Games in Mayagüez, Puerto Rico.

So far in 2026, the Mexican team is delivering again, surging up to 106 total medals as the competition moved through day 5 on Tuesday — a haul that includes 38 gold medals with 11 days still to go.

Mexico sits atop the overall table, more than 40 medals ahead of Colombia with 63 and Cuba with 38. The Dominican Republic and Venezuela rank fourth and fifth, respectively.

Mexico’s lead has been built on familiar strengths, such as the taekwondo team registering 14 podium finishes, including gold medals for Daniela Souza and Iker Casas.

In skeet shooting, flag bearer Gabriela Rodríguez — the silver medalist at the 2025 ISSF Shotgun World Championships — delivered as expected, taking the women’s crown, while teammate Luis Gallardo won the men’s event.

Open water swimmer Paulo Strehlke won gold in the 10‑kilometer race, part of a four‑medal haul for Mexico’s open water swimmers over the weekend.

Rowers Melissa Márquez and Aylin Ibarra each won three gold medals, with other gold medals coming in badminton and rhythmic gymnastics.

Other sports being contested include basketball, figure skating, soccer, baseball, cycling and diving, along with netball, basque pelota (similar to racquetball and jai alai), billiards, chess and esports — high‑level video‑game competitions making their debut at these Games.

Mexico sees its performances in Olympic‑core sports in Santo Domingo as a stepping stone toward the Los Angeles Summer Games in 2028.

It has sent over 600 athletes and its A teams in several sports, notably diving, open water swimming, cycling and taekwondo. Last week, a ceremony for the Mexican delegation was led by President Claudia Sheinbaum.

The next major test will be the Pan American Games in Lima, Peru, scheduled for July 23 to Aug. 8, 2027.

With reports from La Jornada, AP, Olympics.com and El Economista

World.title: Mexico eyes tariff retaliation to level playing field for tequila exports
World.content:
Mexico will introduce stricter trade tariff measures for imported alcohols to encourage other countries to reduce tariffs on Mexican tequila, Mexico’s Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard announced during National Tequila Day celebrations on Friday.

National Tequila Day, celebrated annually on July 24, recognizes the world-famous spirit for its economic and cultural value. Tequila production is a source of employment for thousands of families dedicated to agave cultivation and distillation.

Reconocimiento a la industria del Tequila y plan de acción conjunto para aumentar exportaciones a todo el mundo. pic.twitter.com/R06kE34c6N — Marcelo Ebrard C. (@m_ebrard) July 28, 2026

In a presentation, Ebrard emphasized the need to review and dismantle all trade restrictions facing tequila exports to achieve more balanced treatment for Mexican products. “If another country applies 150 tariffs on me, I will say, ‘Hey, I’m going to impose restrictions on your products too,’” explained Ebrard. “It’s going to have to be more balanced.”

The economy minister said that while Mexico is one of the most open countries to international trade, some markets continue to impose tariffs of up to 150% or regulatory restrictions on tequila imports. Meanwhile, Mexico imposes few restrictions on the import of similar products from other countries.

In 2024, tequila exports achieved a value of almost US $4.2 billion, solidifying the product’s position as Mexico’s second most important agro-industrial export, behind beer, according to Agriculture Ministry (Sader) data. Mexican tequila is exported to over 120 countries, with annual exports exceeding 400 million liters.

It was the only spirit to register growth during the past year, with an increase of 1.2%. Global tequila volumes increased at a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 7% between 2019 and 2025, and are expected to expand at a CAGR of 2% to 2030, according to the global beverage data company IWSR.

Tequila was granted Denomination of Origin (DO) status in 1974, for its historical connection to specific Mexican regions and traditional production practices, making it the first Mexican product to gain this certification.

The Director General of the Mexican Institute of Industrial Property (IMPI), Vidal Llerenas Morales, said that the status guarantees that only tequila produced in the states of Jalisco, Nayarit, Guanajuato, Michoacán and Tamaulipas can legally use this designation, which helps preserve the alcohol’s traditional characteristics and quality.

Other Mexican alcohols have since been granted DO certification, including mezcal, bacanora, sotol, charanda and raicilla.

With reports from El Financiero and El Informador

World.title: Opinion: Beyond better buses. A transportation vision for San Miguel de Allende
World.content:
When Mexico News Daily recently asked how San Miguel de Allende can remain the “Best City in the World,” one recommendation stood out: improve the buses. That is an excellent, perhaps obvious, place to start — but it should not be the city’s only transportation priority. San Miguel’s larger challenge is deciding what kind of city it wants to become over the next decade and beyond, as well as what kind of transportation system will support that vision.

Transportation decisions shape far more than how quickly people travel. They affect air quality, noise, safety, neighborhood vitality, economic opportunity, public health and the simple pleasure of walking the streets. The most successful historic cities understand that transportation is not primarily about moving vehicles. It is about helping people reach the places they need or want to go to, while preserving the qualities that make a city worth living in and visiting.

San Miguel has already achieved something extraordinary. Residents and visitors enjoy walking its streets, lingering in its plazas, gathering in cafés and experiencing a vibrant public life. As the city grows, transportation investments should strengthen those qualities — not gradually erode them. That requires a different way of thinking. The question should not simply be, “How do we move more cars or buses?” It should be, “How do we help more people reach more places more easily, while making the city quieter, healthier, safer and more enjoyable?”

The city’s buses remain the backbone of mobility for thousands of residents and handfuls of visitors, connecting neighborhoods with schools, workplaces, markets, hospitals, churches and Centro. But today’s network reflects decades of incremental change rather than deliberate planning. Neighborhoods have expanded, employment centers have shifted and travel patterns have evolved. Tourists have grown in number and diversified in the variety of places they want to visit. Route redesign should begin with understanding how San Miguelenses, expatriates and visitors actually travel today. Rider surveys, passenger counts, GPS data, employer input and travel analysis could identify where people are going, when they travel and where the current system fails them. Bus service should reflect current travel patterns while avoiding unintended consequences — such as increased noise, congestion or safety concerns — that could diminish quality of life on particular streets or in specific neighborhoods.

The city should also consider whether a system focused primarily on Centro still reflects current demand. Direct cross-town routes connecting residential neighborhoods with employment centers, hospitals, schools and shopping areas could shorten trips without necessarily adding more buses. Frequent service on key corridors, coordinated transfers and reliable schedules may serve riders better than infrequent service spread across too many streets.

But better bus routes are not enough; the experience of using transit must also improve. Replacing aging diesel buses with quieter, cleaner electric or low-emission vehicles would reduce noise, improve air quality and make transit more attractive to everyone — not only residents who depend upon it, but also expatriates and visitors who often choose to drive because the system seems unfamiliar, unattractive or unsafe.

Making transit easy to understand is equally important. Clear route branding, well-designed stops, digital maps, QR codes, real-time arrival information and integration with Google Maps can transform uncertainty into confidence. The goal should be simple: riding a bus should feel as intuitive as taking a taxi.

As transit improves, the city has an opportunity to rethink its streets. Historic cities around the world have adopted Complete Streets — streets designed to accommodate pedestrians, transit riders, people with disabilities, deliveries and automobiles rather than prioritizing cars alone. Wider sidewalks, safer crossings, accessible design, better bus stops and carefully managed loading areas can allow transportation and public life to reinforce one another. Cities such as Copenhagen, Curitiba, Pontevedra and San Antonio have shown that giving more space to people can support local businesses, improve safety, reduce pollution and create more vibrant public places.

San Miguel already has examples of its own. Calle San Francisco near the Jardín illustrates how reducing automobile traffic can transform a street from a transportation corridor into a destination. As public transportation improves, the city should identify additional streets where pedestrian activity already exceeds automobile demand. This should lead to identifying opportunities to expand pedestrian-priority corridors while maintaining access for residents, deliveries and emergency services.

Parking should also be part of the discussion. Building more parking rarely solves congestion and often encourages more driving. A better strategy would be to develop mobility hubs at strategic locations outside the most constrained parts of the city. These facilities could combine parking with frequent transit, bicycle parking, taxi services, visitor information and public restrooms. Commuters into and visitors to the city could leave their cars once and continue their journey without adding traffic to the historic center.

Over time, the hubs might also connect with low-speed, electric, autonomous circulators. Pilot programs around the world are testing autonomous shuttles that connect transit stops, pedestrian districts, shopping areas and major destinations. They would not replace buses, but they could eventually provide another option for reducing automobile dependence while preserving San Miguel’s pedestrian character.

None of these ideas requires overnight implementation. The city could begin with demonstration projects: one redesigned bus corridor, a small fleet of cleaner vehicles, improved passenger information, a mobility hub, a temporary pedestrian-priority street or others. Pilot projects allow residents, visitors, businesses, existing transportation providers and public officials to see what works, identify unintended consequences and make adjustments before committing to larger investments.

How can progress — and ultimately success — be measured? Traditionally, this begins with a baseline needs assessment, followed by continuous monitoring as initiatives are implemented. Success can then be evaluated by whether workers can reach jobs more easily, children can travel to school more safely, neighborhoods become quieter and more livable, businesses become more vibrant and more people choose to walk, use public transit or spend time in the city’s public spaces.

San Miguel’s transportation decisions over the next decade will determine whether it becomes more congested — or more livable. Cleaner buses, smarter routes, Complete Streets, expanded pedestrian districts and mobility hubs are not separate projects. They are pieces of a single vision for preserving what makes San Miguel extraordinary. The world’s most admired historic cities are not remembered because they accommodated the most automobiles. They are remembered because they created places where people want to live, work, visit, and resettle.

San Miguel is already one of those cities. Now it has the opportunity to build a transportation system worthy of that distinction.

Johanna Zmud and her husband, Carlos, owned a transportation research consultancy in the U.S. They now live in San Miguel de Allende, where they own and manage a boutique hotel. Johanna continues transportation consulting.

World.title: Mexico gets favorable ruling in Vulcan trade accord violation case — but it’s far from over
World.content:
The International Centre for Settlement of Investment Disputes (ICSID) — an arm of the World Bank — issued a mixed ruling in the arbitration process initiated against Mexico by U.S.-based Vulcan Materials Company.

In what is being framed as a favorable ruling for Mexico, the ICSID dismissed almost all of the company’s claims, except for one measure related to the expropriation of a property operated by a Vulcan subsidiary.

In that regard, the ICSID ruled that Mexico violated the North American Free Trade Agreement, which was still in effect when the complaint was filed in 2018, by shutting down quarrying operations managed by Calica, a Vulcan subsidiary.

Although Vulcan sought US $1.53 billion in damages plus interest and costs, the tribunal awarded the company only negligible monetary damages.

The final decision remains confidential until officially released. Vulcan said it will discuss the ruling during its Q2 earnings call on Wednesday.

Mexico’s Economy Ministry (SE) said the government is “carefully analyzing the ICSID decision to determine what legal actions are available.”

The government had been negotiating with Vulcan to permanently end limestone extraction in what is now a protected natural area in the state of Quintana Roo. Earlier this month, President Claudia Sheinbaum said any agreement would require the company to relocate operations to an environmentally viable site and fund environmental remediation of the affected zone.

In a statement, the SE said that Mexico “reaffirms its commitment to foreign investment that brings innovation, good wages and environmental protection, as well as to respecting the rules and procedures contained in international treaties as a fundamental element to provide the legal certainty that makes economic development possible.”

Vulcan, a producer of ready-mixed concrete and asphalt, filed the complaint with the tribunal in 2018, accusing Mexico of violating NAFTA by repudiating an agreement to unlock a portion of Vulcan’s aggregates reserves and arbitrarily shutting down its quarrying operations in the state of Quintana Roo.

Mexican environmental authorities closed parts of Calica’s limestone operations in Quintana Roo in 2018. The government canceled deepwater port access and shipping privileges even though Vulcan’s concession over the property is valid until 2037.

Operations were completely shuttered in May 2022 (the government claimed underwater limestone extraction was causing environmental damage) and Navy personnel seized the company’s port in March 2023.

In September 2024, the government designated 53,000 hectares between Playa del Carmen and Tulum, encompassing the port and limestone operations, a protected natural area.

With reports from El Economista, Reforma, Aristegui Noticias and Mexico Business News

World.title: CFE: Power outages reduced by nearly 40% since 2024
World.content:
The Federal Electricity Commission (CFE) reported that power outages fell 39% during the first half of 2026 compared to the same period in 2024, attributed to a “historic investment” in the expansion and modernization of the country’s transmission and distribution networks.

Speaking at the Industrial Exhibition of the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE), Mexico section, head of CFE Emilia Calleja said that system restoration times were also “significantly reduced,” typically resolved within one to three hours.

Calleja noted that improvements in electricity coverage respond to CFE’s updated strategy to enhance and modernize distribution network capacity, as attention had long been focused primarily on generation.

The head of CFE explained that “modern, robust and intelligent grids” allow for the integration of new energy sources, remote operation, anticipation of failures and, above all, a better response to natural disasters.

The latter has a direct precedent in the aftermath of Hurricane Otis, which in October 2023 devastated much of Guerrero’s electrical infrastructure, leaving more than 500,000 customers without power. It took the CFE a record time of seven days to restore service in that region.

“This experience showed us the importance of having a resilient infrastructure, qualified and well-trained personnel, and above all, technology that allows us to respond quickly,” Calleja said.

For this purpose, between 2024 and 2030, CFE is implementing a program exceeding 244 billion pesos, including 15 billion pesos (US $859 million) in 2025-2026 alone, to strengthen distribution with new poles, meters and conductors.

The move is enhanced by the renewable energy plan recently presented by Energy Minister Luz Elena González. In June, González explained that the government aims to add 32,475 megawatts of generation capacity to the national electricity system by 2030, of which approximately 22,376 megawatts — roughly 70% — will come from renewable sources.

Speaking at Sheinbaum’s mañanera, Calleja also highlighted the emblematic project of the Rafael Galván Maldonado Solar Park in Puerto Peñasco, Sonora, which upon completion of its four stages will reach 1,000 megawatts, becoming the largest solar installation in the Americas.

With reports from La Jornada and El Heraldo de México

World.title: Spain’s Repsol is selling half its Gulf oil project to Talos Energy, a US company
World.content:
Spanish oil company Repsol has agreed to sell half of its Block 29 oil and gas development project in the Gulf of Mexico to Talos Energy.

Repsol will bring the U.S. company into its project by selling it a 50% stake in exchange for two payments totaling more than US $50 million.

The transaction is subject to approval by Mexico’s Energy Ministry and the National Antitrust Commission.

Headquartered in Houston, Texas, Talos is acquiring a working interest in Block 29, located in the Salinas-Sureste Basin approximately 88 kilometers offshore of the state of Tabasco. This 3,254 square-kilometer area in the southern Gulf of Mexico has seen more than a dozen deepwater discoveries.

Block 29 contains the Polok and Chinwol oil discoveries, which together are estimated to contain more than 200 million barrels of oil equivalent in gross recoverable resources, along with multiple additional exploration prospects.

The block features a floating production, storage- and offloading-based development concept anchored by existing oil discoveries described by Energy-pedia news as “well-positioned to serve as a hub for future developments and nearby discoveries.”

The two payments offered by Talos are a contingent payment of US $30 million at the time of the final investment decision (FID) and a cash stake of up to US $20 million in the next exploration well. Talos will also be asked for the reimbursement of “certain pre-closing costs.”

Upon closing, Talos will hold a 50% working interest and, together with Repsol, will be the sole participants in the block. The partners expect to reach a FID early next year.

Repsol acquired 100% of the rights to Block 29 in 2025, assuming full operational and strategic responsibility for the asset, after Petronas (Malaysia’s national oil and gas corporation) and Harbour (the largest London-listed independent oil and gas company) relinquished their stakes.

In a statement, Talos Chairman and CEO Paul Goodfellow expressed confidence in working alongside Repsol as progress is made on Block 29.

“This stake adds a high-quality, large-scale development opportunity and significant exploration potential in a proven deepwater basin, further boosting the third pillar of our strategy and strengthening our long-term growth portfolio,” he said.

Talos said the “discoveries and identified prospects target amplitude-supported Miocene reservoirs analogous to fields [the company] has successfully developed and produced in the Gulf of America [sic].” The investment reinforces Talos’ “strategic focus on opportunities where its deepwater subsurface expertise provides a competitive advantage.”

With reports from El Economista, Economía Digital, Energy-pedia news and Offshore Engineer Magazine

World.title: Great escapes: Summertime adventures accessible from Guadalajara
World.content:
Guadalajara is the perfect location for people looking for a quick escape from noise and congestion on a fine summer day. The city is bordered to the north by gorgeous Oblatos Canyon and to the west by Bosque la Primavera, a magnificent pine and oak forest the size of 42,657 World Cup soccer fields.

Guadalajara also happens to sit at the center of an area where all five of Mexico’s main ecosystems converge. This puts tapatios (Guadalajara residents) within a day’s drive of mountains, beaches, deserts, rivers, slot canyons, hot springs and Mexico’s largest lake.

My wife and I described 90 of these sites in our three-volume series “Outdoors in Western Mexico,” no longer in print but available in digital form.

The importance of finding a good guide

These days, I suggest that hikers contact local guides to arrange for excursions out in the blue. The guides know the territory, the people who live there, the weather patterns and the feasibility of transit on a given day. On top of that, you’ll have a chance to contribute to the local economy.

One of those knowledgeable guides is outdoor enthusiast Mike Gallegos. Mike is the founder of Senderismo Guadalajara, which organizes hikes and climbs all over Western Mexico.

500 meters straight down

As I mentioned above, Guadalajara has some great outdoor sites located immediately adjacent to the city. For example, you can take a bus to Parque Puerta de la Barranca at the northern edge of town for a good look at magnificent, 500-meter-deep Cañon de Oblatos, also called Cañon de Huentitán. Very near the park, there’s a steep trail — once part of the famed Camino Real — which takes you to the Santiago River at the bottom. Here you’ll find graceful Puente de Arcediano, the second suspension bridge built in the Americas.

To get back up to the city, Senderismo Guadalajara offers two unforgettable, adrenaline-raising routes. One is via the Árbol de la Bruja (“Witch’s Tree”), while the other takes you up an abandoned cable-car track. Hang on to your hat!

Hot river, cool forest

At its Western edge, greater Guadalajara butts up against the Primavera Forest. Here, Senderismo Guadalajara has an exciting hike following the forest’s famed Río Caliente to the bizarre Cascada Esmeralda, which looks cold and alpine from a distance, but turns out to be hot and steamy up close. At its source, this river literally boils its way out of a spot you may be tempted to call the “Gates of Hell.”

For a totally different experience in this forest, you can hike seven kilometers atop mesas covered with pine and oak trees to reach Nejahuete Tower, better known as Torre Dos. Here you can climb up to a platform manned by forest-fire spotters 24 hours a day. The view from this tower is truly breathtaking.

‘The Tooth’

Another outstanding site on Guadalajara’s perimeter is “El Diente,” located only six kilometers north of the City’s busy Periférico or Ring Road. A veritable forest of giant rocks stands here in total silence except for the grunts of rock climbers who consider the monoliths ideal for perfecting their techniques. These hard rocks were once part of the Earth’s mantle and may be 30 million years old. You’ll enjoy taking Senderismo Guadalajara’s six-kilometer loop hike around the mass of monoliths.

Once you drive out of the city, you’ll find great summertime escapes at every turn.

Stargazing on Ceboruco Volcano

Ceboruco is a massive, still active volcano, 2,280 meters high, in the state of Nayarit, a two-hour drive from Guadalajara. The camino to the top is in good condition — and don’t be surprised if you see road runners along the way.

Senderismo Guadalajara will arrange for you to camp on the flat, grassy floor of an old crater a few meters below a billowing and hissing fumarole, with a spectacular view of the starry sky. The next day, you can hike to another of Ceboruco’s seven craters, from whose rim you can gaze down at a dramatic tongue of lava stretching off into the distance. Those “ants” you see crossing the rubble far, far away are actually buses and semi-trailers!

Comala Falls: Am I in paradise?

A two-hour drive to the southwest of Guadalajara brings you to the foot of an utterly spectacular waterfall. You can practically jump out of your car and straight into the delightful, bubbling pool at the foot of the cascade. “What more could I ask for?” you say, and Mike Gallegos replies: “More than you would ever believe.”

There are, in fact, 11 more waterfalls upstream. Welcome to paradise!

There are other falls and volcanoes near Guadalajara, too. But in case you get a yen for a jungle experience instead, you might drive to Huilotán Ecological Park, 90 minutes north of town, where you can camp next to spring-fed pools beneath mango and fig trees, your eyes peeled for military macaws flying overhead. Oh, did I mention the 100-meter-tall waterfall and the fish-fry dinner?

14 geysers and a psychedelic bell

Next, for something truly different, I recommend the 14 geysers of Los Patitos River, located 30 kilometers north of Huilotán. Of course, there are hot pools, too, so don’t forget your swimsuit.

Finally, how about a little mountain that stands in a category all its own? La Campana (“The Bell”), located 160 kilometers west of Guadalajara, features giant wave-shaped rock formations that look as if they could have been designed by Antoni Gaudí. Don’t forget your camera!

To start exploring Guadalajara’s natural wonders, contact Mike Gallegos at WhatsApp +52 (331) 136-8254.

John Pint has lived near Guadalajara, Jalisco, for more than 30 years and is the author of “A Guide to West Mexico’s Guachimontones and Surrounding Area” and co-author of “Outdoors in Western Mexico.” More of his writing can be found on his website.

World.title: MND Local: Balancing preservation and growth in Puerto Vallarta
World.content:
Puerto Vallarta has always known how to attract people. For decades, visitors have arrived searching for the same things: beautiful beaches, a welcoming community, incredible food and the feeling that life moves just a little differently here. But success brings its own challenges for the people living here year-round.

This week, three stories highlight different aspects of life in Puerto Vallarta: federal concerns about water quality at one of the city’s beaches, the arrival of electric buses aimed at modernizing public transportation, and the ongoing work of protecting the sea turtles that return to the region’s coastline each year.

Playa del Cuale flagged in federal water quality monitoring

One of Puerto Vallarta’s most recognizable beaches, Playa del Cuale, has been classified as unsuitable for recreational use following the latest federal water quality monitoring program.

The Federal Commission for the Protection against Health Risks (Cofepris) included the beach among five in Mexico that exceeded permitted bacteria levels during its most recent testing between June 15 and July 1. Cofepris tests beaches by measuring levels of enterococci bacteria, an indicator used to determine whether seawater meets health standards for activities such as swimming. Beaches that exceed established limits are classified as not suitable for recreational use until conditions improve.

The classification doesn’t mean Puerto Vallarta’s beaches as a whole failed inspection. Cofepris reported that 98.3% of beaches tested nationwide met the required standards for recreational use. However, the result draws attention to Playa del Cuale and raises questions about what contributed to the elevated bacterial levels and what measures will be taken to address the issue. Located near the mouth of the Cuale River, the beach is an area where factors such as rainfall runoff, drainage systems and coastal conditions can all influence water quality.

For residents, the report serves as a reminder of the importance of monitoring and maintaining the environmental systems that support a growing coastal city.

Puerto Vallarta receives first electric buses as public transport changes begin

Puerto Vallarta has taken its first step toward introducing electric public transportation, with the arrival of new electric buses designed to operate along one of the city’s busiest corridors.

The first units arrived as part of a state-backed electromobility project led by the government of Jalisco. Seven articulated electric buses are expected to serve the Francisco Medina Ascencio corridor, connecting important areas of the city, including the hotel zone, Marina Vallarta, Ixtapa and the Centro Universitario de la Costa area.

The buses are designed to carry high passenger volumes and include features such as air conditioning and accessibility improvements.

The introduction of electric buses represents one of the most significant changes to Puerto Vallarta’s public transportation system in years. For residents, however, the success of the project will ultimately be measured by how it performs in daily life.

Public transportation is a major issue for many people who depend on buses to travel to work, school and essential services. As Puerto Vallarta continues to grow, questions about traffic congestion, reliability and accessibility have become increasingly important.

The arrival of electric units marks the beginning of a transition, but residents will be watching how quickly the new system expands and what improvements it brings to everyday commuting.

Boca de Tomates turtle camp reports thousands of hatchlings released

While Puerto Vallarta continues to develop, conservation groups are working to protect one of the species that’s long been part of the region’s natural identity.

The Boca de Tomates turtle camp reported the release of 30,864 sea turtle hatchlings during the latest nesting season, following efforts that protected 521 nests containing more than 36,000 eggs.

The conservation program, located along the northern coastline of Puerto Vallarta, works throughout the nesting season to monitor beaches, protect nests from threats and help ensure hatchlings can safely make their way into the Pacific Ocean. The annual effort depends on the work of conservation staff, volunteers and community members who patrol nesting areas, relocate vulnerable nests when necessary and organize releases once the young turtles are ready to begin their journey.

For residents, the results highlight the role that local conservation organizations play in protecting Puerto Vallarta’s natural environment. While discussions about coastal growth often focus on development pressures, programs like Boca de Tomates demonstrate the ongoing work taking place to preserve local wildlife.

As Puerto Vallarta continues to change, the annual return of sea turtles and the thousands of hatchlings given a better chance of survival through these efforts remains an important part of the region’s environmental story.

Together, these stories offer a snapshot of a city continuing to evolve. Puerto Vallarta’s growth brings new opportunities, but it also highlights the importance of investing in the systems, services and natural resources that support the community that calls it home.

Charlotte Smith is a writer and journalist based in Mexico. Her work focuses on travel, politics and community. You can follow along with her travel stories at www.salsaandserendipity.com.

World.title: Argentina’s Central Bank Pauses Dollar-Buying Streak After IMF Praise
World.content:
Argentina · Monetary Policy

Key Facts —The pause. The BCRA did not buy dollars on 28 July 2026, ending a 135-session streak that began on 2 January 2026. —Reserve build-up. The central bank accumulated roughly US$13 billion in gross reserves during the nearly seven-month buying streak. —Gross reserves level. Gross foreign reserves stood at US$48.391 billion at the close of trading on the pause day. —IMF encouragement. IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva visited Buenos Aires days before and explicitly told authorities to “keep buying” dollars. —Peso management. The pause was partly tactical, aimed at keeping the wholesale dollar from breaching the ARS 1,500 per US$ threshold.

Argentina’s central bank ended its historic dollar-buying streak on Tuesday, pausing after 135 consecutive sessions of purchases that added US$13 billion to reserves, just days after the IMF chief visited Buenos Aires and praised the accumulation programme.

A 135-session dollar-buying streak comes to a tactical halt

The Banco Central de la República Argentina (BCRA) stepped back from the foreign-exchange market on 28 July 2026, breaking a run of daily dollar purchases that had stretched unbroken since 2 January. The central bank confirmed it made no intervention, citing heavy buying by energy-sector firms that supplied enough dollars to the market without official participation.

The pause was not a policy reversal but a calculated move to prevent the wholesale peso from weakening past the closely watched ARS 1,500 per US$ line. The wholesale exchange rate closed the session at ARS 1,499.84, barely inside the threshold that authorities have defended under the crawling-peg regime.

By halting purchases, the BCRA also slowed the injection of pesos into the economy, a side effect of its reserve-building that requires the Treasury to absorb excess liquidity through regular debt auctions. The decision underscored the balancing act between shoring up reserves and maintaining exchange-rate stability.

Reserves surge to near US$49 billion on the back of aggressive buying

The BCRA’s sustained intervention transformed the country’s reserve position over the first seven months of 2026. Gross foreign reserves reached US$48.391 billion on the day of the pause, a level not seen since 2019, after starting the year significantly lower.

The accumulation averaged roughly US$98 million per day, with several outsized sessions punctuating the trend. A single-day jump of over US$1.2 billion on 7 July pushed gross reserves to US$49.536 billion, while a US$532 million purchase on 14 July marked the largest daily acquisition since late 2022.

By late July, year-to-date net purchases had surpassed US$13.1 billion, comfortably exceeding the BCRA’s annual goal of US$10 billion. The reserve build-up has been a cornerstone of President Javier Milei’s economic programme, aimed at rebuilding credibility with international creditors and eventually dismantling capital controls.

IMF chief visits Buenos Aires and says “keep buying”

The pause came just days after IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva visited Buenos Aires and delivered a clear message on the reserve programme. Speaking during her late-July trip, Georgieva praised Argentina’s shift from fiscal deficit to primary surplus and the decline in annual inflation from roughly 210 percent to around 30 percent.

She pointed specifically to the US$13 billion in reserve accumulation since January and told authorities to “keep buying.” The Fund had already modified Argentina’s net-international-reserves target earlier in 2026, effectively instructing the Milei government to continue the dollar-purchase programme while maintaining some exchange-rate flexibility.

Net reserves rose by about US$7 billion under the programme, putting Argentina very close to its US$8 billion end-2026 target under the IMF agreement. The Fund’s public endorsement signalled confidence that the buying streak, even with its tactical pauses, remains aligned with programme objectives.

The peso tightrope: crawling-peg discipline meets market pressure

The official peso has been managed through small daily depreciations under a crawling-peg policy, keeping it at the very top of its 52-week range. On the day of the pause, the official rate stood at ARS 1,497 per US$, virtually unchanged, before weakening 0.18 percent to ARS 1,500 the following session.

The tight management of the official rate contrasts with persistent premia in parallel markets. By mid-July, the blue dollar traded between ARS 1,510 and ARS 1,530, while the MEP dollar sat at about ARS 1,514 and the CCL dollar reached roughly ARS 1,560, reflecting continued demand for financial-dollar hedges.

The Merval stock index rose 0.65 percent to 3,305,316 points on the pause day, as markets digested the tactical shift without alarm. Investors appeared to treat the halt as a routine operational adjustment rather than a signal of stress in the FX programme.

What the dollar-buying streak pause means for investors and expats

For international investors, the pause reinforces that Argentina’s reserve-building strategy is pragmatic rather than dogmatic. The BCRA has shown it will step aside when private-sector flows are sufficient, prioritising exchange-rate stability over mechanical accumulation.

The broader trajectory remains one of reserve strengthening, which improves Argentina’s capacity to meet external obligations and edges the country closer to lifting capital controls. Expats and businesses operating in Argentina should expect the crawling-peg to persist, with the official peso continuing its gradual, controlled depreciation.

The key risk to watch is whether the BCRA can resume purchases without pushing the wholesale rate decisively above ARS 1,500. A sustained breach would test the central bank’s commitment to the crawling-peg framework and could trigger a faster pace of depreciation, with knock-on effects for inflation and parallel exchange rates.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why did Argentina’s central bank pause its dollar-buying streak?

The BCRA paused purchases on 28 July 2026 for two stated reasons. Strong dollar buying by energy companies provided sufficient FX supply that day, and the central bank wanted to prevent the wholesale peso from weakening past the ARS 1,500 per US$ threshold.

The pause also slowed the injection of pesos into the economy, reducing the need for the Treasury to absorb liquidity through debt auctions.

How much did Argentina’s reserves grow during the dollar-buying streak?

The BCRA accumulated roughly US$13.128 billion in gross reserves between 2 January and 28 July 2026, averaging about US$98 million per day across 135 consecutive sessions. Gross foreign reserves reached US$48.391 billion on the pause day, the highest level since 2019, comfortably exceeding the central bank’s US$10 billion annual accumulation goal.

What did the IMF say about Argentina’s reserve-buying programme?

IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva visited Buenos Aires in late July 2026 and explicitly encouraged authorities to “keep buying” dollars. She highlighted the US$13 billion reserve accumulation, the shift to a primary fiscal surplus, and the drop in annual inflation from about 210 percent to around 30 percent.

The Fund noted Argentina was very close to its US$8 billion net-international-reserves target for end-2026.

World.title: Milei’s Central-Bank Charter Reform Would End State Money-Printing
World.content:
Argentina Policy

Key Facts —Announcement. President Milei will detail the BCRA charter reform in a national broadcast on 30 July 2026. —Single Mandate. The bill proposes restoring the Central Bank’s sole mission to preserving the currency’s value. —Financing Ban. It explicitly prohibits BCRA financing of the national government, provinces, and municipalities. —Privatisation Path. The separate Ley de Bases framework already authorises the sale of eight state-owned companies. —IMF Alignment. The Fund has explicitly requested the charter reform to strengthen institutional independence.

Argentina central bank reform will enter Congress in early August 2026, as President Javier Milei seeks to constitutionally ban monetary financing of the state and enshrine a single mandate for the peso, while a parallel privatisation drive advances under existing law.

Milei to Send Argentina Central Bank Reform and Privatisation Plan to Congress (Photo: Wikimedia Commons)

The Core of the Argentina Central Bank Reform

President Milei will outline the project in a pre-recorded national address on 30 July 2026 at 20:00 local time. The government then plans to send the legislation to Congress in the first days of August, though it has not yet decided whether the Senate or the Chamber of Deputies will debate it first.

The central pillar is a return to a single legal mandate for the BCRA: preserving the value of the currency. This would undo the 2012 reform that gave the bank multiple objectives, including employment and financial stability, which Milei calls a “declaration of ignorance.”

The bill explicitly prohibits the Central Bank from financing the State at any level. This covers the National Treasury, provincial governments, municipalities, and any primary-market purchase of public debt, effectively ending the practice of “adelantos transitorios” that historically funded deficits.

Governance, Independence, and the End of Letras Intransferibles

The reform strengthens institutional firewalls around the BCRA’s leadership. Removing the governor or board directors would require a two-thirds majority in both houses of Congress, a high bar designed to insulate monetary policy from political cycles.

A version under study also mandates Senate consent for appointments and removals of directors. The project further eliminates the 2012 charter changes and abolishes non-transferable Treasury letters, the instruments that swapped BCRA reserves for illiquid government paper for years.

On profits, valuation gains from price changes would be locked in a non-distributable technical reserve. Only results from active portfolio management could flow to the Treasury, and solely to cancel existing debt, closing a long-standing loophole.

A Second Phase: Criminal Penalties and Shutdown Mechanisms

The government is considering splitting the package to improve its legislative chances. A second tranche of bills would address the criminalisation of monetary issuance to fund the deficit, treating it as counterfeiting under the Penal Code.

This follow-up package would also introduce a “shutdown” mechanism. It would restrict or halt State operations when budget appropriations are exhausted, reinforcing the administration’s commitment to a zero-deficit rule.

As of late July 2026, this second legislative tranche has no fixed submission date. Officials indicate it may arrive within the second half of the year, giving the government time to build a coalition for the more contentious provisions.

The Privatisation Track: Ley de Bases in Action

While the BCRA reform grabs headlines, the privatisation of state-owned enterprises runs on a separate, already-operational track. The Ley de Bases, Law 27,742 of 2024, provides the legal framework for total or partial sale of eight public companies.

The U.S. State Department’s 2025 Investment Climate Statement confirms the law aims to optimise resource allocation and reduce the fiscal burden of SOEs. An IMF staff report names Aerolíneas Argentinas, Energía Argentina, Radio y Televisión Argentina, Intercargo, and water utility AySA among the entities up for privatisation.

Four companies are already in the active privatisation pipeline, with five more under consideration. This process is not tied directly to the BCRA charter bill but forms part of the broader stabilisation programme that Milei is pursuing with IMF backing.

Political Reactions and the IMF Factor

A group of former BCRA presidents criticised the reform, arguing a single mandate is too narrow and rigid. Milei responded on 2 July by calling them “economic illiterates” and insisting the multi-objective framework allowed emission “for anything.”

The IMF has explicitly requested reform of the BCRA charter as part of its conditionality framework. Milei presents the project as fully aligned with the Fund’s requirements, which strengthens its credibility with international investors watching Argentina’s stabilisation effort.

The government remains uncertain of legislative support and is holding intensive briefing sessions with La Libertad Avanza legislators. Splitting the package into more digestible parts is the clearest signal yet that the administration is prepared to negotiate rather than gamble on a single high-stakes vote.

What the Argentina Central Bank Reform Means for Investors and Expats

For foreign investors, the reform is a structural signal. A legally independent Central Bank with a single mandate and no obligation to fund the Treasury removes a primary driver of Argentina’s chronic inflation, which averaged over 100% annually in recent years.

The parallel privatisation pipeline offers concrete opportunities in transport, energy, media, and utilities. The Ley de Bases framework provides a legal entry point for private capital, and the IMF’s involvement adds a layer of oversight that international players typically require.

Expats living in Argentina should watch the shutdown mechanism closely. If passed, it could mean more austere public services when budgets run dry, but also a more predictable macroeconomic environment if the zero-deficit rule holds and inflation continues its downward trend.

Frequently Asked Questions

When will Argentina’s Central Bank reform be sent to Congress?

The government will announce the reform on 30 July 2026 and send it to Congress in early August 2026. The exact chamber of origin, whether the Senate or the Chamber of Deputies, has not yet been decided.

What are the main changes in the BCRA charter reform?

The reform establishes a single mandate of preserving the currency’s value, explicitly bans BCRA financing of the State at all levels, strengthens governance by requiring a two-thirds congressional majority to remove bank leadership, and eliminates non-transferable Treasury letters.

Which state-owned companies are being privatised in Argentina?

Under the Ley de Bases framework, eight companies are authorised for total or partial privatisation, including Aerolíneas Argentinas, Energía Argentina, Radio y Televisión Argentina, Intercargo, and water utility AySA. Four are already in the active pipeline, with five more under consideration.

World.title: Chile Private Mining to Pay Record US$8 Billion to State
World.content:
Chile Fiscal Windfall

Key Facts —Record payment. Private miners will pay US$8,039 million to the Chilean state in 2026, a 32% jump from 2025. —Budget share. The sum equals 9.1% of all projected central government revenues for the year. —Copper driver. High copper prices and strong export volumes are the main engine behind the record contribution. —Royalty effect. A new mining royalty law, fully active since 2024, adds roughly US$1.35 billion annually to state income. —Regional share. About US$450 million of the royalty revenue is legally earmarked for regional and municipal funds.

Chile private mining companies are projected to transfer a record US$8,039 million to government coffers in 2026, reshaping the fiscal landscape for Latin America’s richest mining economy.

Chile’s Private Mining to Deliver Record US$8 Billion to State Coffers (Photo: Wikimedia Commons)

One-stop reference Company Intelligence Every listed company in Latin America — financials, ownership and structure for 1,450+ companies across 26 exchanges, in one place. Browse the directory →

A Historic Payment Reshapes the Budget

Chile’s Budget Office (Dipres) has pencilled in US$8,039 million from large private mining operators for 2026. The figure marks the largest payment from the industry since records began.

The sum represents a 32% increase over 2025 private mining payments. It also shatters the previous record of US$6,207 million set during the commodity super-cycle of 2007.

Total central government revenues for 2026 are projected at US$88,842 million. Private mining alone will cover roughly 9.1% of that total, giving the sector outsized weight in national accounts.

Copper Remains the Undisputed Fiscal Engine

Copper is the dominant force behind the numbers. In the first half of 2026, copper exports reached US$30.236 billion, accounting for 50.1% of all Chilean exports.

The Ministry of Finance explicitly links the revenue jump to high copper prices and robust production volumes. Each US$0.01 per pound increase in the copper price adds an estimated US$27–35 million to fiscal revenues.

Copper provided 43% of all mining-related government revenue in 2024, a year when total mining income stood near US$5 billion. The 2026 projection shows that dependence intensifying rather than easing.

The New Royalty Law Delivers on Its Promise

A structural shift underpins the record. The Mining Royalty Law, fully in force from 2024, combines a 1% ad valorem tax on copper sales with a margin-based royalty of 8–26% on adjusted mining operating income.

The government estimates the law will generate about US$1.35 billion annually from 2025 onward, equivalent to 0.45% of GDP. The total tax burden for the largest producers is capped at 46.5% of operating profit.

Bank reports for 2025 already showed private mining revenues rising 47–50% year-on-year. Dipres projections simply extend that trend into 2026, confirming the royalty is working as designed.

Where the Money Goes: Regions Get a Guaranteed Slice

Not all the new revenue stays in Santiago. Roughly US$450 million of the annual royalty take is legally earmarked for regional and municipal funds.

The Regional Productivity and Development Fund receives about US$225 million. A Territorial Equity Fund for lower-income municipalities gets roughly US$170 million, while a Mining Municipalities Compensation Fund takes around US$55 million.

This distribution mechanism is designed to ease local opposition to mining projects. Communities that host operations now have a direct fiscal stake in the industry’s success.

Codelco and Lithium Add Further Fuel

The private sector is not the only contributor. State-owned Codelco is projected to transfer US$3,188 million to the state in 2026, its largest contribution in five years and a 58% real increase over 2025.

Lithium property rents administered via development agency Corfo are set to reach US$1,231 million, a 234% jump versus the prior year. Combined, total mining-related public revenue will comfortably exceed US$12 billion.

Mining accounts for 10–12% of Chile’s GDP and 50–60% of exports. The 2026 figures confirm the sector’s role as the irreplaceable backbone of public finance.

What Investors and Expats Should Watch Next

The record contribution signals a stable, rules-based fiscal framework for mining investors. The royalty law’s cap on total tax burden provides predictability that global boards value.

However, the heavy reliance on copper prices cuts both ways. Part of the windfall flows into the Economic and Social Stabilization Fund, a sovereign wealth vehicle designed to smooth budget swings when commodity cycles turn.

For expats and professionals in Santiago, the fiscal bounty could ease pressure on public services and infrastructure spending. The regional distribution of royalty funds may also unlock new opportunities in mining-adjacent communities across the north.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much will Chile private mining pay the state in 2026?

Chile’s Budget Office projects private mining companies will contribute US$8,039 million in 2026. This is a 32% increase over 2025 and the largest payment from the industry on record.

What is driving the record mining revenue in Chile?

High copper prices and strong export volumes are the main drivers. The new Mining Royalty Law, which combines an ad valorem tax and a margin-based royalty, is also contributing roughly US$1.35 billion annually from 2025 onward.

Where does the mining royalty money go in Chile?

About US$450 million of the annual royalty revenue is legally earmarked for regional and municipal funds. This includes money for a Regional Productivity and Development Fund, a Territorial Equity Fund for lower-income municipalities, and a compensation fund for mining communes.

World.title: OceanPact Buys Dock Brasil in a US$23 Million Ship-Repair Deal
World.content:
Brazilian Maritime Services

Key Facts —The price. OceanPact will pay a base price of R$119 million (US$23.1 million) for 100% of Dock Brasil. —The structure. The deal runs through OceanPact’s wholly owned subsidiary Estaleiro Farol de São Tomé, not the listed parent directly. —The conditions. Closing requires Dock Brasil to restructure and extinguish certain debts before the deal can complete. —The CBO merger. CADE approved the OceanPact-CBO combination without restrictions on 27 July, creating a 73-vessel offshore fleet. —The strategy. OceanPact aims to cut operating costs and strengthen vertical integration by internalising ship repair and maintenance.

OceanPact buys Dock Brasil for R$119 million, adding a dedicated ship repair yard just as regulators clear its blockbuster merger with CBO to create Brazil’s largest offshore support vessel operator.

OceanPact Buys Dock Brasil in R$119 Million Ship Repair Deal (Photo: Wikimedia Commons)

What OceanPact buys Dock Brasil for and how the deal works

OceanPact Serviços Marítimos S.A. (OPCT3) disclosed on 28 July 2026 that its subsidiary Estaleiro Farol de São Tomé signed a binding contract to acquire 100% of Dock Brasil’s shares. The base price is approximately R$119 million, structured on a debt-free, cash-free basis.

The transaction remains subject to customary suspensive conditions, including the prior restructuring and extinguishment of certain Dock Brasil indebtedness. OceanPact has not yet disclosed a closing date or provided guidance on the timing for definitive completion.

The price includes standard update and adjustment mechanisms, along with price-retention arrangements to secure indemnification obligations agreed in the contract. Dock Brasil is described in coverage as an existing, operational naval repair infrastructure focused on ship repair, maintenance, and docking capacity.

Why OceanPact buys Dock Brasil now

OceanPact frames the acquisition as another step in its strategy to expand maritime infrastructure capabilities. The company expects to significantly increase its capacity to provide repair, maintenance, and docking services for both its own vessels and third-party client vessels.

The move aims to boost operational efficiency, reduce operating costs, and strengthen vertical integration by internalising repair and maintenance activities. OceanPact argues this will enhance its competitiveness in the Brazilian maritime services market through better control over support infrastructure.

The acquisition also positions the company to respond more quickly to growing demand for specialised services linked to offshore, port, and maritime support sectors. Incorporating an established, operational yard allows OceanPact to improve its service offering for an expanding fleet and client base.

The CBO merger clears, creating a 73-vessel offshore giant

Brazil’s antitrust authority CADE approved the OceanPact-CBO business combination without restrictions on 27 July 2026, one day before the Dock Brasil announcement. The combined company will operate 73 offshore support vessels with projected annual revenue above R$4 billion (US$778 million).

The all-stock deal will see OceanPact issue approximately 274 million to 275 million new shares to CBO’s shareholders. CBO shareholders will hold roughly 57.86% to 58% of the combined company, while existing OceanPact shareholders retain about 42% to 43%.

The combined backlog stands at about R$14 billion (US$2.7 billion), providing strong revenue visibility. OceanPact’s Investor Relations director indicated at the Brazil Investment Forum 2026 that roughly 95% of the company’s revenue comes from long-term contracts of three to four years, reducing exposure to oil price volatility.

OceanPact’s offshore services profile and what it means for investors

Founded in 2007 in Rio de Janeiro, OceanPact started as an environmental consulting and oil spill response firm before evolving into a broad maritime services group. It now serves oil and gas, ports, mining, energy, and telecom clients across three main business units: environmental protection, subsea services, and maritime logistics and engineering.

Chartering of maritime support vessels accounts for about 67% of total revenue, while services in marine environments contribute roughly 33%. The company maintains dedicated bases for environmental protection and offshore logistics, including one of the largest environmental protection bases in Latin America at Porto do Açu in Rio de Janeiro state.

Decommissioning has become a major growth avenue within OceanPact’s services segment, supported by a large Petrobras budget for decommissioning in the 2026-2030 period. The Dock Brasil acquisition adds in-house repair capacity that should improve margins on both its own fleet maintenance and third-party work.

What the Dock Brasil deal signals for Brazil’s maritime sector

The acquisition reflects a broader consolidation trend in Brazil’s offshore services industry, where scale and vertical integration increasingly determine competitiveness. OceanPact is building an integrated platform that spans vessel ownership, subsea operations, environmental response, and now dedicated repair infrastructure.

For international investors and expats watching Brazil’s maritime sector, the deal signals confidence in sustained offshore activity despite global energy transition pressures. The long-term contract profile and Petrobras’s decommissioning budgets provide a multi-year demand floor that makes infrastructure investments like Dock Brasil economically rational.

The timing is notable: securing repair capacity immediately after CADE cleared the CBO merger suggests OceanPact is moving quickly to capture synergies and prepare the combined fleet for efficient operations. Investors should watch for the debt restructuring milestone at Dock Brasil as the next concrete signal on deal completion.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much is OceanPact paying for Dock Brasil?

OceanPact is paying a base price of approximately R$119 million (US$23.1 million) for 100% of Dock Brasil’s shares, on a debt-free, cash-free basis. The price is subject to customary adjustment mechanisms and price-retention arrangements to secure indemnification obligations.

What does Dock Brasil do and why does OceanPact want it?

Dock Brasil operates naval repair infrastructure focused on ship repair, maintenance, and docking services. OceanPact wants the yard to internalise these services, cutting operating costs and strengthening vertical integration across its growing fleet of 73 offshore support vessels following the CBO merger.

Has the OceanPact-CBO merger been approved?

Yes, Brazil’s antitrust authority CADE approved the OceanPact-CBO business combination without restrictions on 27 July 2026. The combined company will operate 73 offshore support vessels with projected annual revenue above R$4 billion and a backlog of approximately R$14 billion.

World.title: Liberia’s IMF Review Unlocks About US$50 Million for the Economy
World.content:
Africa · Western

Key Facts —IMF Board decision. On 27 April 2026, the IMF Executive Board approved a new Resilience and Sustainability Facility arrangement for Liberia. —Total package size. The RSF is worth SDR 193.8 million, approximately US$266 million, disbursed over 21 months. —Immediate cash unlocked. The third ECF review released an immediate disbursement of about US$26.5 million. —Short-term liquidity. Combined with parallel World Bank flows, roughly US$50 million in near-term cash becomes available. —Climate-macro link. The RSF explicitly ties long-term, low-interest financing to climate-resilience reforms.

Liberia’s latest IMF review has unlocked roughly US$50 million in short-term cash, anchoring the fragile West African economy to a Bretton Woods reform programme at a moment of intensifying global competition for influence.

Liberia: un accord avec le FMI ouvre la voie à un décaissement de 50 millions $ (Photo internet reproduction)

What the Liberia IMF deal actually contains

On 27 April 2026, the IMF Executive Board approved a 21-month Resilience and Sustainability Facility arrangement for Liberia worth SDR 193.8 million, roughly US$266 million. The board simultaneously completed the third review of Liberia’s existing 40-month Extended Credit Facility, releasing an immediate disbursement of SDR 19.3 million, about US$26.5 million.

Liberia’s Ministry of Finance confirmed the figures the following day, noting that total ECF disbursements now stand at approximately US$106 million. When seen alongside parallel World Bank development-policy financing, the combined short-term inflow reaches roughly US$50 million.

The RSF is not a blank cheque. Its tranches will be released over 21 months only when Liberia meets specific reform triggers tied to climate resilience, fiscal governance, and public financial management.

Why a climate-linked facility matters for a fragile economy

Liberia carries a heavy climate-exposure burden: a long coastline, rainfall-dependent agriculture, and weak infrastructure. The RSF is designed to build macroeconomic buffers against precisely those shocks, funding reforms that reduce climate-related risks to the national budget.

The facility also serves as a signalling tool. IMF endorsement of Liberia’s climate-policy trajectory is meant to crowd in additional concessional finance from other multilateral and bilateral partners, creating a reform-financing ecosystem.

For a country that has cycled through repeated IMF programmes since the 1960s, the RSF represents a newer instrument that links long-term, low-interest money directly to environmental governance. That linkage is increasingly central to how Western-backed institutions compete for influence in Africa, as explored in our pillar Africa: The New Scramble.

The power dynamics behind the Liberia IMF deal

IMF conditionality gives the Fund substantial policy leverage inside Liberia. Every RSF tranche and every future ECF disbursement depends on meeting performance criteria, from introducing a Value Added Tax to strengthening oversight of state-owned enterprises.

That leverage translates into a governance framework shaped in Washington. The current administration’s ARREST Agenda reform programme is benchmarked against IMF targets, constraining how freely Monrovia can increase spending or delay politically sensitive reforms.

Historically, this pattern has delivered short-term macro gains but also social pushback. Austerity-type measures, wage freezes, and currency reforms have repeatedly accompanied IMF programmes in Liberia, from the post-war debt workout to the Ebola and COVID-19 emergency facilities.

The great-power contest and the Bretton Woods anchor

Liberia has been an IMF member since 1962, and the Fund describes itself as a longstanding partner. The new RSF-ECF package reinforces that relationship at a moment when Western powers are using multilateral institutions to reassert leadership in climate finance across Africa.

For a small, debt-vulnerable state, the IMF-World Bank route offers concessional financing and debt relief in exchange for reforms. Large-scale Chinese or private-market borrowing would likely be more expensive and less forgiving in distress, which makes the Bretton Woods option structurally attractive despite its policy strings.

Regional stability also factors into the calculus. Economic collapse in Liberia could spill over into migration and security risks affecting Sierra Leone, Guinea, and Côte d’Ivoire, all within ECOWAS, a zone Western governments have a clear interest in stabilising.

What the Liberia IMF deal means for investors and businesses

The immediate practical effect is reduced near-term macro risk. With US$266 million in RSF commitments and cumulative ECF disbursements topping US$106 million, Liberia has more predictable external financing through 2027.

IMF oversight signals policy continuity to foreign investors, particularly in taxation, exchange-rate management, and financial-sector regulation. The Fund itself emphasises that the programme is designed to unlock additional financing from other international financial institutions and development partners.

Climate-linked RSF resources may also generate project pipelines in infrastructure, energy, agriculture, and forestry, potentially open to private capital under blended-finance structures. However, tight fiscal stances mandated by conditionality could limit rapid public-investment expansion unless grant financing rises substantially.

What to watch next

The first RSF tranche disbursement will test whether Monrovia can meet the initial reform triggers on schedule. Any delay would signal implementation friction and could slow the broader financing cascade from the World Bank and other partners.

Domestic politics will also matter. The VAT introduction and public-sector governance reforms required under the ECF are politically sensitive, and social pushback could intensify if growth and job creation lag behind the government’s projections of 4.6 percent in 2025 and 5.4 percent in 2026.

Finally, watch the broader geopolitical choreography. How visibly the IMF and World Bank package is presented as a Western-led alternative to Chinese or Gulf financing will shape perceptions of who holds the upper hand in West Africa’s evolving scramble for influence.
