Frequently Asked Questions

How much money does the Liberia IMF deal actually release immediately?

The immediate ECF disbursement is approximately US$26.5 million. Combined with parallel World Bank development-policy financing flows, roughly US$50 million in short-term cash becomes available. The larger US$266 million RSF will be disbursed in tranches over 21 months, conditional on meeting specific reform triggers.

What is the Resilience and Sustainability Facility?

The RSF is a relatively new IMF instrument that provides long-term, low-interest financing to low-income and vulnerable countries. It supports reforms that reduce climate-related macroeconomic risks, such as floods, coastal erosion, and food insecurity. For Liberia, the RSF is explicitly designed to build buffers against climate shocks while signalling policy credibility to other lenders.

Why does Liberia repeatedly turn to the IMF?

Liberia has relied on IMF concessional facilities for decades to regain market credibility after crises, from post-war debt restructuring to Ebola and COVID-19. The Bretton Woods route offers cheaper financing and debt relief compared to commercial or bilateral borrowing. In exchange, Monrovia accepts policy conditionality that shapes its fiscal, governance, and now climate-reform agenda.

World.title: Gabon-Equatorial Guinea Deal Ends 50-Year Oil Islands Dispute
World.content:
Africa · Central

Key Facts —The Agreement. Gabon and Equatorial Guinea signed a joint commitment mechanism in Addis Ababa on 28 July 2026. —The Ruling. The deal implements a 19 May 2025 ICJ judgment awarding Mbanié, Cocotiers, and Conga to Equatorial Guinea. —The Trade-off. Gabon cedes roughly 0.4 km² of insular territory but gains about 50 km² of mainland territory. —The Resource. The surrounding Corisco Bay waters are considered highly prospective for offshore oil and gas. —Next Step. Both nations must now negotiate the precise maritime boundary to define their Exclusive Economic Zones.

Gabon and Equatorial Guinea have turned a half-century territorial dispute over three tiny islands into a framework for cooperation, signing an African Union-brokered deal that promises to unlock offshore energy investment in the Gulf of Guinea.

Le Gabon et la Guinée équatoriale signent un accord sur un contentieux portant sur trois îles (Photo internet reproduction)

A Handshake in Addis Ababa Ends a 50-Year Standoff

On 28 July 2026, the foreign ministers of two of Central Africa’s oil-producing heavyweights met in Ethiopia to close a chapter that had remained open since the early 1970s. Gabon’s Dieudonné Aba’a Owono and Equatorial Guinea’s Simeón Oyono Esono Angüe signed a “joint commitment mechanism” on the sidelines of the African Union’s 49th ordinary session.

The document, witnessed by AU Commission Chair Mahmoud Ali Youssouf, does not reopen the question of who owns the islets of Mbanié, Cocotiers, and Conga. It simply binds both states to implement the International Court of Justice’s ruling peacefully and to create a technical committee that will manage the practical consequences.

What the ICJ Decided Over the Gabon Equatorial Guinea Islands

The Hague spoke clearly on 19 May 2025. The ICJ unanimously recognised Equatorial Guinea’s sovereignty over Mbanié, Cocotiers, and Conga, tracing legal title back to the Franco-Spanish Convention of 1900. The court explicitly rejected a 1974 “Bata Convention” that Gabon had presented as proof of its ownership, finding that the original text was missing and that the document never carried the force of law.

The ruling was not a total loss for Libreville. Gabon was ordered to withdraw its soldiers from Mbanié, which it had occupied for decades. The court’s judgment focused on sovereignty over the islands and the land and maritime boundary, with the common land boundary fixed by the 1900 Franco-Spanish Convention.

The Real Prize: Offshore Oil and Maritime Boundaries

Sovereignty over the islets matters because of what lies beneath the waves. The Corisco Bay sits within the Gulf of Guinea, one of the world’s most productive offshore hydrocarbon basins. Control of Mbanié influences how the maritime boundary is drawn, which in turn determines which country can award exploration licences for the surrounding blocks.

The ICJ deliberately left the precise maritime delimitation unresolved. It set the legal parameters but instructed both states to negotiate the exact line themselves. The new AU-supervised mechanism will frame those negotiations, effectively deciding who gets to license future deepwater drilling, gas monetisation, and associated infrastructure projects worth billions of dollars.

A Test Case for Africa’s New Scramble

The settlement fits a broader pattern of African coastal states legalising their maritime claims before external powers can exploit the ambiguity. The Gulf of Guinea is a crowded strategic space where Nigerian, Angolan, and Equatoguinean offshore zones overlap with European, American, and Chinese naval interests. Clear borders reduce the risk of incidents that could draw in outside forces.

This is precisely the dynamic tracked in our pillar coverage of Africa: The New Scramble. The Gabon-Equatorial Guinea deal shows how African institutions are taking ownership of dispute resolution. The AU has moved from observer to active guarantor, appointing former Burundian foreign minister Albert Shingiro as a special envoy to accompany the implementation process.

Domestic Politics and the Investor Lens

In Gabon, the ICJ loss on Mbanié triggered sharp criticism. Opposition figure Alain-Claude Bilie By Nzé called the decision “a catastrophe” in French and African media, arguing the government had sacrificed maritime claims. The administration of Brice Oligui Nguema will now need to show that the mainland gains and the chance to shape the final maritime line represent a strategic victory.

For international investors, the calculus is simpler. A 50-year territorial dispute has been replaced by a binding court ruling and a joint implementation agreement. Political risk for offshore projects in the Corisco Bay area has dropped measurably. The next licensing rounds will reveal whether oil majors and independent explorers agree that the legal fog has lifted.

What to Watch Next

The technical committee created in Addis Ababa must now oversee Gabon’s troop withdrawal from Mbanié. That process will be the first test of whether both capitals intend to honour their commitments on the ground, not just on paper. Any delay or friction will immediately raise questions about the viability of the maritime negotiations that follow.

The larger prize remains the maritime boundary. Once the EEZ line is drawn, both Libreville and Malabo will be able to market specific blocks to international oil companies. The settlement also sets a precedent for other unresolved disputes in the Gulf of Guinea, from Nigeria-Cameroon to Equatorial Guinea-São Tomé and Príncipe, where hydrocarbons and sovereignty remain tangled.

Frequently Asked Questions

Which country now owns the three disputed islands?

Equatorial Guinea holds legal sovereignty over Mbanié, Cocotiers, and Conga following the ICJ ruling of 19 May 2025. The court based its decision on the 1900 Franco-Spanish Convention, which defined colonial borders in the Gulf of Guinea. Gabon has accepted the ruling and agreed to withdraw its military forces from Mbanié under the July 2026 implementation deal.

Why are these tiny islands so important economically?

The islets sit in the Corisco Bay, part of the hydrocarbon-rich Gulf of Guinea. Control over them influences where the maritime boundary is drawn, which determines which country can award offshore oil and gas exploration licences. The surrounding waters are also valuable for industrial fishing and shipping lanes connecting Central African energy exports to global markets.

What happens next in the Gabon-Equatorial Guinea border process?

A joint technical committee, supervised by the African Union and special envoy Albert Shingiro, will oversee Gabon’s troop withdrawal from Mbanié and manage the practical implementation of the ICJ ruling. The two countries must then negotiate the precise maritime boundary to define their Exclusive Economic Zones, a process that will directly shape future offshore energy investment in the region.

World.title: Afungi Shuttle Links Mozambique’s US$20 Billion LNG Project
World.content:
Africa · Southern

Key Facts —The service. MSC announced the Afungi Shuttle on 22 July 2026, a dedicated coastal feeder linking Afungi to Nacala and Maputo. —The project. Mozambique LNG at Afungi is a $20 billion megaproject led by TotalEnergies, targeting first gas in 2029. —The restart. Construction resumed fully in January 2026 after a five-year freeze caused by an Islamist insurgency in Cabo Delgado. —The money. US EXIM backs the project with a $4.7 billion loan, its largest ever in Sub-Saharan Africa. —The stakes. The shuttle signals that global capital is returning to Cabo Delgado faster than humanitarian aid.

MSC’s new Afungi Shuttle is far more than a logistics upgrade—it is the clearest signal yet that the $20 billion Mozambique LNG project has moved from frozen ambition to full-scale execution, pulling a web of great-power finance, Asian shipyards, and African security forces into its orbit.

MSC lance une liaison maritime dédiée au chantier gazier d’Afungi (Photo internet reproduction)

What the Afungi Shuttle actually does

On 22 July 2026, Mediterranean Shipping Company (MSC) announced a new dedicated maritime service called the Afungi Shuttle. It connects the remote Afungi peninsula in northern Mozambique to the country’s two main ports, Nacala and Maputo, via regular feeder rotations.

The service is built for one purpose: moving construction materials, heavy machinery, industrial equipment, and project cargo to the Mozambique LNG site. Customers can book an entire movement from any origin port to Afungi under a single MSC contract, simplifying the paperwork and planning that a $20 billion megaproject demands.

MSC framed the launch as “opening a new gateway to northern Mozambique.” In practice, it creates a controlled logistics corridor that plugs a security-sensitive construction site directly into the company’s global network spanning Europe, Asia, the Americas, and the Middle East.

The megaproject behind the shuttle

Mozambique LNG is the largest foreign direct investment in the country’s history. The consortium, led by French major TotalEnergies with a 26.5 percent stake, plans to produce 13.12 million tonnes of LNG per year across two liquefaction trains, with first gas targeted for 2029.

The ownership structure reveals the project’s geopolitical weight. Three Indian state-linked firms—ONGC Videsh, Bharat Petroleum, and Oil India—hold a combined 30 percent. Japan’s Mitsui controls 20 percent, and Mozambique’s national oil company ENH holds roughly 15 percent.

By late March 2026, the site was 42 percent complete with over 6,000 workers on the ground. The Mozambican state expects up to $35 billion in revenue over the project’s lifetime, a figure that dwarfs the country’s annual GDP.

From insurgency to restart: why the Afungi Shuttle matters now

The Afungi peninsula sits in Cabo Delgado province, where an Islamist insurgency linked to Islamic State has killed thousands since 2017. In March 2021, militants attacked the nearby town of Palma, leaving more than 1,400 people dead or missing, including foreign nationals.

TotalEnergies declared force majeure in April 2021 and evacuated the site. Financing from US EXIM and other lenders was suspended. The project—and Mozambique’s hopes of becoming a top-tier LNG exporter—went into deep freeze.

The picture shifted dramatically in late 2025. The consortium lifted force majeure on 7 November, and on 29 January 2026, President Daniel Chapo and TotalEnergies CEO Patrick Pouyanné stood together at Afungi to announce the full restart of onshore and offshore activities. The Afungi Shuttle is the logistical backbone of that restart.

The security architecture protecting the gas

The return to Afungi was made possible by a foreign military presence. Rwanda deployed an estimated 2,500 troops to Cabo Delgado under bilateral arrangements, though some reports cite up to 5,000, with the European Union providing roughly €20 million in funding for counter-insurgency operations.

That security umbrella is fragile. Rwanda has signalled it may withdraw its forces if EU funding is not extended beyond May 2026. The Afungi Shuttle will operate in a zone where the line between stability and renewed violence depends on decisions made in Kigali and Brussels.

Meanwhile, humanitarian conditions remain dire. The UN’s 2026 response plan for Cabo Delgado requested $348 million but had received only $102 million by mid-year—about 25 percent of what is needed for roughly 919,000 people classified at the highest severity level.

Great-power money and the new scramble for African gas

The Afungi Shuttle is a cog in a much larger machine of great-power competition. The US Export-Import Bank has committed $4.7 billion to Mozambique LNG—its largest deal in Sub-Saharan Africa and a direct counter to Chinese and Russian interest in financing the project.

Asian lenders have reconfirmed roughly $5 billion in financing. South African commercial banks and state-backed institutions have committed over $2.2 billion combined. The UK, by contrast, withdrew $1.15 billion in export credit support in 2025, citing climate and human rights concerns.

The project will require at least 16 new LNG carriers worth about $2.9 billion, built mainly by Hyundai Heavy Industries and Samsung Heavy Industries in South Korea. Japanese shipping lines NYK, MOL, and K Line will operate 12 of those vessels, with Greece’s Maran Gas Maritime taking the remaining four. This is the full architecture of a global energy play, and the Afungi Shuttle is the feeder that connects it all. Readers following the broader contest for African resources will recognise the pattern described in our pillar, Africa: The New Scramble.

What the shuttle tells investors and professionals

For business readers, MSC’s decision to launch a dedicated service is a market signal. Shipping companies do not invest in tailored feeder routes for projects that might happen. They do it for projects that are happening now, with cargo already moving and contractors demanding reliable lead times.

The shuttle also functions as a risk-mitigation tool. By controlling the coastal corridor, MSC reduces dependency on ad-hoc shipping and road convoys through a province with a recent history of insurgent attacks. That matters to insurers, lenders, and the engineering firms sending expensive equipment to site.

For Latin American readers, the parallels are instructive. Mozambique LNG mirrors the scale and complexity of Brazil’s pre-salt developments, where dedicated logistics chains turned remote offshore fields into national revenue engines. The difference here is the overlay of active conflict and great-power military and financial positioning.

What to watch next

The immediate question is whether Rwanda’s troop deployment will be extended past May 2026. A withdrawal would test the security assumptions underpinning both the construction schedule and MSC’s logistics calculus.

Beyond security, watch the financing. Several European banks and insurers had yet to reconfirm their commitments as of early 2026. Any further withdrawals would shift more weight onto US and Asian lenders, deepening the geopolitical character of the project.

Finally, watch the humanitarian gap. The contrast between returning capital and shrinking aid is already sharp. If that gap widens, the project’s social licence—and the stability of the communities around Afungi—will come under strain, with consequences that no shuttle service can insulate against.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Afungi Shuttle and why was it launched?

The Afungi Shuttle is a dedicated coastal shipping service launched by MSC on 22 July 2026. It connects the Mozambique LNG construction site at Afungi to the ports of Nacala and Maputo, moving construction materials, heavy machinery, and project cargo. It was launched to secure the supply chain now that the $20 billion megaproject has fully restarted after a five-year freeze.

Who owns and finances the Mozambique LNG project?

TotalEnergies leads the consortium with a 26.5 percent stake. Indian state-linked firms hold 30 percent, Japan’s Mitsui holds 20 percent, and Mozambique’s ENH holds roughly 15 percent. Financing comes from a $14.9 billion debt package backed by eight export credit agencies and 19 commercial banks, with US EXIM providing the largest single loan at $4.7 billion.

Is the Cabo Delgado region safe for the project to proceed?

Security has improved enough for TotalEnergies to lift force majeure in November 2025 and restart construction in January 2026. Roughly 5,000 Rwandan troops, partly funded by the EU, provide security around Afungi. However, the situation remains fragile, and Rwanda has indicated it may withdraw its forces if EU funding ends in May 2026.

World.title: Strike at BAIC’s Coega plant will set a precedent, says union
World.content:
Africa · Southern

Key Facts —Strike duration. About 350 workers at BAIC’s Coega plant have been on strike since 15 June 2026, with production at a standstill. —Wage gap. BAIC pays production workers R40–R48 per hour, less than half the R121 per hour rate under the industry’s National Bargaining Forum agreement. —Union demands. NUMSA wants BAIC to join the National Bargaining Forum, align wages with sector norms, and provide a 13th cheque and pension benefits. —Investment size. BAIC’s Coega facility is its first overseas plant, built with approximately US$226 million in investment and intended as a global export base. —Market context. Chinese brands now command roughly 15% of South Africa’s new-car market, up from about 3% in 2022, reshaping the competitive landscape.

The BAIC Coega strike has entered its second month with no resolution, and the union representing 350 workers says the outcome will determine whether Chinese automakers must accept South Africa’s industry-wide collective bargaining framework or can operate outside it.

Strike at Chinese carmaker BAIC’s Coega plant will set a precedent, says union (Photo internet reproduction)

What the BAIC Coega strike is about

Workers at BAIC South Africa’s assembly plant in the Coega Special Economic Zone near Gqeberha downed tools on 15 June 2026. The plant assembles the Beijing X55 crossover SUV using a semi-knocked-down process.

The dispute centres on wages that were slashed after a two-month plant shutdown in mid-2025. BAIC laid off workers citing refurbishment, then rehired them at R48 per hour (roughly US$2.60), down from R121 per hour previously paid under the automotive industry’s National Bargaining Forum agreement.

The National Union of Metalworkers of South Africa, which represents roughly 400,000 members nationally, is leading the action. NUMSA’s Eastern Cape regional secretary Mziyanda Twani has framed the strike as a test case for labour standards across the sector.

The union’s demands go beyond wages

NUMSA wants BAIC to join the National Bargaining Forum, the industry body that sets wage floors for automakers including Toyota, Volkswagen, BMW, and Mercedes-Benz. BAIC is not a member and currently operates outside that framework.

The union’s formal demands include a minimum rate of R144 per hour, closure of the wage gap with NBF rates by June 2028, a guaranteed 13th cheque, pension or provident fund benefits, and conversion of fixed-term contracts to permanent positions. Spray painters at BAIC earn R84 per hour against an industry entry rate of R163.24.

BAIC has largely declined public comment. Negotiations have repeatedly broken down, with the company withdrawing from talks at least once as the strike passed the one-month mark. Previous attempts at dispute resolution through the Commission for Conciliation, Mediation and Arbitration have failed.

Why the BAIC Coega strike sets a precedent

The outcome will signal whether Chinese manufacturers operating in South Africa must accept the same collective bargaining architecture as Western and Japanese original equipment manufacturers. If BAIC can sustain wages far below sector norms, it could pull the floor down for the entire industry.

The strike also tests the rules inside Special Economic Zones. Coega is one of South Africa’s flagship SEZs, designed to attract foreign direct investment with incentives. Unions argue those incentives cannot create a low-cost labour enclave inside an otherwise highly unionised sector.

For other African governments watching Chinese manufacturing investments expand across the continent, the Coega outcome will serve as a reference point. A NUMSA victory would strengthen the hand of labour movements elsewhere. A BAIC victory could encourage tighter cost control in future plants.

Chinese auto capital and South Africa’s industrial strategy

BAIC’s Coega plant represents approximately US$226 million in investment and is the Chinese state-linked automaker’s first overseas production facility. It was intended as a global export base targeting Africa, Europe, the Middle East, and Latin America.

Chinese brands now command roughly 15% of South Africa’s new-car market, up from about 3.1% in 2022. Competitive pricing and long warranties have driven the surge, with some analyses projecting Chinese makers could reach 40% of the market by 2028.

South Africa’s government is caught between welcoming Chinese investment and protecting domestic manufacturing. Policymakers are negotiating with BAIC, Chery, BYD, and Great Wall Motor to localise production, while considering tariffs of up to 50% on Chinese and Indian automotive imports to protect local producers.

The great-power contest over African automotive value chains

The BAIC Coega strike sits inside a larger geopolitical competition over the future of automotive and electric-vehicle manufacturing. Western governments have moved towards tariffs on Chinese vehicle imports, citing overcapacity and subsidy concerns, while Chinese firms are building local assembly capacity in Africa to tariff-jump and access European markets.

Chery has already taken over a retrofitted plant in Rosslyn, previously used by Nissan, for local internal-combustion and EV production. The company plans to export from South Africa to other African markets and Europe from around 2027. Labour costs at Chinese-owned plants become a competitive variable in these global supply chains.

This dynamic is part of the broader pattern covered in our pillar series Africa: The New Scramble, which tracks how great powers are competing for critical minerals, manufacturing bases, and supply-chain footholds across the continent.

What to watch next

The immediate question is whether BAIC returns to negotiations or the strike extends further, deepening production losses. The Department of Labour has inspected the plant and confirmed wages exceed the national minimum wage of R30.22 per hour, but has not certified alignment with NBF sectoral rates.

For investors and policymakers, the precedent cuts both ways. If BAIC joins the NBF and aligns wages, it signals that Chinese capital must accept South Africa’s social-compact model. If it holds out, SEZs may become zones of cheaper labour, reshaping the competitive landscape for every automaker operating in the country.

The strike is also being watched across BRICS. South Africa and China are both members, and the bloc’s rhetoric emphasises South-South cooperation and mutual benefit. How this labour dispute is resolved will test whether that rhetoric translates into shared standards on the factory floor.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why is the BAIC Coega strike considered precedent-setting?

The strike will determine whether Chinese automakers must join South Africa’s National Bargaining Forum and accept industry-wide wage agreements. If BAIC can operate outside that framework with significantly lower labour costs, it could undercut established manufacturers and reshape the sector’s wage floor.

How much are BAIC workers paid compared to industry norms?

BAIC production workers earn R40–R48 per hour, while the National Bargaining Forum rate for Skill Level 1 workers is R121 per hour. Spray painters at BAIC earn R84 per hour against an industry entry rate of R163.24. The national minimum wage is R30.22 per hour.

What is BAIC’s investment in South Africa worth?

BAIC invested approximately US$226 million in the Coega plant near Gqeberha, its first overseas production facility. The plant assembles the Beijing X55 crossover SUV and was intended as an export base for Africa, Europe, the Middle East, and Latin America.

World.title: Ride-app protest could slow your drive across the Valle Central this morning
World.content:
If you have a flight out of Juan Santamaría today, a shuttle booked to the airport, or a drive between Cartago and San José, leave earlier than you planned. Ride-app drivers have called a protest for 9 a.m. today, and the roads they say they will use are the ones that carry nearly everyone.

Organizers say the convoy will roll along Ruta 1 in Alajuela, through Ochomogo, past Sabanilla and onto Circunvalación, finishing at Casa Presidencial in Zapote. Those details come from the drivers themselves. As of first light Wednesday, the Policía de Tránsito had not published an advisory confirming the route, so treat that list as the plan rather than the result. Plans like this one shift, shrink or start late.

What the drivers have called is a tortuguismo, a go-slow. Nobody blocks anything. The convoy simply travels in a pack at a crawl, and every vehicle behind it travels at the same speed. That distinction is the whole story for you. A closure gets you a detour, an officer waving you around, and a police post you can see from a distance. A go-slow gets you none of that. There is no sign, no announcement, and no way to tell you are in it until you already are. Once you are boxed in on a divided highway, your only real option is to wait.

Ruta 1 is the reason this matters to travelers. It is the corridor between San José and Juan Santamaría, so anything that slows it slows every airport transfer, every hotel shuttle and every rental car heading for a return desk. Ochomogo sits on the climb between Cartago and San José and is the pinch point for that whole side of the valley. Circunvalación is the ring road that absorbs traffic coming off Ruta 27 and feeds it around the capital toward Zapote. Between them, those three points decide whether the Valle Central moves.

If you are flying out this morning and have not left yet, go now. Whatever cushion you would normally give yourself, add an hour on top of it. That sounds excessive on a normal Wednesday, and on a normal Wednesday it would be. The problem with a go-slow is that the delay is not proportional to the protest.

A few dozen vehicles moving at 20 kilometers per hour (about 12 miles per hour) for half an hour can leave a line that takes two hours to drain, because the road behind them keeps filling at normal speed while the front of it empties at a crawl. You do not lose the time the protest lasts. You lose the time it takes the backlog to clear.

Check in online before you leave, and if you have a bag to drop, know your airline’s cutoff rather than guessing at it. If you are running late, call the airline from the road rather than waiting until you reach the counter. Missing a bag cutoff by ten minutes is a different problem than missing a flight, and airlines can sometimes do something about the first if they hear from you early.

If you are already on Ruta 1 and traffic ahead of you dies, stay in the lane you are in. Weaving between lanes to get past a convoy does not work, and on that stretch it puts you alongside heavy trucks that cannot stop quickly. Do not try to overtake the group. If you have not yet committed to the highway, Ruta 3, the old road through Heredia and Alajuela, runs roughly parallel and gives you a way to reach the airport without joining the line. It is slower on a good day and it will be crowded today, but a slow road that is moving beats a fast road that is not.

Coming from Cartago, the alternative to Florencio del Castillo is the old road, and this week that carries a complication of its own. The Romería is already underway. Tránsito started its operation on July 25 with about 150 officers on that corridor and reinforces it between July 31 and August 2, and pilgrims are walking the shoulder in numbers. The old road is an option this morning, but drive it expecting people on foot rather than a clear run.

If you are not traveling and have nothing that cannot move, the simplest answer is to not drive between roughly 9 a.m. and midday. Reschedule the Zapote appointment. Take the errand in the afternoon. Every vehicle that stays home is one that is not in the line in front of somebody trying to catch a plane.

Behind all of this is a bill that has been moving through the Legislative Assembly for years. Expediente 23.736 would regulate transport offered through platforms such as Uber and DiDi, requiring drivers to register with the CCSS and Hacienda, pay an annual permit, and meet insurance and background requirements. The Comisión de Gobierno y Administración finished working through 282 mociones de fondo on Tuesday and approved nine of them, sending the revised text back to the plenary. That vote is what put drivers on the road this morning.

The drivers want two things added before it passes. They want a ceiling on the commission platforms take from each fare, and they want guaranteed benefits and due process when a company deactivates an account. Drivers made both demands at the Assembly earlier this month, saying they had not been heard during the drafting.

Aprimotec, an association representing platform drivers, asked the Assembly and the Executive on July 20 to stop the bill’s advance altogether, arguing the text was written around the traditional taxi sector and would push drivers out of the work rather than formalize it. The taxi sector sees it differently. Canatrans, Fenacotaxi, the Foro Nacional de Taxistas and other transport groups have publicly backed the bill, framing it as legal certainty and fair competition.

Neither side is likely to settle it this morning. What will be settled by lunchtime is whether you made your flight.

World.title: Costa Rica Urged to Repair Early Defects on Circunvalación Norte
World.content:
Cracks, open joints, drainage problems and rapidly fading road markings have appeared along the newest section of Circunvalación Norte, just 17 months after the $60 million project was officially completed. The problems were identified on the section connecting Calle Blancos with Guadalupe, known as Unit V. The route forms the final link in Circunvalación Norte, one of the most important road projects completed in the San José metropolitan area in recent years.

The inspection found cracks in the driving surface of the viaduct, open joints between sections of the structure and protective and drainage work that remains unfinished. Open joints are a particular concern because rainwater, dirt and other debris can enter the gaps. Over time, that can accelerate damage to the roadway and the structure beneath it, especially during Costa Rica’s prolonged rainy season.

Inspectors also found no evidence of adequate corrosion protection on some supports beneath the viaduct. Without that protection, exposed structural components may become more vulnerable to moisture and deterioration. Water accumulation was documented near the exit toward the Guadalupe roundabout, creating another potential risk for motorists. Parts of the drainage system remain incomplete or have not shown that they can remove water effectively during heavy rainfall.

Road markings are also deteriorating faster than expected. Crosswalks, lane lines, traffic islands and other painted markings have already lost visibility in several areas despite being installed relatively recently. The findings do not mean the highway is structurally failing. Tests showed that the basic pavement structure continues to have good load-bearing capacity and that the driving surface remains generally smooth.

Resistance to skidding was also satisfactory across most of the inspected section. However, some areas inside the tunnel recorded lower levels of friction. Those results were not considered critical, but continued monitoring was recommended in case conditions worsen. The distinction is important. The immediate concern is not that the viaduct is unsafe or close to collapse, but that defects appearing so soon after completion could become more expensive and disruptive if they are not corrected now.

Authorities were advised to carry out a full evaluation of the viaduct, calculate the cost of repairs and use the project’s construction guarantees to correct the problems. Acting while those guarantees remain available could prevent taxpayers from assuming higher maintenance costs later.

Construction of the Calle Blancos–Guadalupe section began in August 2021 under the H. Solís-Estrella consortium. The viaduct opened to traffic on October 4, 2024, even though some surrounding work was still unfinished. The project was declared fully completed on February 28, 2025.

Circunvalación Norte was designed to complete a northern bypass around central San José and improve travel between La Uruca, Route 32, Calle Blancos and Guadalupe. The corridor has reduced the need for many drivers to pass through the center of the capital. The early defects now put pressure on transportation authorities to determine which problems fall under the contractor’s responsibility and ensure repairs are completed before routine maintenance becomes a larger public expense.

World.title: Motagua lashes up Verdes 5-0 in Central American Cup blowout
World.content:
Motagua lashes up Verdes 5-0 in Central American Cup blowout

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): It was a night to forget for Belizean football. Verdes FC suffered a heavy 5-0 defeat to Honduran club Motagua in Concacaf Central American Cup action.

Motagua dominated from the opening whistle, controlling possession and punishing Verdes’ defensive mistakes with clinical finishing. The scoreline was harsh, but the pattern was clear: every error was made to cost.

For a half, Verdes hung in the fight. The Belizean champions reached the break trailing just 0-1, still within a goal of level. Then came the collapse. Four second half goals turned a competitive contest into a rout, as the Honduran giants shifted gears and Verdes had no answer.

The gulf in class between Belizean clubs and the region’s heavyweights has been a recurring story in this competition, and Motagua, one of Honduras’ most decorated sides, showed exactly why.

Verdes must now regroup quickly, with pride and points still to play for in the tournament. Nights like this sting. What matters is the response.

Minister Martinez and delegation strengthen collaboration with CABEI during Taiwan visit

By Zoila Palma: Osmond Martinez, Minister of State in the Ministry of Economic Transformation, and his delegation are visiting Taiwan from July 27 to 31, 2026.

Discussions focused on continued collaboration, technical assistance, and financing for projects related to hospitals, municipal climate-resilient initiatives, and the sugar sector.

Minister Martinez was accompanied by Carlos Pol, CEO of the Ministry of Economic Transformation, and Katherine Meighan, Belize’s Ambassador to Taiwan.

World.title: International News: CONCACAF expresses concern regarding proposed FIFA forward enterprise
World.content:
International News: CONCACAF expresses concern regarding proposed FIFA forward enterprise

By Zoila Palma: Today, Concacaf issued a statement saying that it was only made aware of this matter through media reports and, subsequently, via a media release.

“We are deeply concerned by the lack of due process.

We share the disappointment of many within our region and the game that this level of detail has been designed and shared publicly before any discussion with the relevant governance bodies and stakeholders has taken place,” Concacaf explained.

Concacaf says that as leaders within football, “we are the custodians of the game. Collectively, FIFA, the Confederations and every Member Association have a responsibility to always act in the best interests of the sport. Every decision we make must be guided by good governance, robust processes and long-term stewardship.”

Concacaf further said that it trusts that all within the FIFA family will act in the same manner.

World.title: Late summer and fall are the smart seasons to escape to Las Terrazas
World.content:
Late summer and fall are the smart seasons to escape to Las Terrazas

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Seasoned travelers know a secret about Ambergris Caye: the island at its best is not always the island at its busiest. As late summer rolls into fall, the crowds thin, the pace softens, and resorts like Las Terrazas Resort and Residences come into their own.

Located on the quiet beachfront north of San Pedro, Las Terrazas is a member of the L.V.X Collection of Preferred Hotels and Resorts, an international stamp of quality carried by only a select group of Caribbean properties. The resort describes itself as a place where nature calls for adventure and discreet sophistication meets guilt-free indulgence, and the low season is when that promise breathes easiest.

The months ahead offer calmer beaches, easier restaurant tables, and a reef every bit as spectacular as in the winter rush, with snorkeling, diving and fishing all steps from the resort’s dock. For Belizeans, it is also the season when a staycation splurge makes the most sense, and the resort’s stay four nights, get the fifth free offer runs through December 15.

Plan the escape at the resort’s website or reach the team through the Las Terrazas Resort and Residences Facebook page.

Sophisticated Caribbean splendour, minus the crowds. That is the fall play.

World.title: No social media ban
World.content:
Health and Wellness Minister Dr Christopher Tufton (left) in discussion with Dr Ganesh Shetty (right), acting director, adolescent mental health, Ministry of Health & Wellness, as well as lead researcher and fellow at The University of the West Indies and consultant with the Ministry of Health Dr Stephen Johnson during Tuesday’s media briefing to present the findings from a National Study on Social Media Use and the Protection of Children. (Photo: Naphtali Junior)

In what is said to be “one of the most comprehensive national assessments ever undertaken” on social media use by minors in Jamaica, the majority of citizens surveyed have baulked at a total ban but say Government must lead the way in implementing policy with strong parental involvement when it comes to enforcement.

“The results show overwhelming public support for some level of Government action,” said Health and Wellness Minister Dr Christopher Tufton.

He was delivering the main address, Tuesday, during a press conference to release findings of the National Study on Social Media Use and the Protection of Children.

The event was held at the Courtyard by Mariott Hotel in St Andrew.

According to Tufton, nine out of every 10 respondents, or 90.2 per cent, support Government regulation of minors’ social media use, while 2.9 per cent expressed opposition. In addition, he said, nearly 84 per cent believe Jamaica should establish a clear national policy framework governing minors’ use of social media.

Tufton said from reading the study he formed the opinion that the subject has been “a long-standing concern, but not talked about as much”.

“I was surprised when I saw the results. A strong message: The Jamaican people recognise that this is an issue requiring national attention, and they expect thoughtful leadership on the issue. But perhaps the most significant finding is not simply that Jamaicans support some levels of Government action; it is that they believe this responsibility must be shared, and I was very heartened at that,” the minister stated.

Citing the report, he said only 12.7 per cent of respondents believe Government should lead this effort alone.

“Again, that’s very good to know, because it means people will want to engage,” Tufton said, while adding that 40.5 per cent of respondents believe parents/guardians should play the leading role, while another 39 per cent favoured shared responsibility among parents, schools, Government, communities, and other stakeholders.

“The finding is especially important, because it reminds us of something we already know: No Government policy can replace active parenting, and that’s very important to note. No legislation can replace guidance within the home. No technology platform can replace the influence of families, teachers, and communities. Protecting children online, therefore, must be a national partnership, and that’s a very big theme. A takeaway from this: A national partnership,” said the minister.

He noted that the survey also revealed that Jamaicans favour balance rather than extremes, and the preferred approach was not simply stronger legal restrictions.

While acknowledging the positives brought by social media the health minister emphasised that the results of emerging research from 2025-2026 for Jamaica “confirms a strong link between social media use and increased anxiety, depression, and digital addiction, particularly among young persons and content creators”.

He said youth under 24 spend an average of six hours daily on social media, compared to five hours for adults and four hours for seniors.

Tufton stressed that the study is “intended for public consumption and discourse in the first instance, not any decision”, while at the same time assuring that there was no intention to “just wholesale adopt what entails elsewhere” as far as regulations are concerned.

Delving into the study during the event, Dr Stephen Johnson, lead researcher and fellow at The University of the West Indies and a consultant with the Ministry of Health, said the use of social media by minors has become a public health issue.

“We have data from the National Council on Drug Abuse [NCDA] indicating that 70 per cent of our minors sleep less than eight hours on an average school night. In terms of body image, [there is] low self-esteem; [we see] digital addiction from excessive screen time [of] three hours or more; having 68 per cent of our population being addicted. [There are issues of] online safety, cyberbullying, grooming, and being exposed to harmful content. Now, of course, there’s a need for Government not necessarily to be preventative, but to be proactive,” he said.

The sample of 1,027 individuals surveyed included Gen Zers, millennials, Gen X, and Boomers educated at the primary, vocational, and tertiary levels.

Dr Johnson emphasised that while the overwhelming majority, over 80 per cent of those interviewed, supported “a clear policy framework for minors’ social media use… the appetite for an outright ban it’s not really here… Persons are saying, while you’re doing this, be mindful that minors have rights,” the lead researcher disclosed.

Dr Ganash Shetty, acting director, adolescent mental health in the Ministry of Health, who pointed out that the algorithms behind social media platforms are created by behavioural specialists, spoke directly to youngsters in attendance.

World.title: Bounty Killer gets key to Kingston
World.content:
Rodney “Bounty Killer” Price delivering his acceptance speech Tuesday after receiving the Keys to the City of Kingston and the renaming of Wenchman Road in his honour.(Photo: Karl Mclarty)

FROM the inner-city community of Seaview Gardens in western St Andrew that raised him to conquering the global dancehall stage, Rodney “Bounty Killer” Price returned home Tuesday to receive the Key to the City of Kingston and the renaming of a road in his honour.

“It’s official, the king of Kingston with the keys to Kingston,” a jubilant Price declared as he accepted the city’s highest civic honour during a ceremony at Seaview Gardens Primary School.

In a further tribute to the dancehall icon, Wenchman Road — where Price spent much of his youth — was officially renamed Rodney Price Drive, following a petition from Seaview Gardens’ residents and approval by the Kingston and St Andrew Municipal Corporation (KSAMC).

Visibly moved by the recognition Price, who has also received the Order of Distinction for his invaluable contribution to Jamaica’s music scene, described the occasion as another meaningful milestone in his career, admitting that words could not fully express his gratitude.

“Today is really the unfolding of another historical chapter in my career. And this milestone is a very unusual and an uncommon accomplishment — the Keys to the City of Kingston,” he said, thanking the KSAMC, mayor of Kingston Andrew Swaby, and other officials for the honour.

Pointing to the road which now bears his name, Price recalled how his life was defined by it, noting that it had witnessed both the beginnings of his journey and some of his darkest moments. “This is more than just a ceremony. This is a celebration of troubles and trial and triumph and greatness. It’s just right round the road, that’s where I got shot when I was 16, right around there,” he said.

He thanked the KSAMC for immortalising the name, the battles, and the triumphs he carried long before he became known to the world as Bounty Killer.

“Our community is a golden garden. Hard work and dedication leads to these accomplishments and accolades in life. And then they say a king has never been crowned in his town, so what is this then?” questioned an evidently elated Price.

The entertainer who has won a Grammy award for his feature on No Doubt’s multi-platinum hit song Hey Baby and received a solo Grammy nomination, told the ceremony that the significance of the occasion far surpassed international acclamation.

“This is more than a Grammy to me. These are people who watched me emerge as a young artiste. These people are people who are personally involved in my upbringing, and for them to decide that I deserve the key to Kingston, this is something phenomenal,” he said.

For his part, Kingston Mayor Andrew Swaby congratulated Price and noted that the recognition is more than celebrating the successful musician, describing it as a statement about the values of the city and the potential that exists within communities such as Seaview Gardens.

“Too often communities like Seaview Gardens are viewed through the lens of their challenges rather than their possibilities. People sometimes make assumptions about what someone can achieve based on where they come from, but as we all should know by now an address does not determine one’s personal potential. What Bounty Killer’s life demonstrates is the clearest possible term that potential exists in every community; talent discipline and determination can emerge from anywhere for our young people,” said Swaby.

Announcing the renaming of Wenchman Road to Rodney Price Drive, Swaby said the tribute would ensure that the artiste’s legacy remains permanently etched in the community that shaped him.

“His name will remain fixed to this day, in this very community that raised him, so that anyone who passes through Seaview Gardens will know that greatness comes from these streets. So Bounty Killer, on behalf of the citizens of Kingston and St Andrew, thank you. Thank you for your music, for your mentorship, and for the contribution that you have made to Jamaica’s culture. This city is proud to recognise you as a son of Kingston, and it is an honour today to place this key in your hands,” said the mayor.

World.title: Grand day-long celebrations for Rita Marley’s 80th
World.content:
These young performers enjoyed the kids’ zone. (Photo: Rahyme McKenzie)

The Bob and Rita Marley foundations brought together supporters, partners, artistes, and community members to honour Alferita “Rita” Marley as she celebrated her 80th earthstrong under the theme ‘Thank You Jah 80’.

The day-long tribute celebrated Marley’s extraordinary legacy as a musician, philanthropist, entrepreneur, cultural advocate, and matriarch whose impact continues to inspire generations around the world.

Celebrations began at 6:30 am with Rise in Grace, a wellness and fitness experience at Bob Marley Museum that invited participants to embrace healthy living while reflecting on Rita Marley’s lifelong commitment to holistic well-being.

From 11:00 am to 3:00 pm Tuff Gong International came alive with a Family Fun Day, offering free entertainment and activities for all ages. Families enjoyed interactive games, storytelling, face painting, karaoke, water attractions, creative activities for children, dominoes, ludo, and complimentary health screenings. The activation reflected Rita Marley’s lifelong commitment to strengthening families, promoting wellness, and building resilient communities.

The festivities officially began with a prayer and blessing led by the Ethiopian Orthodox Church, followed by cultural performances from students of Half-Way Tree Primary, Linstead Primary, Central Branch Primary, Meadowbrook Primary and Old Harbour Bay Culture Camp.

Music then took centre stage during the lunch hour concert, held from 1:00 pm to 2:00 pm and powered by Tapedeck, an independent music streaming and digital download platform.

Through a partnership with the Jamaica Cultural Development Commission (JCDC), the concert also provided a national stage for the 2026 Festival Song Competition finalists, reinforcing both organisations’ shared commitment to preserving and celebrating Jamaican culture.

Tim Quirk, founder of Tapedeck, commented: “Rita Marley’s musical journey is a living blueprint for creative independence. What she and Bob Marley established through Tuff Gong by leveraging their voices to amplify other independent artistes and producers resonates strongly with us at Tapedeck. We are honoured to be a part of this milestone birthday celebration as we welcome Tuff Gong International Distributors to Tapedeck and look forward to bringing Jamaica’s creative community to our audience.”

The day’s celebrations culminated with the highly anticipated Thank You Jah 80 Digital Celebration Concert at 5:00 pm, streamed on the Tuff Gong TV YouTube channel and Bob Marley’s Tuff Gong Radio on SiriusXM Channel 19. Hosted by Kamila McDonald and Ron Muschette, the concert featured performances by Tessanne Chin, Nadine Sutherland, Romain Virgo, Alaine, and Makeda, reaching audiences around the world and allowing supporters everywhere to join in celebrating the milestone.

CEO of the Bob Marley Group of Companies Cedella Marley shared: “We celebrate mommy every day, but turning 80 is a milestone that deserves to be honoured in a truly special way. She has spent her entire life showing up for us — not just as our mother, but as a guide, a protector, and an unwavering source of love. Beyond our family, she’s poured that same love into communities around the world, serving others with grace, compassion, and humility. Everything she has done has been rooted in love, so celebrating her is one small way for us to say thank you. She deserves every flower, every tribute, and every moment of appreciation. This celebration is our way of letting her know just how deeply she is loved.”

World.title: ‘WALK STRONG’
World.content:
Gordon Swaby, CEO of EduFocal Limited, as the Junior Market-listed company reports early operating gains from its restructuring while working to stabilise its balance sheet.

SHAREHOLDERS of loss-making EduFocal Limited will vote on September 10 on renaming the listed company Walstron Limited, widening its mandate beyond education technology and authorising directors to issue shares to executives, advisers, employees and business partners.

The renamed company would be permitted to operate across education technology, technology, commerce and real estate, but the annual general meeting (AGM) documents identify no acquisition target, property project or commerce venture. Chief Executive Officer Gordon Swaby said there was nothing in those areas to announce, while the EduFocal brand and its existing products would continue.

The vote comes as EduFocal’s auditors warn of material uncertainty over its ability to continue as a going concern. At December 2025, the group had a $163.02-million equity deficit and only $104,315 in cash.

Swaby told the Jamaica Observer in written responses that Walstron was derived from the phrase “walk strong”.

“You know how we tell people ‘walk good’ when they’re heading off? Walstron is our version of that, except it’s about how you carry yourself through the challenging parts,” he said.

The AGM resolution says the change would reflect an expanded business focus and long-term growth strategy. Swaby, however, said the broader mandate was intended to give the company room to pursue opportunities rather than signal that a transaction was imminent.

“On real estate and commerce, what the resolution does is give us room. That’s really all it is. It widens what the company is allowed to do so we’re not running back to shareholders every time something interesting comes along,” he told the Business Observer.

“But there’s nothing for me to announce today. When there is, it goes through the JSE (Jamaica Stock Exchange) first and you’ll have it the same time our shareholders do.”

He also drew a distinction between the listed company’s proposed new name and the EduFocal operating brand.

“EduFocal is still EduFocal. Same brand, same platform, same everything. Academy runs. Quizzative runs. Engage runs,” Swaby said.

He said the previously disclosed wind-down of EduFocal’s African subsidiary operations would not affect those products or the company’s customers.

Shares for obligations

More immediately for shareholders, Resolution Six would authorise EduFocal’s directors to issue unissued ordinary shares to key partners, executives, legal advisers and other employees of the company or its subsidiaries.

The shares could be issued as compensation for services or other valuable consideration, with the directors determining each allotment at their discretion.

The resolution does not state how many shares could be issued, the proposed issue price, the recipients or the value of the services and obligations involved.

Swaby confirmed that settling some obligations with shares forms part of the plan.

“Yes. Part of what we’re asking shareholders to approve is settling certain obligations by issuing new ordinary shares,” he said.

“You either service those obligations out of cash, or you convert them into equity and free that cash up for the business. I’d much rather put the money into building.”

Issuing shares instead of using cash could reduce liabilities and preserve scarce working capital. It would, however, increase the number of shares in issue and would dilute existing shareholders. The extent of any dilution cannot be determined until the company discloses the number of shares, issue price, recipients and obligations being settled.

EduFocal had 648.45 million ordinary shares in issue at December 2025. Its shares closed Tuesday at $0.18, compared with the $1 price at which the company listed in March 2022.

Rights issue must wait

EduFocal’s audited financial statements list a proposed $250-million rights issue among the measures management intends to use to address its cash-flow difficulties. The other measures include securing $200 million in large contracts and restructuring loans with creditors.

Swaby now says the rights issue will not proceed until the balance sheet has first been repaired.

“We’re not doing a rights issue until the balance sheet is fixed. Simple as that,” he said.

“You don’t go asking people for fresh money on a balance sheet that isn’t right yet. Fix it first. That’s the work we’re in the middle of, and a good chunk of what shareholders are voting on is exactly that work.”

He did not define what would constitute a repaired balance sheet or say how much of the deficit the proposed share settlements are expected to eliminate.

The sequencing is important because the audited accounts presented the rights issue as part of management’s response to the going-concern uncertainty. Existing shareholders would ordinarily be given an opportunity to participate in a rights issue, while allotments to selected parties under Resolution Six would dilute shareholders who do not receive additional shares.

EduFocal has not reported a full-year net profit since listing.

Revenue declined 28 per cent to $70.27 million in 2025, but the company recorded an operating profit of $23.9 million after sharply reducing expenses. Finance costs and impairment losses contributed to a net loss of $29.43 million, although that was an improvement on the $58-million loss recorded in 2024.

At year end, liabilities exceeded the group’s $203.14 million in assets by $163.02 million. Its accumulated deficit stood at $341.23 million.

Approximately $153.09 million, or 75 per cent, of total assets comprised intangible assets such as software and intellectual property. The auditors identified the valuation of those assets as a key audit matter because it depends partly on management’s estimates of future revenue and cash flow.

At the stand-alone company level, current liabilities exceeded current assets by $147.01 million. The auditors said continued operation depended on management’s ability to reduce costs and increase revenue. Their opinion was not modified in respect of the going-concern matter.

EduFocal subsequently reported a net profit of $368,479 for the March 2026 quarter, reversing a $1.34-million loss a year earlier. Revenue, however, declined 53 per cent to $14.11 million.

Late again

The company’s 2025 audited accounts and March 2026 quarterly report have now been published, but both were late.

The first-quarter report, due on May 15, was submitted on July 1. EduFocal was also suspended from trading in both 2024 and 2025 after failing to submit audited financial statements within the Jamaica Stock Exchange’s deadlines. Its most recent suspension lasted from early June until December 5, 2025.

“On the filings, you’re right. We’ve been late, and that’s on me,” Swaby said in his responses.

He said the company had made significant changes to its internal processes and intended to remain current with its reporting obligations.

“When you list, you take on an obligation to keep the market informed on time, and I take that seriously. We intend to be current and to stay current,” he said.

World.title: RAINY DAY BLUES
World.content:
(From bottom to top) Antigua and Barbuda’s Cejhae Greene, Australia’s Edward Nketia, Jamaica’s Ackeem Blake, Canada’s Jerome Blake, Nigeria’s Adekalu Nicholas Fakorede, South Africa’s Gift Leotlela, Lesotho’s Mojela Koneshe and Barbados’s Kuron Griffith compete in the men’s 100m semi-finals during the athletics event at the Scotstoun Stadium in Glasgow, on day five of the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow, Scotland, on Tuesday. (Photo: AFP)

Jamaica failed to add to its medal tally on the second day of track and field at the Commonwealth Games at Scotstoun Stadium in Glasgow, Scotland, on Tuesday as, for the second straight staging, no Jamaican man contested the blue-ribbon 100m final.

There were hopes of adding to the two gold medals won on Monday by high jumper Romaine Beckford and sprint hurdler Demario Prince, but the Jamaicans must wait at least until today if they are to win more medals.

Lamara Distin failed to repeat her success in the women’s high jump, placing fourth, while Jodean Williams was fifth in the women’s 100m final.

Jamaicans are down to contest two finals today — the men’s long jump and women’s shot put — while the 200m events for both men and women will also start.

The afternoon session was held in heavy rain, forcing officials to take the high jumpers off the field. When the competition resumed, Distin, who led in the first half of the event, could only manage 1.87m and missed out on a medal.

Australia’s Eleanor Patterson, the silver medallist in 2022, won the gold with a games record-equalling 1.96m, beating teammate Nicola Olyslagers, who cleared 1.93m, while Nigeria’s Temitope Simbiat Adeshina took the bronze.

Jodean Williams was the only Jamaican who reported for the women’s 100m final, with Jonielle Williams, who had also qualified, withdrawing. Both had qualified on time after placing third in their respective semi-finals.

Jodean ran 11.09 seconds (1.0m/s) as New Zealand’s Zoe Hobbs won with an Oceania Area record 10.93 seconds, beating England’s Amy Hunt, who ran 10.98 seconds. Australia’s Torrie Lewis lowered her national record to 10.99 seconds after running 11.00 seconds in the semi-finals.

Both Ackeem Blake and Rohan Watson failed to get past the men’s semi-finals. Blake was third in the third semi-final in 10.06 seconds (1.1m/s), behind South Africa’s Gift Leotlela, who ran 10.02 seconds, and Australia’s Edward Nketia, who clocked a personal-best 10.03 seconds.

In the first semi-final, Watson was sixth in 10.12 seconds (0.0m/s) as Emmanuel Eseme of Cameroon won in a national-record 9.89 seconds, ahead of Australia’s Lachlan Kennedy, who ran a personal-best 9.94 seconds.

Eseme returned with another national record and a Commonwealth Games record 9.83 seconds (1.3m/s) to win the gold. Kennedy was second with an Area Record 9.85 seconds, while Nigeria’s Kayinsola Ajayi was third in 9.90 seconds.

The last Jamaican to win the men’s 100m was Kemar Bailey-Cole in 2014, while Nigel Ellis was a finalist in 2018.

Nayoka Clunis came up short in the women’s hammer throw final with three fouls after throwing 64.83m in the qualifying round a day earlier.

The NACAC Senior Championships silver medallist has a personal best and national record of 72.03m, set earlier this year, which is the fifth-best mark in the Commonwealth this year.

Zandrion Barnes ran a season’s best 45.13 seconds to lead the semi-final qualifiers in the men’s 400m at the Commonwealth Games at Scotstoun Stadium in Glasgow, Scotland, on Tuesday.

Barnes is one of two Jamaican men who won their first-round heats, including Antonio Watson, as all the Jamaicans in action booked semi-final spots for Thursday.

Former world champion Watson was in total control in his first-round race, running 46.36 seconds, with Delano Kennedy also advancing after placing second in his heat in 45.82 seconds.

Both Jamaicans in the women’s 400m also advanced, with Shana Kaye Anderson placing second in her race in 52.71 seconds and Leah Anderson third in 52.74 seconds.

National men’s 800m record holder Navasky Anderson also made progress after placing third in his first-round heat in 1:48.12.

Today, Tajay Gayle and Jordan Turner are down to contest the men’s long jump, while Lloydricia Cameron will carry the Jamaican flag in the women’s shot put.

Christopher Taylor, Roshawn Clarke and Jevaughn Powell will start their quest for medals in the men’s 200m, with Alana Reid and Lavanya Williams lining up in the women’s heats.

Assinie Wilson will contest the men’s 400m hurdles, while Sanique Walker and Shiann Salmon are in the women’s event. Kelly Ann Beckford and Adelle Tracey will compete in the women’s 800m semi-finals.

World.title: Investor residency plan edges forward
World.content:
Jamaica is moving closer to introducing economic residency for qualifying foreign investors, but the required investment, job-creation targets, and eligible assets remain undisclosed.

JAMAICA’S long-delayed plan to grant residency to qualifying foreign investors has moved closer to Parliament, more than four years after its formal implementation target and more than a decade after Jamaica Promotions Corporation (Jampro) recorded the proposal.



But the Government still has not disclosed how many applicants would have to invest, how many jobs they would have to create or which investments would qualify.

The Government’s latest annual report on Form 18-K, filed with the United States Securities and Exchange Commission, said draft amendments to the Immigration Restriction (Commonwealth Citizens) Act and the Aliens Act are being vetted for submission to the legislation committee.

The wording indicates progress but does not say that the committee has received the Bills or that they have been approved for tabling in Parliament.

“The proposals include the introduction of an economic residency programme which is intended to support a more enabling environment for potential investors who do not present a national security threat to Jamaica,” the report said.

It is the clearest sign of movement since the SEC filings began referring to the draft amendments in 2023. The programme nevertheless remains at a pre-parliamentary stage, with no implementation date announced.

Then Industry, Investment and Commerce Minister Audley Shaw disclosed in May 2021 that Cabinet had approved the proposal for further consultation and determination of the conditions under which permanent residency — not citizenship — would be granted.

But the proposal predates that decision. Jampro’s 2013/14 annual report described the Jamaica Economic Residency Programme as a proposed immigration-residency category for foreign investors undertaking projects involving a predefined amount of capital. It said Jampro and the Passport, Immigration and Citizenship Agency (PICA) had agreed that the programme was feasible.

The National Investment Policy, approved by Cabinet on July 18, 2022, subsequently called for a strategic economic residence programme to encourage direct investment and job creation based on specified criteria, with PICA and Jampro responsible for implementation.

The policy targeted the first quarter of fiscal year 2022/23, covering April to June 2022. That deadline had already passed when Cabinet approved the policy and is now more than four years overdue.

It compared the proposed programme with business-migration arrangements then operating in the United States and Australia, citing investments of US$1.8 million and A$1.5 million, or approximately US$1.03 million at the time. Those were international examples, not proposed Jamaican thresholds.

Successive Government filings show that the legislation remained at roughly the same stage for three years. The 2023 report said the bills were being finalised for submission to Cabinet. The 2024 report said they had been further revised and were being finalised for Cabinet approval. The 2025 report repeated that position.

The latest wording suggests movement beyond the previously stated Cabinet-preparation stage, but several features that will determine the programme’s value and credibility remain unknown.

The Government has not disclosed the minimum investment, the jobs applicants would have to create, how long the investment and jobs must be maintained or whether qualifying investments would be restricted to selected industries.

Nor has it said whether applicants could qualify through new or existing businesses, real estate, Government securities, approved development projects or investment funds. Processing fees, physical-presence requirements, provisions for dependants, renewal conditions and grounds for revoking residency also remain undisclosed.

In November 2022, then Jampro Vice-President Shullette Cox said the programme would be based on “firm, foreign direct investments that are underpinned by job creation”.

The intended applicants could include Diaspora members without Jamaican citizenship. Former State Minister for Industry, Investment and Commerce Dr Norman Dunn said in June 2022 that the programme could facilitate second- and third-generation Jamaicans ready to invest.

Permanent residency allows a foreign national to live and work in Jamaica without restrictions on the length of stay or the need for a work permit. It does not provide the same constitutional rights as citizenship or automatically give the holder a Jamaican passport.

PICA’s published permanent-residence categories cover employment, retirement, marriage and dependency, but not investment. Applicants are interviewed and must provide financial records, police certificates, medical documents and evidence of assets. Business owners must also submit company registration and tax-compliance documents, income tax returns, and audited financial statements.

Economic residency would not itself confer citizenship. Like any other qualifying non-national, a holder could later apply for naturalisation. PICA says applicants must have lived in Jamaica for at least five years in total, including the 12 months immediately before applying, and be of good character.

Because Jamaica is proposing residency rather than citizenship, the economic return would depend largely on the investment and employment attached to each approval, not the sale of a passport.

The programme could give investors greater certainty about living in Jamaica while managing local operations, remove the need for repeated work-permit and immigration applications and make the country more attractive to Diaspora investors and foreign business owners.

But its value will depend on how the Government defines an eligible investment and verifies that promised jobs and capital are maintained. Directing investors towards operating businesses and productive projects could generate employment, exports and tax revenue. Allowing passive asset purchases to qualify could produce less direct economic activity.

The legislation must also establish what happens if an investor withdraws the money, sells the qualifying asset or fails to create or maintain the promised jobs.

Residency-by-investment programmes also require strong background checks. A 2023 report by the Financial Action Task Force and the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development said the programmes can attract foreign direct investment but may also be abused to launder criminal proceeds, evade justice or misrepresent tax residence. It recommended several layers of due diligence rather than reliance on a single background check.

Jamaica’s latest filing says the programme is intended only for investors who do not present a national security threat. It does not identify which agencies would conduct the checks, how applicants’ source of wealth would be verified or whether successful applicants would be monitored after receiving residency.

The bills form part of wider amendments intended to modernise Jamaica’s immigration laws, strengthen anti-terrorism measures and increase PICA’s use of technology.

The next public test will be whether they reach the legislation committee and are subsequently approved for tabling. Until the legislation and accompanying rules are published, investors will not know the price of admission and Jamaicans will not know what economic return the country expects in exchange for residency.
