Edouard le Grix de la Salle, who runs Château du Grand Verdus with his brother, said official appeals to avoid the region threatened its wine-tourism trade. "How did they not think about protecting that sector?" he told The Associated Press.

At one point the Gironde blaze created a black thundercloud, electrified and lit from within, that generated lightning, violent winds and new fires beyond the original front. The pyrocumulonimbus was the first recorded in France.

More than half of the UK is now drought-declared as unusually dry conditions persist through summer. (Reuters: Toby Melville)

Two firefighters died Wednesday while battling a wildfire in the Rethymno region of Crete, Greece's fire department said. They were among about 125 firefighters confronting flames fanned by strong winds, with four helicopters and four water-dropping planes deployed.

The circumstances of their deaths were not immediately clear. The department said they died "in the line of duty to protect the lives and property of citizens and the natural environment".

Tens of thousands begin returning home in Spain

At the height of the crisis, roughly 330,000 people were driven from homes and vacation sites across France and Spain.

Tens of thousands of people began returning home in central Spain after firefighters made progress around Madrid and Ávila. Evacuation orders were lifted for about 20,000 people in the Madrid region, while stay-at-home restrictions ended for another 14,000.

Major fires have been burning for days near the Spanish cites of Madrid and Valencia. (Reuters: Pedro Nunes)

But 10,000 people remain under evacuation orders in Castellón, where a fire was still out of control as Spain braced for its fourth heat wave of the summer.

More than 1,160 square kilometres have burned across France this year, according to the Interior Ministry.

Europe is the world's fastest-warming continent, warming at more than twice the global average, according to the European Union's Copernicus climate service. Western Europe recorded its hottest June on record, with extreme heat and widespread dryness contributing to the spread and intensification of fires in France and Spain, Copernicus said.

AP

World.title: Three dead in Sydney house fire as police launch investigation
World.content:
Three people have died in a house fire in Sydney's south-west, New South Wales police say.

An investigation into what caused the blaze is underway.

A crime scene has been established at the address on Cornelia Street, Wiley Park

Emergency services were called to reports of a house fire on the street about 9.45pm Wednesday evening.

Extensive damage to the property was reported, with Fire and Rescue NSW extinguishing the blaze.

Three bodies were later located inside the house, following a search by authorities.

In a statement, NSW Police said they were yet to formally identify the victims, and that a report would be prepared for the coroner.

World.title: Norwegian teen guilty of UK murder plot tied to Iran-linked group
World.content:
A Norwegian teenager has been convicted of conspiracy to commit murder in Britain after being recruited by a Swedish organised crime group that prosecutors said was being used by the Iranian government.

Johannes Natland, now 19, was arrested in a hotel room in Huddersfield, northern England, in March last year with two firearms and ammunition in his possession.

Prosecutors said Natland had been recruited by the Foxtrot Network, a Swedish organised crime group used by the Iranian state and sanctioned by both Britain and the United States.

Natland had admitted possessing a semi-automatic pistol, a revolver and ammunition, but denied conspiracy to murder, saying he did not intend to carry out the plan.

After a retrial at London's Old Bailey court, Natland was found guilty of conspiracy to murder. A jury at his initial trial in June could not reach a verdict on that charge.

Prosecutors say the intended target of the plot has never been identified.

Natland is the latest young adult to stand trial in Britain and elsewhere over serious criminal acts allegedly carried out after being recruited online for money, often as an unwitting proxy for a foreign state.

Prosecutor Alistair Richardson told jurors that Natland was recruited by the Foxtrot Network, after someone using the name "Agent 47" organised hiring an assassin with 25,000 euros ($40,000) "in the pot" to pay for it.

Natland "neither knew, nor cared who he was to kill … to him, this was all about the money", Mr Richardson said.

Footage posted on social media by the UK's Crown Prosecution Service after the conviction showed Natland using his hands to pretend to shoot at officers during his arrest.

The vision also shows him walking through woodland to retrieve ammunition and firearms in Huddersfield.

During a police raid, which prosecutors said was carried out two days before the planned hit, officials found live ammunition, firearms and cash.

Frank Ferguson, Head of the Crown Prosecution Service's Special Crime and Counter Terrorism Division, said the case demonstrated how organised crime networks were operating across borders and using young people.

"This conviction sends a clear message: if you come to this country to commit serious violence on behalf of organised criminals, you will be caught and we will make sure you are brought to justice," he said.

The CPS said in a statement that a 17-year-old had been convicted and sentenced to 14 years in Norway in relation to recruiting Natland to the conspiracy, while a 16-year-old in Norway was awaiting trial for alleged involvement in the conspiracy.

World.title: Trump vows to retaliate 'hard' against Iran in expletive-laden warning
World.content:
Donald Trump has unleashed another fiery threat against Iran after a missile barrage launched towards American forces in Jordan.

In a phone interview with Fox News, which was not broadcast, the US president reportedly said the US would "beat the f****** s***" out of Iran in response to the surprise strikes on Tuesday night, local time.

He added that the US military would be "hitting them hard, they're going to get a beating".

Mr Trump paused US attacks against Iran over the weekend, after 13 straight days of strikes.

In turn, Iran had stopped launching retaliatory strikes against American personnel and bases across the Middle East, including in the Gulf states and in Jordan.

A number of US media outlets had reported the decision to halt strikes was made, in part, because of concerns that interceptor missiles used to defend American bases and allies from Iranian attacks were running low — something US officials publicly rejected.

The aftermath of an airstrike on a Popular Mobilization Forces base in Mosul, Iraq. (AP: Farid Abdulwahed)

But on Tuesday, local time, the US joined with Saudi Arabian forces to hit Iranian-backed militia groups in Iraq, which US Central Command (CENTCOM) said had been directed by Tehran's powerful Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) to attack Saudi and US forces in the region.

"The unwarranted attacks against US forces were not successful," CENTCOM said in a statement.

" The IRGC and its terrorist proxies must cease these attacks to avoid further US military response. "

The Iraqi Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF) had said at least 20 of its members were killed and 32 injured in the US and Saudi strikes.

If Mr Trump followed through on his latest threat, it would shatter the current calm in the region and once again risk returning the region to all-out war.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and US President Donald Trump met face to face on Tuesday for the first time since the war began. (X: Benjamin Netanyahu)

The US president had said he was prepared to attack Iran again if negotiations on a lasting peace deal remained stalled, while Iran had accused the US of consistently undermining progress toward any agreement by making repeated threats.

On Tuesday, in Washington DC, Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu held his first face-to-face meeting with Mr Trump since the start of the war in late February.

Despite being one of the instigators of the war, Israel had held fire and refrained from joining the US in attacking Iran after the interim deal to end the war, signed in June, collapsed.

That had been triggered by the ongoing dispute over control of the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow and busy shipping channel which Iran has blocked for much of the war.

Hours before the US and Saudi strikes, a new proposal by Oman on management of the waterway had been rejected by Iranian negotiators.

World.title: Russia charges Telegram founder with aiding terrorism
World.content:
Russia says it has charged Telegram founder Pavel Durov with facilitating terrorist activity, alleging that his hugely popular messaging app is being used by Ukrainian spies to organise attacks inside Russia.

In response, Telegram's official account on X posted an image of the Russian-born billionaire making an obscene gesture with his middle finger.

The charges, announced by the Federal Security Service (FSB), marked the culmination of a long investigation against Dubai-based Durov and Telegram.

Moscow has effectively throttled the service as part of a wider campaign to cut off access to foreign tech platforms and tighten control over the internet.

What is Telegram and why was its founder arrested? French authorities arrest Pavel Durov under unusual circumstances in Paris. He is being questioned over alleged criminal activity on Telegram, which has been enabled through a lack of moderation.

Russians can only access Telegram now by using a VPN to encrypt traffic and conceal their location. Yet state bodies including the Kremlin and the defence ministry continue to post to it on a daily basis.

The app has been described as a "virtual battlefield" in the war between Russia and Ukraine, where it is used by officials, soldiers and influential bloggers on both sides.

In statements, the FSB and the state Investigative Committee said a chatbot available on Telegram called "Daivinchik/Leo" had been used by Ukrainian special services to recruit young Russians to carry out sabotage and terrorist operations.

Daivinchik/Leo is a popular dating chatbot in Russia, where Tinder is no longer available. The statement said Ukrainian spies posting as young women were using it to contact and entrap Russians before coercing them into committing crimes.

The FSB said 46 Russians aged 12 to 22 had been arrested in the past year after being recruited in this way to carry out attacks on law enforcement officers or set fire to transport, energy, communications or financial infrastructure.

Vladimir Putin unsuccessfully attempted to block Telegram between 2018 and 2020. (Reuters: Anastasia Barashkova)

There was no immediate comment from Ukraine.

The FSB statement said Mr Durov was being placed on an international wanted list, but it did not specify what mechanism Russia would use to do this.

The global police organisation Interpol did not immediately respond to a request for comment. If Moscow does request a Red Notice, however, the process is unlikely to be quick, said a source with knowledge of the situation.

Dubai, where Mr Durov lives, has friendly relations with Moscow and growing ties in energy, business and finance. But handing him over to Russia could risk damaging the Emirate's image as an attractive hub for enterprise and technology.

Mr Durov posted that he was in Georgia last week, but his current whereabouts are unclear.

Born in Russia, he now holds Emirati and French passports. He founded Russia's Facebook equivalent, VKontakte, before selling his remaining stake in 2014 amid pressure from Russian authorities.

In 2024 he was arrested in France over allegations that Telegram failed to adequately counter criminal activity on the platform and did not sufficiently cooperate with law enforcement requests. He was later allowed to leave the country while investigations continue.

Mr Durov denies wrongdoing and says Telegram has exceeded its obligations to moderate content and cooperate with authorities to fight crime.

A Russian government newspaper reported in February that Durov was under investigation in a terrorism-related case. In April, he posted on Telegram that a summons for "Suspect P.V. Durov" had been delivered to an apartment in Russia where he lived 20 years ago.

"They must be suspecting me of defending Articles 29 and 23 of the Russian Constitution — which guarantee freedom of speech and the right to private correspondence. Proud to be guilty!" he wrote at the time.

Reuters

World.title: Nasty crash denies Aussies chance to hit back at defector Richardson
World.content:
One of the most hotly anticipated showdowns of the 2026 Commonwealth Games has been unceremoniously called off with the news England's Matt Richardson will not ride in the track cycling.

The sprint champion who represented Australia before defecting to the country of his birth following the Paris Olympics in 2024 has been ruled out by injury, Team England announced.

Richardson was racing in Japan and had been set to arrive in Scotland just before the track cycling program in Glasgow gets underway on Thursday.

Live: Commonwealth Games day six We are past the halfway mark in Glasgow, which means the end of the swimming program as athletics kicks into high gear. Follow live.

He sustained an undisclosed injury after taking a nasty fall while riding in the Keirin World Series in Tachigawa.

"We wish him a speedy recovery and look forward to seeing him back on the track soon," the English team said.

Richardson was set to compete in the men's individual and team sprints in Glasgow, setting up a high-profile showdown with his former Australian teammates.

"It's definitely weird seeing him in GB kit," Australian sprinter Leigh Hoffman said before the withdrawal was announced.

"At the time it just came out of nowhere, we'd just finished the [Olympic] Games, brought a few medals back for Australia and then he went on holiday and never came back.

"I'm not really going to be sad about it or anything, I'm just going to focus on riding my bike and I think he does the same as well."

The Aussies generally played down the match-up earlier at the Games.

Matt Richardson (left) and Leigh Hoffman have competed before, but on friendlier terms. (Supplied: AusCycling/Mackenzie Sweetnam)

"I'm excited to beat everyone in the world, he's just another domino to fall, hopefully," said Hoffman, who won 2022 Commonwealth Games gold and 2024 Olympic bronze in the team sprint with Richardson.

"The Australia-England rivalry goes back very far with the Ashes and all our other sports. It's always Australia vs England, [but] for the Commonwealth Games, we've got some really stacked riders.

"Azizul Awang from Malaysia, who's come in in great form; Trinidad and Tobago, Nicholas Paul — there's a lot of great riders.

"But the fans are definitely looking forward to an Australia-England match-up."

Hoffman admitted to being hurt by Richardson's defection after years riding together.

"We'd never experienced something like that," Hoffman said.

"You grow up racing with someone and you think you're both Aussies and then he's not. That's life."

On the way out the door, Richardson fired shots at the AusCycling set-up — comparing riding in Australia vs England to attending a normal high school vs Hogwarts — a quote Hoffman chuckled about "biting [Richards] in the arse".

World.title: Oscar-winning Irish musician Glen Hansard dies in motorcycle crash
World.content:
Irish musician Glen Hansard, who won a Best Original Song Oscar and was lead singer for rock group The Frames, has died in a motorcycle crash at the age of 56.

Irish police said a man in his 50s had died after a single-vehicle motorcycle collision in the west of Dublin.

Emergency services were alerted shortly before 04:30 am local time and the man was pronounced dead a short time after being treated at the scene.

Newstalk Radio and the Irish Independent reported that Hansard died in the crash.

In a statement ot the ABC, ATC Management "with broken hearts" confirmed Hansard's death.

"We are still dealing with the shock of it all, so we kindly ask that the privacy of Glen’s family, colleagues and friends is respected at this difficult time," a spokesperson said.

Glen Hansard was the frontman of The Frames. (Reuters: Stephan Savoia/Pool)

Hansard combined acting and a musical career.

He played a member of a Dublin soul band in 1991 movie The Commitments and won an Oscar in 2008 for the song Falling Slowly from the film Once, in which he starred alongside Markéta Irglová.

He was the long-serving frontman for rock band The Frames, half of rock duo The Swell Season and released solo albums including Didn't He Ramble, which was nominated for a Grammy for Best Folk Album in 2016.

For years, Hansard led the Christmas Eve charity busk outside Dublin's Gaiety Theatre, where members of the public gathered to see famous Irish musicians perform in aid of the Dublin Simon Community.

At the funeral of The Pogues frontman Shane MacGowan in 2023, Hansard performed The Pogues' song Fairytale Of New York with Irish singer Lisa O’Neill, which prompted dancing in the aisles of the church.

Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin said he was "deeply saddened to learn of the passing of Glen Hansard".

"A talented musician and actor who made a significant contribution to Ireland's cultural landscape over many years," Mr Martin posted on X.

Reuters/AP

World.title: New data shows Indigenous children face lengthy periods on remand
World.content:
Under the vast outback sky of Mount Isa, community leader Corina James is a familiar face at the local courthouse, a place she visits weekly out of a deep-seated commitment to supporting her young relatives and other local children.

"I go there every week; I'm still going to the courthouse because I worry," she said.

Corina also heads to the local police station when she gets a call that someone she knows has been arrested. Those visits are tough on her heart.

"I just broke down and cried for the little fella. It makes you feel really sad for them," she said.

With 30 grandchildren and seven great-grandchildren, Corina's home serves as an open-door sanctuary for many young people in the community seeking guidance.

Corina James believes the youth justice system is broken. (ABC News: Abbey Halter)

"I support … anyone else that wants to come along and ask for a bit of support … I point them in the right direction," she said.

While families like Corina's work to keep kids out of trouble, First Nations children continue to be over-represented in the criminal justice system.

The latest Closing the Gap data shows little progress to reach the nationally agreed target of at least a 30 per cent reduction in the number of Indigenous children behind bars by 2031.

The Productivity Commission's annual data compilation report found that First Nations children nationally have been held without a sentence on average for 57 days while they await trial, sentencing or a bail decision.

Over the past five years, the rate has increased from 69 per cent to 76 per cent.

Queensland has the highest proportion of children detained without a sentence, ranging from 80 to 90 per cent, with an average of 96 days, the highest in the country.

Corina opens her Mt Isa home as a safe place for youth. (ABC News: Abbey Halter)

Corina keeps detailed records about the children she supports who are navigating the youth justice system.

She knows one child who recently spent 48 days unsentenced in the Cleveland Youth Detention Centre in Townsville, followed by a 24-hour curfew upon release.

"[He] was in custody for a very long time because he had to wait for a lawyer," Corina said.

"They kept chopping and changing his lawyer, and it's really sad because they had to deal with lawyers from Brisbane."

She said he was "really sad and frustrated" while in custody.

At home, families are doing what they can to stop kids ending up behind bars.

Christine says she is often out on the streets looking for her grandchildren in the middle of the night. (ABC News: Abbey Halter)

Christine Doyle, Corina's sister, said it is often the exhausted grandparents and parents who take to the streets to track down the kids.

"When we go to bed at night, we all go to sleep here, [but] our kids are sneaking out the door," said Christine.

" Then when we wake up at like three o'clock in the morning, the kids are all gone … I drive around and look for my grandsons. "

Target to reduce youth in detention not on track

The Closing the Gap National Agreement is a formal commitment by all Australian governments to work in partnership with Indigenous communities to achieve equal life outcomes.

But the latest Productivity Commission assessment released today found there has been no significant improvement since the target to reduce young people in detention was established, and it is not on track to be met.

Indigenous young people continue to make up more than half of all people held in juvenile detention.

Sue-Anne Hunter says it is easier to demonise children than to deal with the root problems. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

National Commissioner for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Children and Young People Sue-Anne Hunter said the picture was damning.

"These numbers should worry every Australian; this is active harm, and it's compounding every year," she said.

"Most First Nations young people sitting in detention today have not been sentenced; they have not been found guilty of anything."

She said the detention figures reflected how governments respond to children in contact with the justice system, rather than a simple measure of youth offending.

" We see a demonisation in this country of youth, it's easier to lock them up. "

A rise in unsentenced detention

The data highlighted how limited access to secure housing could be a factor contributing to Indigenous children being exposed to longer periods of incarceration.

Katherine Hayes, the CEO of Youth Advisory Centre in Brisbane, said unstable homes were just one of the reasons why young people are detained without a sentence.

Katherine Hayes is working to reduce the number of children in custody through early intervention and diversionary programs. (Supplied)

"They don't have an appropriate bail address, so they don't have a permanent home or a safe home, and so they're held on remand," she said.

"[But also] it takes a really long time for their matters to get to the trial stage and that can be multifaceted … but also the way that defence lawyers conduct the matter or the police prosecutors can be slow to provide briefs of evidence."

Of all the states and territories in Australia, the highest number of children incarcerated are in Queensland.

More children are being held in unsentenced detention, with Queensland holding kids for more than 90 days. (ABC News: Abbey Halter)

Ms Hayes said detaining children in custody was not the solution fit for all youth crime.

"Give them a safe home, engage them in education, address all the mental health concerns and make sure that they have a safe home that is free from domestic and family violence," she said.

A spokesperson for Queensland's Department of Youth Justice and Victim Support told the ABC the state was prioritising "the rights of victims".

"The Queensland government is addressing youth crime and restoring safety where Queenslanders live by introducing tough new laws to prioritise the rights of victims and deliver consequences for actions for youth offenders," the spokesperson said.

"The Queensland government is also investing in early intervention and rehabilitation to reduce offending and reoffending and break the cycle of crime."

Experts say that prison is not rehabilitating for children. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

Anne Hollonds, spokesperson for Justice Reform Initiative and former National Children's Commissioner, said incarcerating children without a sentence was "completely unacceptable".

"These are children who have not been found, at this stage, to have been guilty of any crime, [and] some of them are as young as 10," Ms Hollonds said.

"To deprive them of their liberty in these places of incarceration … is really punishing them for circumstances that are beyond their own control."

The data also revealed more than one in 10 First Nations young people who completed a community-based sentence in 2022-23 were back in detention within a year.

Community supervision is intended to keep young people out of detention by allowing them to serve court orders in the community.

Ms Hollonds said governments were failing to stop vulnerable children from becoming entrenched in the justice system once they have come in contact with it.

"The recidivism rates in Australia are extraordinarily high, and what that's demonstrating is that incarcerating children, whether on remand or sentenced, is doing no one any good," she said.

"It's not keeping the community safer, but it's certainly harming these children who just go on to commit more serious crimes."

The emotional toll of remand

Skye Cooney, a youth service coordinator at Darwin's CAAPS Aboriginal Corporation, works closely with vulnerable adolescents aged 10 to 17.

Many of her clients are navigating the aftermath of juvenile detention.

Skye says she has seen the negative impacts that holding children in unsentenced detention can have. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

"When they get released to us, they participate in our Youth Service AOD program, so our goal is obviously to support them and try and give them a bit more of a positive life while they're still either serving [a] sentence or they have coming court dates," she said.

Skye frequently supports youth who have been held in unsentenced detention. She said these types of cases exacerbate substance dependency as a coping mechanism for confinement.

"If a client has been on remand in prison for two months or three months for committing a crime, [and] if they are not found guilty of that crime, then they're trying to cope with what's just happened," she said.

A 'blueprint' for success

The Productivity Commission updated nine out of the 19 Closing the Gap targets with new data.

Out of the nine updated targets, child protection continues to worsen, as well as suicide rates and adult incarceration.

The target for preschool enrolment has been met for the first time.

Employment, land rights and sea rights are on track to be met, while youth detention and babies born with a healthy birth weight have seen no significant change from the baseline.

Indigenous young people make up more than half of all people held in juvenile detention. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

The minister for Indigenous Australians said in a statement it was an "encouraging" result that the gap in preschool enrolments had officially closed.

"This is a significant milestone and shows that collective efforts can drive meaningful and lasting change," Senator Malarndirri McCarthy said.

But she noted it was "very concerning" that other critical targets for early childhood development, children in out-of-home care, suicide and adult incarceration continued to worsen.

Senator McCarthy urged states and territories that have primary responsibility for prisons, youth detention and child protection systems to do more.

"State and territory governments must also back in their commitments under the National Agreement with investments and policies that improve outcomes for First Nations people," she said.

The commissioner, Sue-Anne Hunter, said handing over power to community-controlled organisations was the way forward.

Ms Hunter wants to see the government use the successful targets as "blueprints" for addressing youth crime and child protection targets, with more funding into early intervention and support for family services.

World.title: Fauci pleads Fifth Amendment on COVID-19 origins, lawyer thrown out of tense hearing
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaCoronavirus pandemic Fauci pleads Fifth Amendment on COVID-19 origins, lawyer thrown out of tense hearing Michael Koziol July 30, 2026 — 2:45am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Washington: Republicans have slammed former US chief medical adviser Anthony Fauci after he refused to answer questions about the origins of COVID-19 during a heated congressional hearing, citing his Fifth Amendment right not to incriminate himself. Fauci, an infectious diseases expert who helped steer the US through the pandemic – first under Donald Trump and then under Joe Biden – accused Republican committee chairman Rand Paul of having an “unhinged obsession” with him. Dr Anthony Fauci appears before the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee at the Capitol. AP Photo/Allison Robbert “The only conclusion I can reach is that the sole reason he is calling me before this committee is to get me to say something – anything – that could vindicate his repeated public pledges that I end up behind bars,” Fauci told the Senate. “Although it pays me to do so ... under the advice of my attorneys, I will invoke my right under the Fifth Amendment of the Constitution to refrain from answering your questions.”



Republican lawmakers still attempted to question Fauci over the ensuing several hours, prompting him to plead the Fifth each time. The high-profile hearing came just two days after Paul – Fauci’s long-time congressional nemesis – released more than 1000 pages from the doctor’s personal diary during the pandemic. Senator Rand Paul of Kentucky, who has long had a fraught relationship with the now-retired infectious-disease expert. AP Photo/Allison Robbert Among other things, the entries painted a picture of a health bureaucrat who, having become the public face of the pandemic, meticulously tracked his media appearances and how he was being portrayed in various TV, newspaper and magazine profiles. “The situation with my national and international fame is explosive and really unimaginable,” he wrote after a “very flattering” front-page piece about him in The Washington Post in May 2020.



“It is not hyoperbole [sic] to say that today I am the most famous and talked about person in the country and one of the most recognizable peson [sic] in the world.” Related Article Coronavirus pandemic Leaked diary reveals US COVID chief’s view on a ‘rambling’ Trump and his own fame Fauci’s diary included appearances on Australia’s 60 Minutes and a discussion with the Doherty Institute’s director Sharon Lewin, who “said that I am a ‘household name’ in Australia”. In late October 2020, as Melbourne emerged from its record-breaking COVID lockdown, Fauci praised the actions of then-Victorian premier Daniel Andrews. “The Australians had zero new infections in the entire city of Melbourne yesterday proving that pure public health measures such a mandatory mask wearing ($1000.00 fine) and avoiding crowds actually works,” Fauci wrote on October 27, 2020.



The primary purpose of Paul’s committee hearing, five years after the pandemic subsided, was to interrogate Fauci about US government-funded research at a laboratory in Wuhan, China where some believe COVID-19 originated. The National Institutes of Health (NIH) for years gave grants to a New York non-profit called EcoHealth Alliance, which used some of the funds to help conduct “gain of function” research with Chinese laboratories studying coronaviruses commonly carried by bats. In his opening statement, Fauci said Paul has an “obvious obsession with calling for my prosecution”. AP Photo/Allison Robbert Gain of function research is the practice of enhancing a virus in a lab to study its potential real-world impacts. It includes general research as well as especially risky experiments. Fauci and the NIH have long maintained that the viruses studied using EcoHealth Alliance funding were genetically distinct from the one that caused COVID-19, including in his private diary entries. At Wednesday’s hearing, Paul accused Fauci of semantics.



“When you defended this research you described its benefits in the broadest terms,” he said. “But when Congress demanded accountability, you hid behind the narrowest possible definition. You can’t have it both ways.” At one point, one of Fauci’s lawyers, David Schertler, attempted to speak from the witness table on behalf of his client, leading Paul to ultimately order his removal from the room. David Schertler, Anthony Fauci’s lawyer, is escorted out of the hearing room by security after being ejected by the Republican chairman. AP Photo/Allison Robbert “You’re disputing the proceedings. You are not recognised, sir,” Paul said. “Security, please remove him from the room.” Some people in the gallery applauded, and Schertler was escorted outside by a security guard. Paul also threatened consequences for Fauci’s failure to answer questions. “It’s against the law to obstruct an investigation of Congress. There will be repercussions to your refusal to testify today.”



For years, the libertarian-leaning Republican senator from Kentucky has accused Fauci of lying to Congress over the NIH funding of coronavirus research, and called for him to be indicted. In his opening statement, Fauci pointed out he briefed or testified before Congress “well over 200 times” during his 38 years as director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases. US President Joe Biden with Anthony Fauci and Kizzmekia Corbett at the National Institutes of Health in Maryland. Bloomberg That included multiple appearances during and after the pandemic, including “several days-long transcribed interviews, answering questions about the very issues that are now the subject of this hearing”. Fauci, who is now 85, retired at the end of 2022. Democrats defended Fauci. Gary Peters, the top Democrat on the committee, said Wednesday’s hearing was a witch-hunt, abuse of congressional power and re-litigation of the past.



“One-sided investigations designed to validate pre-determined conclusions do not serve the American people,” he said. Paul told reporters Fauci did not need to invoke the Fifth Amendment and the committee would hold a vote next week on whether to hold Fauci in contempt of Congress. Anthony Fauci with President Donald Trump in April 2020 as the pandemic took hold. AP The Department of Justice would then decide whether to bring criminal charges through a grand jury. “All I can do is recommend prosecution,” Paul said. Before leaving office in 2025, Biden pre-emptively pardoned Fauci for any offences he may have committed in his official roles since 2014. But that would not cover a criminal contempt charge in 2026.



Related Article Coronavirus pandemic The married scientists torn apart by a COVID bioweapon theory Republicans rounded on Fauci following Wednesday’s hearing. “[During the pandemic] there was no camera he couldn’t find. No interview he couldn’t give. No American life he wouldn’t micromanage,” said Republican senator Ted Cruz of Texas. “Today, when the country finally demanded answers, the man who never stopped talking suddenly went silent.” Trump posted on Truth Social that he warned Biden at the time that Fauci “either didn’t have a clue or was dishonest”. Biden “went on to give Fauci vast destructive power”, Trump said. “The rest is history!”

World.title: Three dead in house fire in Sydney’s south-west
World.content:
NationalNSWFire Three dead in house fire in Sydney’s south-west Sarah McPhee July 30, 2026 — 12:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Three people have died in a house fire in Sydney’s south-west. Emergency services were called to a fire at the home on Cornelia Street in Wiley Park about 9.45pm on Wednesday. Fire and Rescue NSW (FRNSW) crews extinguished the blaze and found the bodies of three people inside. The victims are yet to be formally identified. The property suffered extensive damage, police said. Officers from Campsie Police Area Command have established a crime scene and are investigating the circumstances surrounding the fire. A report will be prepared for the coroner.



While the cause is still being investigated, earlier this month FRNSW issued a safety reminder about “the most dangerous time of the year for house fires”. As of July 15, FRNSW had already attended 480 residential fires this winter and 2025 this year. FRNSW Commissioner Jeremy Fewtrell encouraged residents to use the service’s free home fire safety visit program which includes smoke alarm checks. “You can also take some simple steps to keep you and your family safe. For example, regularly check your smoke alarm, always keep looking when cooking, keep a fire blanket and extinguisher in your kitchen, keep flammable materials a metre from the heater, and don’t overload power board or power points,” Fewtrell said. “Always check electric and heated blankets before turning them on, and look for frays, scorch marks, exposed wires or controller damage. If anything looks off, bin it.”

World.title: Alzheimer’s blood test to give Australians invaluable gift of time
World.content:
NationalHealthcare Alzheimer’s blood test to give Australians invaluable gift of time Rachel Rasker and Kate Aubusson July 30, 2026 — 12:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Australians will soon have access to the first diagnostic blood test for Alzheimer’s disease that researchers say will transform early detection, treatment and potentially prevention. The Therapeutic Goods Administration has approved a blood plasma test known as pTau217, paving the way for a blood test for Alzheimer’s disease to become part of routine GP health checks. John Gethin-Jones with his wife, Felicity Nicholson. John was diagnosed with Alzheimer’s disease in 2021. Eddie Jim On Thursday, Health Minister Mark Butler will launch the new Asia-Pacific Centre of Excellence for Alzheimer’s Diagnosis in Sydney, capable of running the pTau217 test in 18 minutes, as well as processing a suite of other biomarkers linked to Alzheimer’s disease. “I think it’s going to transform Alzheimer’s disease and eventually dementia,” said neurologist Dr Emma Devenney, who will oversee the new centre at Randwick – a collaboration between Neuroscience Research Australia (NeuRA) and Roche.



“It’s going to very quickly transform the field in terms of how we move towards prevention [and] move us much closer to early diagnosis, early treatments; and dementia and Alzheimer’s disease will become treatable.” Related Article Dementia Almost 50 per cent of dementia cases could be prevented. This new advice tells us how Dementia is the leading cause of death in Australia, and an estimated 446,500 Australians currently live with dementia. Alzheimer’s disease accounts for roughly two-thirds of cases, and there is no cure. The current gold-standard diagnostic tools to confirm Alzheimer’s disease pathology are lumbar punctures to sample cerebrospinal fluid or specialised PET scans costing thousands of dollars. Alzheimer’s disease is caused by the build-up of two proteins in the brain: amyloid-beta, which forms sticky plaques, and tau, which forms tangles inside neurons, disrupting cell-to-cell communication and causing neuronal death.



“We know that changes in amyloid and tau proteins happen 20 to 30 years before people develop symptoms, so that process has been going on for a long time [before people become symptomatic],” Devenny said. The pTau217 test detects elevated levels of phosphorylated tau protein, a reliable biomarker for amyloid-beta plaques. Trials show the test has a diagnostic accuracy of about 90 per cent. “Earlier diagnosis really gives people something incredibly valuable, which is time,” said Dr Anand Vairavan, Managing Director of Roche Diagnostics. “Time to understand what’s happening, time to plan for the future, and to access care and treatment sooner.” New technology mean Alzheimer’s can be detected in just 18 minutes. Peter Rae Felicity Nicholson knows that an earlier diagnosis would not have solved everything for her husband, John Gethin-Jones.



“But it would have taken some of the heartache out of the long, painful process,” she said. John was 60 when Nicholson noticed small signs. He could no longer write lovely messages in her birthday cards, held his knife and fork the wrong way up, and confused his right from his left. Now he cannot dress or feed himself. It took two years to get John’s diagnosis after multiple assessments and scans. “When we were finally told, he’s got Alzheimer’s, we still weren’t ready,” Nicholson said. “We just cried and cried and cried in the hospital foyer. “If we had got an earlier diagnosis, he would have embraced life and used it differently. We would have had conversations about what John wanted, made better decisions … we didn’t even look at [care] homes. Whether it’s six months or a year, it’s a game-changer.”



NeuRA’s Matthew Kiernan and Emma Devenney will oversee the Alzheimer’s centre. Peter Rae In October, the TGA approved another blood test called pTau181, known as a “rule-out test” used as part of assessments for people with mild cognitive impairment to clear individuals without the Alzheimer’s pathology. However, the pTau217 test is a “rule-out” and “rule-in” test that identifies people with Alzheimer’s pathology and those without it. A “grey zone” intermediate result suggests confirmatory tests are needed. “It’s a better test,” said Professor Scott Ayton, director of the Centre of Research Excellence in Enhanced Dementia Diagnosis at the Florey Institute. The pTau217 test has typically been useful to confirm a diagnosis of Alzheimer’s in people with symptoms.



“In the future, it might be used for screening for the early stages of Alzheimer’s disease even before they present with symptoms,” said Ayton, who leads a study that makes the test available to clinicians working up patients who may have Alzheimer’s disease. The TGA approval means, for the first time, the test can be used clinically. “As a researcher I’m really excited by this, but I’m also cautious about everyone in the community knocking on their doctor’s door to say, ‘I want this blood test’,” Ayton said. “There is still a developmental training phase to be rolled out over several years.” NeuRA is leading the development of national guidelines that will set the parameters for the blood test’s use, including who to test and when. The centre will process blood tests and cerebrospinal fluid samples for clinical trials. Clinicians are expected to be able to refer patients in six to nine months.



NeuRA CEO Professor Matthew Kiernan said the centre would create clinical pathways to receive blood samples from doctors across Australia and the Asia-Pacific. Related Article Healthcare Charlie’s dad died of a rare disease often misdiagnosed as depression The centre would produce the reference information for pTau217 necessary to apply for a Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme listing. “Then any doctor in Australia can order it,” Kiernan said. “For a long time, there was this feeling that there wasn’t much that we could do, but that has changed so much,” Kiernan said. “An earlier diagnosis means people can access the right supports earlier … we have disease-modifying therapies, and we know the sooner we start those, the better the outcome will be.”



Studies of recently approved amyloid-targeting therapies lecanemab and donanemab have shown a modest effect at slowing down cognitive impairment. Ayton said: “The hope of the field is that if we intervene even earlier, then we might be able to stop the development of Alzheimer’s disease.” Devenney is also leading an investigation aimed at detecting Alzheimer’s pathology in people with early-onset genetic dementia, and treating them with amyloid-targeting drugs before they develop symptoms. World.title: Superquiz, Thursday, July 30
World.content:
NationalSuperquiz Superquiz, Thursday, July 30 July 29, 2026 — 11:59pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Welcome to the new-look Superquiz! Easier to play on your mobile, the new quiz features a fresh design and more interactive features. Click here to tell us what you think of the new format. Got questions or want to know more? Scroll past the quiz to see our FAQs. By Andrew Brooks Why has the quiz changed?



Our new quiz format is faster, smoother and easier to play on your mobile. We’ve also introduced several new features. For the first time, you’ll see how other players scored in real time and be able to share your result with friends and family on Facebook, X and WhatsApp. We have more exciting updates on the horizon too. Tell us what you think about the new experience here. We’re keen to hear from you. Although it has a new look, this is the same Superquiz you know and love. Our regular quizmaster is excited to put your general knowledge to the test with a new set of 15 crafty questions every day. Can I see the number of questions in the quiz?



Yes, the total number of questions is displayed next to the progress bar at the top of the quiz. The number of your current question is also shown (e.g. 3/15). Want to keep track of your score? You can find a running tally in green at the top right of the quiz. Can I see all the quiz questions at a glance? No, we challenge players to complete the quiz one question at a time. When I answer a question, there’s a percentage next to the correct and incorrect answers. Why?



Thanks for noticing! This is a new addition to the quiz. It lets you track how your score compares to other readers by showing the percentage of players who chose that particular answer. It will also help you gauge the difficulty of each question after you’ve answered. Can I reset the quiz for other players on my device? Yes, click or tap ‘Play Again’ at the end of the results screen to reset the quiz.

World.content:
The Scottish men’s 3x3 team have made history winning their nation’s first Commonwealth Games basketball medal after beating New Zealand in a heart-stopping bronze medal game.

The Scots won 18-16 with New Zealand have two chances to tie the game in the final seconds.

Kyle Jimenez of Team Scotland is challenged by Christian Martin of Team New Zealand. Getty Images

Scotland were unlucky to missed out on a men’s basketball medal at 2018 Commonwealth Games on the Gold Coast with respected Australian coach Rob Beveridge leading the team to the last four before they fell just short in the bronze medal game.

This time, they have their medal and have done it at home in Glasgow.

Scottish guard Kyle Jimenez capped off an exceptional tournament with nine points in the win.

World.title: A pointed accusation
World.content:
Paul Taylor of Winston Hills detects a conflict of interest: “I think the spike in the number of porcupine/echidna recipes of late is merely a cunning ploy by Granny to promote her culinary sideline. A quick online search reveals a recipe for Homemade Meat Hedgehog with Italian Recipes on a Facebook page entitled Granny’s Homestyle Cooking and Recipes.”

“Band-Aids? Surely, nothing is worse than a pair of scissors packaged in hard plastic that can’t be opened (C8) without … a pair of scissors?” We thank Eric Scott of Bondi Junction and Vicki Brownless of South Maroota, who’s also feeling a bit snippy.

Geoff Carey of Pagewood wondered about this one for openers: “How about the cruelty of arthritis medication in a childproof bottle?”

“I just want to remind us all of the astonishingly fine margins in elite racing,” writes Kate Coates of Wangi Wangi. “Lachlan Kennedy was pipped into second place in the Commonwealth Games 100m sprint by 0.02 seconds. That’s 20 milliseconds. An average human eye takes between 100 and 400 milliseconds to blink. He was beaten by less than a blink of an eye! Far less!”

Merilyn McClung of Forestville was watching and thinks “it’s nice to see that technology hasn’t overtaken the humble, yet reliable, safety pin in holding on the track and field athletes’ number bibs. Invented in 1849, it has certainly stood the test of time.”

World.title: Boy, woman injured as large tree branch falls on popular playground
World.content:
Updated NationalQueenslandEmergency services Boy, woman injured as large tree branch falls on popular playground Courtney Kruk Updated July 29, 2026 — 8:48pm ,first published 6:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A large tree branch has fallen on a playground injuring a woman and child at a popular inner-city park in Brisbane. Emergency services rushed to Guyatt Park in St Lucia about 6pm on Wednesday when the tree branch, running the length of the playground, struck an eight-year-old boy and a 29-year-old woman. A weekly community dinner run by Greens MPs Elizabeth Watson-Brown and Michael Berkman was taking place nearby. Neither was in attendance. The large branch, which extends the full length of the playground, which struck the woman and boy. Felicity Caldwell The boy suffered head injuries and the woman’s arm was injured by the falling tree.



Queensland Ambulance Service confirmed four crews attended the scene, and said the woman was taken to the Royal Brisbane and Women’s Hospital, while the boy was taken to the Queensland Children’s Hospital. In a statement posted online, Berkman praised park goers and dinner attendees for providing prompt assistance to the pair. A witness described a huge police presence alongside fire and ambulance crews at the park. Felicity Caldwell “Around 5.45pm a large tree branch fell in the playground area at Guyatt Park, seriously injuring one woman and a young boy. My community meals team was there at the time for our regular dinner,” he wrote. “I hear that there was an incredible effort from everyone in the park to move the tree, get firies and ambos there, and help out wherever possible. I couldn’t be prouder of our community right now.



“Obviously medical professionals are still assessing the situation, but I understand the woman is receiving treatment for traumatic injuries to her arm. One of the Greens’ free community dinners, held weekly at Guyatt Park in St Lucia. Michael Berkman “The young boy sustained more serious injuries, including a head injury, but thankfully is responsive. “I am grateful that there were no lives lost in this frightening accident.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

The primary purpose of Paul’s committee hearing, five years after the pandemic subsided, was to interrogate Fauci about US government-funded research at a laboratory in Wuhan, China where some believe COVID-19 originated. The National Institutes of Health (NIH) for years gave grants to a New York non-profit called EcoHealth Alliance, which used some of the funds to help conduct “gain of function” research with Chinese laboratories studying coronaviruses commonly carried by bats. In his opening statement, Fauci said Paul has an “obvious obsession with calling for my prosecution”. AP Photo/Allison Robbert Gain of function research is the practice of enhancing a virus in a lab to study its potential real-world impacts. It includes general research as well as especially risky experiments. Fauci and the NIH have long maintained that the viruses studied using EcoHealth Alliance funding were genetically distinct from the one that caused COVID-19, including in his private diary entries. At Wednesday’s hearing, Paul accused Fauci of semantics.



“When you defended this research you described its benefits in the broadest terms,” he said. “But when Congress demanded accountability, you hid behind the narrowest possible definition. You can’t have it both ways.” At one point, one of Fauci’s lawyers, David Schertler, attempted to speak from the witness table on behalf of his client, leading Paul to ultimately order his removal from the room. David Schertler, Anthony Fauci’s lawyer, is escorted out of the hearing room by security after being ejected by the Republican chairman. AP Photo/Allison Robbert “You’re disputing the proceedings. You are not recognised, sir,” Paul said. “Security, please remove him from the room.” Some people in the gallery applauded, and Schertler was escorted outside by a security guard. Paul also threatened consequences for Fauci’s failure to answer questions. “It’s against the law to obstruct an investigation of Congress. There will be repercussions to your refusal to testify today.”



For years, the libertarian-leaning Republican senator from Kentucky has accused Fauci of lying to Congress over the NIH funding of coronavirus research, and called for him to be indicted. In his opening statement, Fauci pointed out he briefed or testified before Congress “well over 200 times” during his 38 years as director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases. US President Joe Biden with Anthony Fauci and Kizzmekia Corbett at the National Institutes of Health in Maryland. Bloomberg That included multiple appearances during and after the pandemic, including “several days-long transcribed interviews, answering questions about the very issues that are now the subject of this hearing”. Fauci, who is now 85, retired at the end of 2022. Democrats defended Fauci. Gary Peters, the top Democrat on the committee, said Wednesday’s hearing was a witch-hunt, abuse of congressional power and re-litigation of the past.



“One-sided investigations designed to validate pre-determined conclusions do not serve the American people,” he said. Paul told reporters Fauci did not need to invoke the Fifth Amendment and the committee would hold a vote next week on whether to hold Fauci in contempt of Congress. Anthony Fauci with President Donald Trump in April 2020 as the pandemic took hold. AP The Department of Justice would then decide whether to bring criminal charges through a grand jury. “All I can do is recommend prosecution,” Paul said. Before leaving office in 2025, Biden pre-emptively pardoned Fauci for any offences he may have committed in his official roles since 2014. But that would not cover a criminal contempt charge in 2026.



Related Article Coronavirus pandemic The married scientists torn apart by a COVID bioweapon theory Republicans rounded on Fauci following Wednesday’s hearing. “[During the pandemic] there was no camera he couldn’t find. No interview he couldn’t give. No American life he wouldn’t micromanage,” said Republican senator Ted Cruz of Texas. “Today, when the country finally demanded answers, the man who never stopped talking suddenly went silent.” Trump posted on Truth Social that he warned Biden at the time that Fauci “either didn’t have a clue or was dishonest”. Biden “went on to give Fauci vast destructive power”, Trump said. “The rest is history!”

World.title: Three dead in house fire in Sydney’s south-west
World.content:
NationalNSWFire Three dead in house fire in Sydney’s south-west Sarah McPhee July 30, 2026 — 12:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Three people have died in a house fire in Sydney’s south-west. Emergency services were called to a fire at the home on Cornelia Street in Wiley Park about 9.45pm on Wednesday. Fire and Rescue NSW (FRNSW) crews extinguished the blaze and found the bodies of three people inside. The victims are yet to be formally identified. The property suffered extensive damage, police said. Officers from Campsie Police Area Command have established a crime scene and are investigating the circumstances surrounding the fire. A report will be prepared for the coroner.



While the cause is still being investigated, earlier this month FRNSW issued a safety reminder about “the most dangerous time of the year for house fires”. As of July 15, FRNSW had already attended 480 residential fires this winter and 2025 this year. FRNSW Commissioner Jeremy Fewtrell encouraged residents to use the service’s free home fire safety visit program which includes smoke alarm checks. “You can also take some simple steps to keep you and your family safe. For example, regularly check your smoke alarm, always keep looking when cooking, keep a fire blanket and extinguisher in your kitchen, keep flammable materials a metre from the heater, and don’t overload power board or power points,” Fewtrell said. “Always check electric and heated blankets before turning them on, and look for frays, scorch marks, exposed wires or controller damage. If anything looks off, bin it.”

World.title: Alzheimer’s blood test to give Australians invaluable gift of time
World.content:
NationalHealthcare Alzheimer’s blood test to give Australians invaluable gift of time Rachel Rasker and Kate Aubusson July 30, 2026 — 12:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Australians will soon have access to the first diagnostic blood test for Alzheimer’s disease that researchers say will transform early detection, treatment and potentially prevention. The Therapeutic Goods Administration has approved a blood plasma test known as pTau217, paving the way for a blood test for Alzheimer’s disease to become part of routine GP health checks. John Gethin-Jones with his wife, Felicity Nicholson. John was diagnosed with Alzheimer’s disease in 2021. Eddie Jim On Thursday, Health Minister Mark Butler will launch the new Asia-Pacific Centre of Excellence for Alzheimer’s Diagnosis in Sydney, capable of running the pTau217 test in 18 minutes, as well as processing a suite of other biomarkers linked to Alzheimer’s disease. “I think it’s going to transform Alzheimer’s disease and eventually dementia,” said neurologist Dr Emma Devenney, who will oversee the new centre at Randwick – a collaboration between Neuroscience Research Australia (NeuRA) and Roche.



“It’s going to very quickly transform the field in terms of how we move towards prevention [and] move us much closer to early diagnosis, early treatments; and dementia and Alzheimer’s disease will become treatable.” Related Article Dementia Almost 50 per cent of dementia cases could be prevented. This new advice tells us how Dementia is the leading cause of death in Australia, and an estimated 446,500 Australians currently live with dementia. Alzheimer’s disease accounts for roughly two-thirds of cases, and there is no cure. The current gold-standard diagnostic tools to confirm Alzheimer’s disease pathology are lumbar punctures to sample cerebrospinal fluid or specialised PET scans costing thousands of dollars. Alzheimer’s disease is caused by the build-up of two proteins in the brain: amyloid-beta, which forms sticky plaques, and tau, which forms tangles inside neurons, disrupting cell-to-cell communication and causing neuronal death.



“We know that changes in amyloid and tau proteins happen 20 to 30 years before people develop symptoms, so that process has been going on for a long time [before people become symptomatic],” Devenny said. The pTau217 test detects elevated levels of phosphorylated tau protein, a reliable biomarker for amyloid-beta plaques. Trials show the test has a diagnostic accuracy of about 90 per cent. “Earlier diagnosis really gives people something incredibly valuable, which is time,” said Dr Anand Vairavan, Managing Director of Roche Diagnostics. “Time to understand what’s happening, time to plan for the future, and to access care and treatment sooner.” New technology mean Alzheimer’s can be detected in just 18 minutes. Peter Rae Felicity Nicholson knows that an earlier diagnosis would not have solved everything for her husband, John Gethin-Jones.



“But it would have taken some of the heartache out of the long, painful process,” she said. John was 60 when Nicholson noticed small signs. He could no longer write lovely messages in her birthday cards, held his knife and fork the wrong way up, and confused his right from his left. Now he cannot dress or feed himself. It took two years to get John’s diagnosis after multiple assessments and scans. “When we were finally told, he’s got Alzheimer’s, we still weren’t ready,” Nicholson said. “We just cried and cried and cried in the hospital foyer. “If we had got an earlier diagnosis, he would have embraced life and used it differently. We would have had conversations about what John wanted, made better decisions … we didn’t even look at [care] homes. Whether it’s six months or a year, it’s a game-changer.”



NeuRA’s Matthew Kiernan and Emma Devenney will oversee the Alzheimer’s centre. Peter Rae In October, the TGA approved another blood test called pTau181, known as a “rule-out test” used as part of assessments for people with mild cognitive impairment to clear individuals without the Alzheimer’s pathology. However, the pTau217 test is a “rule-out” and “rule-in” test that identifies people with Alzheimer’s pathology and those without it. A “grey zone” intermediate result suggests confirmatory tests are needed. “It’s a better test,” said Professor Scott Ayton, director of the Centre of Research Excellence in Enhanced Dementia Diagnosis at the Florey Institute. The pTau217 test has typically been useful to confirm a diagnosis of Alzheimer’s in people with symptoms.



“In the future, it might be used for screening for the early stages of Alzheimer’s disease even before they present with symptoms,” said Ayton, who leads a study that makes the test available to clinicians working up patients who may have Alzheimer’s disease. The TGA approval means, for the first time, the test can be used clinically. “As a researcher I’m really excited by this, but I’m also cautious about everyone in the community knocking on their doctor’s door to say, ‘I want this blood test’,” Ayton said. “There is still a developmental training phase to be rolled out over several years.” NeuRA is leading the development of national guidelines that will set the parameters for the blood test’s use, including who to test and when. The centre will process blood tests and cerebrospinal fluid samples for clinical trials. Clinicians are expected to be able to refer patients in six to nine months.



NeuRA CEO Professor Matthew Kiernan said the centre would create clinical pathways to receive blood samples from doctors across Australia and the Asia-Pacific. Related Article Healthcare Charlie’s dad died of a rare disease often misdiagnosed as depression The centre would produce the reference information for pTau217 necessary to apply for a Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme listing. “Then any doctor in Australia can order it,” Kiernan said. “For a long time, there was this feeling that there wasn’t much that we could do, but that has changed so much,” Kiernan said. “An earlier diagnosis means people can access the right supports earlier … we have disease-modifying therapies, and we know the sooner we start those, the better the outcome will be.”



Studies of recently approved amyloid-targeting therapies lecanemab and donanemab have shown a modest effect at slowing down cognitive impairment. Ayton said: “The hope of the field is that if we intervene even earlier, then we might be able to stop the development of Alzheimer’s disease.” Devenney is also leading an investigation aimed at detecting Alzheimer’s pathology in people with early-onset genetic dementia, and treating them with amyloid-targeting drugs before they develop symptoms. World.title: A pointed accusation
World.content:
Paul Taylor of Winston Hills detects a conflict of interest: “I think the spike in the number of porcupine/echidna recipes of late is merely a cunning ploy by Granny to promote her culinary sideline. A quick online search reveals a recipe for Homemade Meat Hedgehog with Italian Recipes on a Facebook page entitled Granny’s Homestyle Cooking and Recipes.”

“Band-Aids? Surely, nothing is worse than a pair of scissors packaged in hard plastic that can’t be opened (C8) without … a pair of scissors?” We thank Eric Scott of Bondi Junction and Vicki Brownless of South Maroota, who’s also feeling a bit snippy.

Geoff Carey of Pagewood wondered about this one for openers: “How about the cruelty of arthritis medication in a childproof bottle?”

“I just want to remind us all of the astonishingly fine margins in elite racing,” writes Kate Coates of Wangi Wangi. “Lachlan Kennedy was pipped into second place in the Commonwealth Games 100m sprint by 0.02 seconds. That’s 20 milliseconds. An average human eye takes between 100 and 400 milliseconds to blink. He was beaten by less than a blink of an eye! Far less!”

Merilyn McClung of Forestville was watching and thinks “it’s nice to see that technology hasn’t overtaken the humble, yet reliable, safety pin in holding on the track and field athletes’ number bibs. Invented in 1849, it has certainly stood the test of time.”

World.title: Boy, woman injured as large tree branch falls on popular playground
World.content:
Updated NationalQueenslandEmergency services Boy, woman injured as large tree branch falls on popular playground Courtney Kruk Updated July 29, 2026 — 8:48pm ,first published 6:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A large tree branch has fallen on a playground injuring a woman and child at a popular inner-city park in Brisbane. Emergency services rushed to Guyatt Park in St Lucia about 6pm on Wednesday when the tree branch, running the length of the playground, struck an eight-year-old boy and a 29-year-old woman. A weekly community dinner run by Greens MPs Elizabeth Watson-Brown and Michael Berkman was taking place nearby. Neither was in attendance. The large branch, which extends the full length of the playground, which struck the woman and boy. Felicity Caldwell The boy suffered head injuries and the woman’s arm was injured by the falling tree.



Queensland Ambulance Service confirmed four crews attended the scene, and said the woman was taken to the Royal Brisbane and Women’s Hospital, while the boy was taken to the Queensland Children’s Hospital. In a statement posted online, Berkman praised park goers and dinner attendees for providing prompt assistance to the pair. A witness described a huge police presence alongside fire and ambulance crews at the park. Felicity Caldwell “Around 5.45pm a large tree branch fell in the playground area at Guyatt Park, seriously injuring one woman and a young boy. My community meals team was there at the time for our regular dinner,” he wrote. “I hear that there was an incredible effort from everyone in the park to move the tree, get firies and ambos there, and help out wherever possible. I couldn’t be prouder of our community right now.



“Obviously medical professionals are still assessing the situation, but I understand the woman is receiving treatment for traumatic injuries to her arm. One of the Greens’ free community dinners, held weekly at Guyatt Park in St Lucia.
