World.title: Scaled-back Scott Base redevelopment plans signed off by Cabinet
World.content:
Plans to redevelop Scott Base have been signed off by Cabinet, after being scaled back to get the project under budget.

The project was previously paused and reset because the Antarctica New Zealand board said it could not be delivered within its budget.

Board chair Leon Grice said the organisation had come up with a more affordable plan, which included refurbishing the Hillary Field Centre instead of replacing it.

"So by getting more life out of a building that didn't need to come down, and by building in a more traditional way, we were able to get it under budget."

Scott Base. Antarctia NZ / Al Chapman

Grice said redeveloping Scott Base was crucial to continuing New Zealand's legacy in the region.

"We've had continuous presence there since 1957. So this project continues that legacy, and continues to support our science programme which is crucial to understanding the planet."

The redevelopment would increase the total size of the base by about 1500 square metres.

That included a new Base Services Building, refurbishment of the Hillary Field Centre, and replacement of ageing water and power infrastructure.

Building in Antarctica was incredibly difficult, due to logistics and the weather, Grice said.

"You can build from October to February. So you have to have all of the building materials supplied the February before your October start."

"You can't make any mistakes in terms of what you're building, because there's no hardware store to pop down to and pick up an extra bag of bolts."

Science in Antarctica was more important now than ever to help understand climate change, Grice said.

"Last year, we did all the logistics and support for a multinational science team that did a 500 metres ice claw drill... to get 20 million years of atmospheric record... so that will be an incredibly rich resource that will be studied for many many years."

World.title: Reserve Bank's dual mandate 'achievable', economist says
World.content:
An economist says the Reserve Bank could successfully bring back its dual mandate of low inflation and full employment.

Countries around the world, including the United States and Australia, had implemented dual mandates, independent economist Cameron Bagrie said.

"Sometimes, in certain situations, the two can cause a few frictions, but by and large, the two are achievable."

His comments come after New Zealand First leader Winston Peters signalled he could resurrect the dual mandate, which was scrapped by the coalition government early in its current term.

It also came as the unemployment rate stood at 5.3 percent, with forecasts suggesting it could nudge higher when Stats NZ released its data next week.

Critics have argued that having an employment mandate sitting alongside inflation targeting could take the focus away from the latter.

"First and foremost, any central bank, when it comes to targeting inflation or full employment, their main priority is going to be inflation," Bagrie said.

Winston Peters has signalled that he could bring the dual mandate back. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

"Realistically, it wouldn't make any material difference in regard to how the Reserve Bank would go about their everyday job."

Assuming New Zealand moved back to the settings that were in place under the previous Labour government, Bagrie said he did not think there would be too many problems.

Parliament passed a bill to remove the Reserve Bank's mandate to consider employment levels in monetary policy decisions in December 2023, shortly after the formation of the current National-led coalition.

It was the first piece of legislation passed by the Government.

Prior to the bill becoming law, Finance Minister Nicola Willis said it gave the Reserve Bank "absolute clarity about its role in our economy".

"It needs to focus on the principal objective of price stability," she said.

World.title: Pandemic preparation: 'You don't want it to be a political fight' - Michael Baker
World.content:
Epidemiologist Michael Baker is urging MPs to keep politics out of preparation for future pandemics.

The government on Wednesday accepted "in some form" all of the Covid-19 inquiry's 63 recommendations - 21 in full, 36 in principle, leaving the remaining six partially accepted.

They focused on pandemic preparedness and response.

Professor Baker said the government's acceptance of the recommendations was pleasing, but he was concerned about their implementation.

"This can't be just business as usual, because many of these activities require a very concerted response by multiple government agencies led by the Ministry of Health," he said.

"It does indicate that wherever possible, these measures will be implemented in the next 12 months, which is quite ambitious."

Many of the measures would continue in perpetuity, which was the nature of pandemic preparedness, he said.

"It is an ongoing, continuous refinement process, and that is why it does require committed resources."

Baker said it was important that work was non-partisan.

"I think that's really important to get cross-party support and processes operating because that's what you need when you have a pandemic or any emergency, you don't want it to be a political fight," he said.

"I hope that government and all our political leaders carry on that tradition of putting New Zealand right above political infighting to say, how do we ensure that New Zealand and New Zealanders are as safe as possible in the future, and protected from what could be far worse pandemics than Covid-19."

But after the government released its response to the inquiry on Wednesday, MPs immediately reverted to party politics.

Prime Minister Christopher Luxon took the opportunity to repeatedly accuse Labour of economic mismanagement during the pandemic, while Labour's Kieran McAnulty said the government's response to the inquiry was a distraction from the fact that "they're doing bugger all" in office.

New Zealand First leader Winston Peters labelled the government's response "pathetic" and called for another inquiry, saying this one was a cover up.

ACT leader David Seymour said the Labour government's overreach during the pandemic was devastating to public finances, education, business and mental health.

World.title: Upper Hutt mayor: Don't force us to amalgamate with Wellington councils
World.content:
Upper Hutt's mayor is urging other Wellington councils not to force it into amalgamating against its will.

Councils across the motu have until August 9 to come up with plans to simplify local government, but in the capital there's still stark disagreement about the details.

The current proposal has Wellington, Upper Hutt, Lower Hutt, and Porirua city councils merging, as well as three Wairarapa councils and potentially Kāpiti District Council.

A layer of community councils would sit beneath that.

An email that Wellington Mayor Andrew Little sent last week to all councillors, which RNZ has seen, said Upper Hutt intended to vote against a plan to merge with the other Wellington councils.

The email said the city's mayor Peri Zee intended to ask councillors in each council to propose an amendment to have Upper Hutt excluded from any amalgamation proposal.

Zee told RNZ she was sceptical of amalgamation.

"I haven't yet heard anybody articulate the value proposition, or the outcomes we expect to get from this project.

"Our region already has strong regional governance in things like transport."

Upper Hutt mayor urging Wellington councils not to force amalgamation Checkpoint Download MP3 3m

Analysis by consultants MartinJenkins showed a Wellington council made up of the city, Hutt Valley and Porirua councils could cost $290 million to set up and result in savings of $930 million over 25 years.

Zee said amalgamation would not deliver enough benefits for ratepayers.

She said she would ask elected members across the region to respect local decision-making if Upper Hutt votes against the idea next week.

"If a council votes no, that means no... and I would expect that they would respect that."

But that plea may be rejected.

Little said the proposal he would submit, if it was backed by his council, would include the region's four metro councils.

He said ministers had ultimately designed the process this way.

"Ministers can say it doesn't make sense for you not to be in it, therefore you're in it."

Little said he wants the Wellington region to decide its own fate, and not leave the plan up to the Government by missing a deadline.

Wellington Mayor Andrew Little RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

He believed the benefits, including savings, from a larger council would be a win for ratepayers in the long run.

"We're not setting up for a few years, we're setting up an arrangement that is intended to last for two or three decades."

A majority of 3016 surveyed Wellington city residents said they wanted councillors to forge ahead with merger plans.

About 85 percent said they supported councillors putting forward plans, with 68 percent strongly supporting that and 17 percent somewhat supporting that.

Little said councillors were still debating amalgamation. He expected a decision next week.

What Wellingtonians think of amalgamation

Resident Ellen Blake believed forced amalgamation jeopardised Wellington city's special character.

"We have lots of council housing, we've got significant nature restoration programmes, those are all unique to Wellington - and not to the rest of the region. So we've got our own local identity, and we want to keep it."

Climate consultant Matt Raeburn was more positive about the idea. On Wednesday he told councillors in the capital that merging would help the region address climate change.

He said in his opinion, Wellington's voice was currently weaker than Auckland council's unified one when it came to climate.

"From central governments over the last few years, and frankly even before that, the message to councils has increasingly been you're on your own.

World.title: Government repeals Holidays Act, 'simpler' leave bill becomes law
World.content:
A major change to how leave is calculated in workplaces has become law.

The Employment Leave Bill passed its third and final reading in Parliament on Wednesday evening.

The legislation repeals the Holidays Act 2003, attempting to simplify the regime for both workers and employers.

Speaking at the third reading, Workplace Relations and Safety Minister Brooke van Velden said the bill delivered long-overdue reform to "one of the most complex and problematic areas of our employment law".

It means annual and sick leave will now be accrued in hours, rather than days.

Additional and casual hours will not accrue annual or sick leave, with employers having to pay a 12.5 percent leave compensation payment for these hours instead.

All employers, including casuals, will be able to access annual, sick, bereavement, and family violence leave from the first day of work.

Workers will also be able to cash in up to 25 percent of their total annual leave balance every year.

Van Velden said the bill removed the need for "confusing conversions" between hours, days, and weeks, and its passing was an "important milestone" for New Zealand's workplaces.

"This bill delivers a simpler, fairer, and more workable system," she said.

All three opposition parties opposed the legislation, with Labour saying it would mean part-time workers would have to choose between going to work sick or losing pay, and people who worked extra hours would not have it reflected in the leave they earn.

In his contribution to the debate, Labour MP Phil Twyford said the legislation took from those who could least afford it.

"From all of the documents, from all of the debates we've had in the House, all the submissions we heard at Select Committee, all of the exchanges with the minister in the Committee Stage, it's clear that she and this government have chosen to prioritise administrative efficiency for employers at the expense of part-time and casual workers, who lose money and lose time off as a result of this law."

The Public Service Association had campaigned heavily against the bill, with national secretary Fleur Fitzsimons saying 200,000 workers faced a pay cut if the bill passed.

World.title: Biggest overhaul of gun regulations in decades passes into law
World.content:
The biggest overhaul of gun regulations in more than 40 years has passed into law.

Among the changes brought by the Arms Bill are a new firearms regulator removing police from oversight duties, restrictions for gang members and a host of new offences and penalties.

National and ACT agreed to rewrite the Arms Act - in place since the early 1980s - as part of its coalition arrangement.

The legislation has had many iterations, more recently a ban on semi-automatics and a new firearms regulator, introduced after the March 15 terror attacks in 2019.

Associate Justice Minister Nicole McKee said the changes would improve public safety, keeping guns out of the hands of criminals while making it easier for licensed firearm owners to comply with the law, and be trusted and respected.

In her speech to Parliament on Wednesday during the third reading, McKee said opposition parties and the media had demonised gun owners and conflated them as criminals.

"The reality is the legislation that went through in 2019 and 2020, rushed as it was, without any consultation, without due select committee process, didn't address the issue of unlicensed criminal behaviour. Instead, it pointed the finger at those that conform and those that do behave," she said.

"These legislative changes that we're making will do some greatness, I think, towards being able to show and build trust and confidence in a regime again."

McKee referenced changes including separating the Firearms Safety Authority from Police, regulating large capacity pistol magazines, introducing infringement notices rather than revoking licenses, extending dealer license durations and banning gang members from having licenses.

For her speech she wore a korowai, gifted from the Council of Licensed Firearms Owners (COLFO).

"They placed it around my shoulders, and they told me that I had the weight of licensed firearm owners around my shoulders," she said.

"I have hung this korowai in my office for the last six years, and every time I've made a decision about firearms, I've looked at the wall and I've looked at that, and I've had the best intent for all firearm licence holders throughout New Zealand in every decision that we've made."

Labour's Duncan Webb told the House that McKee's claim that gun owners had been demonised was not accurate.

"The minister referred to the reforms that all but one member of this House, at the time, supported, which was to put an effective ban on semi-automatic weapons."

Labour supported responsible firearms regulation, and it had cooperated with other parties to make the bill more workable, said Webb.

But the party still disagreed with removing police as the regulator, he said, calling the move "strange".

"We think the police are the proper agency to supervise the use of firearms."

Webb said McKee had listened to COLFO, the lobby group that she was formerly closely involved with.

World.title: Police 'hold serious concerns' for missing 69-year-old in Auckland
World.content:
Police have serious concerns for a 69-year-old reported missing from a residential complex on Auckland's North Shore.

Maree Jennins was reported missing from the complex on Roseberry Rd in Birkenhead on Tuesday evening.

The last confirmed sighting of Jennins was on the afternoon of Friday, July 24.

She had no form of transport, but had been known to use taxis in the past, police said.

"We have made enquiries with taxi firms throughout the day, we know that Maree has recently avoided using her name when she has made taxi bookings. She may have caught a taxi from the Roseberry Rd or wider Birkenhead area," Detective Senior Sergeant Mike Williams, from Waitematā East CIB, said.

"Maree's family and police hold serious concerns for her following recent comments she has made. She stayed in a north Auckland motel recently and it is possible she has done the same again, but we continue to be worried for her wellbeing."

Police want any taxi drivers that might have picked her up on Friday afternoon to contact them. They have asked accommodation providers with information to get in touch as well.

Residents in the wider Birkenhead area that may have seen her should also contact police. Anyone who sees her should call 111 immediately.

World.title: Live: Aussies chasing 3x3 wheelchair basketball gold medal
World.content:
Ollie Saxton secures a weightlifting bronze for Australia, 40 years after his dad did the same for England at the Edinburgh Games.

Ollie Hoare survived a scare after falling in his Commonwealth Games mile heat at Scotstoun Stadium, getting into the final on appeal.

Later, the Diamonds have perhaps their toughest match-up of the group stage against South Africa.

Over in the pool, the swimming wraps up with Lakeisha Patterson trying to equal her haul of three Paralympic gold medals with a third Commonwealth title in the women's 100m S9 freestyle.

Follow all the action in our live blog.

World.title: Rugby Australia tight-lipped on possible Cheika homecoming
World.content:
Rugby Australia boss Phil Waugh has danced around the prospect of Michael Cheika's NSW Waratahs return as the search for a new coach narrows.

Dan McKellar stepped down with a year to run on his three-year deal, citing personal reasons, in a surprise development last month.

Expressions of interest for the vacancy closed last Friday.

It is understood former Waratahs and Wallabies coach Cheika, currently on a one-year deal as an assistant with the NRL's Sydney Roosters, has not yet applied for the role.

The Waratahs' high-performance program is run by Rugby Australia.

Cheika has coached Leicester Tigers, Argentina and the Lebanese rugby league team in recent years. (Getty Images: James Baylis)

Cheika was the first man to win major club titles in the Northern (Leinster in 2009) and Southern (Waratahs in 2014) Hemispheres and won World Rugby's 2015 coach of the year award.

Since his departure from the Waratahs in 2015, they have only played one semi-final, finishing eighth with a 5-9 record this year and struggling to build continuity in their roster.

Waugh refused to say if he had spoken to Cheika about the job, but was open to the prospect of his return to Australian rugby.

Stephen Hoiles, Chris Latham and John Manenti are also reportedly in the mix.

"We want world-class coaches, right across the system," Waugh said.

"That's our focus; there's multiple applicants, and we're working through it.

"We want to provide certainty to players and supporters as quickly as we can.

A schoolboy rugby 'dynasty' It might be more than 60 years ago, but Homebush Boys High's 1965 Waratah Shield win remains a fond memory for the likes of Gordon Bray, John Symond and John Coates.

"I don't like to anchor myself to timelines when it comes to coaching announcements, but we're conscious of getting the right person and the importance of a successful Waratahs in a World Cup year."

Waugh added RA would continue to discuss future opportunities with departed coach Joe Schmidt despite the New Zealander lining up work in Ireland as a consultant with Ulster, offering guidance to the province's age-grade coaches.

The role could reportedly see him make multiple visits, while he also committed to be part of the Australia A coaching set-up under Stephen Larkham.

Waugh on Wednesday said Schmidt was "free to do as he pleased" when asked if his return to Ireland had been flagged.

"We've got a very close relationship with Joe and are appreciative of his contribution," Waugh said.

"We'll continue conversations with how he can be involved and have been pretty open about that."

AAP

World.title: Benji Marshall denies claims of Tigers players vaping in gym
World.content:
Benji Marshall admits Wests Tigers need to address slipping club standards, but has refuted reports of players vaping in the NRL club's gymnasium.

The Tigers coach on Wednesday fronted the media to affirm his "love" for Adam Doueihi, almost a week after the 27-year-old disagreed with a move out of halfback and walked out on the club.

Media suggestions had been that aside from the positional switch, Doueihi was dismayed by a lack of professionalism and accountability at the struggling joint venture, which has not played finals since 2011.

Doueihi expected to return to Tigers training Adam Doueihi is expected to resume training with Wests Tigers on Tuesday after the playmaker underwent crisis talks with coach Benji Marshall and club officials.

The Tigers enter round 22 in 16th place on the ladder, despite sitting third earlier in the year and most recently suffering a 46-point loss to Canberra with their season on the line.

Marshall conceded the Tigers had work to do to improve their standards, but denied the club had a culture problem that contributed to their on-field struggles.

"I don't feel like there's a culture problem," he said.

"[But] if we're talking about standards and that, there's probably a few things we might've walked past recently that we need to address."

Marshall refuted media reports of a culture of vaping during gym sessions.

"I can tell you now that no-one's vaping in the gym. That's actually fabricated or misinformation," he said.

"Is there a vaping problem? Probably, with players, but with young men, you can't tell them whether they vape or smoke.

"I definitely can't control what they do 24/7. I'm not with them all the time."

Meanwhile, a remorseful Doueihi admits he can be "stubborn" and "a hard player to deal with", but insists he is committed to Wests Tigers following his highly publicised dummy spit.

Adam Doueihi cast the Tigers into the spotlight for all the wrong reasons. (Getty Images: Brett Hemmings)

Doueihi conceded he should "definitely" have played the Tigers' must-win game against the Raiders last Saturday, rather than walk out after Marshall's decision to move him from halfback.

The 27-year-old said "miscommunication" had led to friction between he and Marshall, who had hoped to play him at lock against the Raiders.

"Benj knows I'd play front row for him. I never put myself above the team," he said.

"Was there a bit of communication breakdown there, and did I take it the wrong way? Yeah, and I'm happy to wear that."

The star utility was visibly emotional fronting a media scrum at Tigers headquarters on Wednesday, two days after crisis talks brought him back into the fold.

Doueihi said there were multiple factors that had led him to "lose [his] head" last week, including conversations with Marshall, the 16th-placed Tigers' disappointing season and a disruptive week that included a visit to the NRL judiciary.

The Tigers' season has fallen apart in recent weeks. (Getty Images: Mark Nolan)

Those factors notwithstanding, Doueihi conceded he was to blame for bringing yet another off-field drama upon the sputtering joint venture.

"I know that at times, I can be a hard player to deal with," Doueihi said.

"I just put this stubborn head on that I have at times, and put this ego on that I have at times and just couldn't get myself in the right headspace to play. That's the reality of it.

"When you're fighting so hard and you have a big week and you go to the judiciary and you're not used to it, and you're losing, and you just want to see this club winning, add a bit of miscommunication, which I mentioned, to Benj.

"I'm an over-thinker and I love being well-prepared for stuff. You add that all together, and it just got the better of me last week."

AAP

World.title: Son of a gun Hewitt takes top-100 scalp in ATP first
World.content:
Cruz Hewitt's victory in his ATP Tour main-draw debut is set to rocket the son of a gun up the world rankings.

Fresh off a run to the Wimbledon boys final, Hewitt beat former world number 37 Marcus Giron — currently ranked 85 — 6-3, 6-4 in Washington DC on Tuesday (Wednesday AEST).

The Australian, who didn't face a break point, became the fourth man born in 2008 or later to win a tour-level match and the youngest Washington match-winner since Japan's Kei Nishikori in 2007.

The teen qualified thanks to walkovers after leading both Dusan Lajovic and top-seed Zach Svajda and has surged 255 places to number 357 in the ATP's live rankings.

He'll play the winner of countryman and mentor Alex de Minaur and former world number three Stefanos Tsitsipas in the next round.

Cruz Hewitt's (right) win at the DC Open means he could face countryman Alex de Minaur next up in the round of 16. (Getty Images: Paul Morigi)

He had warmed up with father Lleyton, the former world number one, two-time major winner and 2004 Washington champion, who told him to lap up the moment.

"[He told me] mainly to enjoy it, because it was my first tour-level match … and to take every point one-by-one, to enjoy the atmosphere and to enjoy the crowd and that is what I did," he said.

Cruz said he was handling the pressure of carrying the Hewitt name "as best as I can".

"There is obviously a little bit of pressure, but I try to take the positives out of it as well, and I am happy with how I am dealing with it so far," he added.

"I am really happy with how I competed today. I came out and started pretty well, and I am thrilled to get through to the next round."

De Minaur is defending his title in the American capital and fresh off a two-day Portofino honeymoon after marrying fellow pro Katie Boulter in Tuscany last month.

"It was an amazing time, everything we could have ever imagined," said De Minaur, who is coming off the disappointment of an upset fourth-round Wimbledon loss.

"It was like our own little movie. We were able to celebrate with family and friends and have a very small honeymoon.

"Then we're on a flight here to Washington and getting our heads screwed back on and back to being tennis players."

AAP

World.title: FIFA boss unveils $US20b plan to sell World Cup to Kushner consortium
World.content:
FIFA president Gianni Infantino's plan to create a $US20 billion ($29 billion) company running the World Cup with private investors, including the Kushner family, has been attacked by European football body UEFA.

"It is not FIFA's to sell," UEFA said in a statement. "None of us are the owners of football."

Mr Infantino's plans to form a commercial subsidiary, called FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE), to run competitions like the World Cup and Club World Cup, were first reported by The Times of London.

Players and fans made the World Cup a success, but the politics shouldn't be forgotten The biggest ever World Cup brought diverse communities together and galvanised its non-traditional footballing co-hosts, but the concerns raised from the start have not disappeared in the positive afterglow.

FIFA said in a statement FFE would raise up to $US4.2 billion later this year to help fund development programs "based on an initial equity valuation of $US20 billion by carefully selecting long-term investors who will purchase minority, non-controlling interests".

FIFA is working with JP Morgan while intended investors include Thrive Eternal, launched by Joshua Kushner, whose brother Jared Kushner is a son-in-law of US President Donald Trump.

The men's World Cup that finished this month only deepened the political and personal ties between Mr Trump and Mr Infantino, and fuelled concerns about those ties, including from UEFA.

"The soul and governance of football are not assets to trade — especially with zero transparency as to who gains financially," UEFA said, responding to the reports of selling stakes in FIFA competitions.

FIFA is a Swiss-based not-for-profit association of its 211 national member federations worldwide.

The brother of Donald Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner (pictured), is among the potential World Cup investors. (Reuters: Kent Nishimura)

Those members must approve any plan and would get the chance "to access up to $US20 million in one-off capital", FIFA said.

"This is about the democratisation of football worldwide," Mr Infantino said in a FIFA statement, which added that "a consultation process has begun".

UEFA, however, said it took reports of the project "extremely seriously. So should every national Football Association".

"This crosses a line that football's governing institutions should never cross," said UEFA, which comprises 55 of the FIFA members.

FIFA emphasising financial benefits for members

FIFA boss Gianni Infantino has promised to "unleash the commercial potential" of the World Cup. (Getty Images)

FIFA said Mr Infantino had detailed the outline of Tuesday's surprise announcement to members who met in Manhattan on July 18 ahead of the World Cup final.

There, Mr Infantino promised to "unleash the commercial potential and opportunity that FIFA has".

FIFA's statement emphasised how much money each of its 211 members could get in the "FIFA Fast-Forward Program", running until 2038.

Instead of the promised $US8 million each in development funds in the 2027-30 World Cup commercial cycle, it would be $US20 million, then $US22 million and $US24 million in the following cycles.

FIFA banked record World Cup income of about $US12 billion from the 2026 tournament, which had unprecedentedly high prices for tickets and hospitality across the US, Canada and Mexico.

World Cup winners Spain will be one of six nations hosting matches at the 2030 World Cup.

It was unclear how that money could be matched from Spain, Portugal and Morocco co-hosting the 2030 men's edition.

Member federations could choose if they wanted to take part in the new financial opportunities, FIFA said.

"FIFA would retain sole control of FFE and exclusive authority over football governance, competitions, match calendar, and all regulatory and sporting decisions," the soccer body said.

FIFA's integrity standards were called into question during the World Cup, including by team coaches, Norway's soccer federation and a top European public body, the Council of Europe.

FIFA's previous attempt to privatise assets

Infantino has built stronger ties with Saudi Arabia's Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman throughout his tenure as FIFA boss. (Reuters: Evelyn Hockstein)

Mr Infantino's 11-year FIFA presidency has become increasingly controversial, and this is the second time he has tried to push through a multi-billion-dollar deal with private backers.

In 2018 he proposed a secretive $US25 billion offer over 12 years with SoftBank of Japan to create new global competitions, including an expanded men's Club World Cup, seemingly backed by Saudi Arabian money.

That ultimately failed after meeting fierce resistance from UEFA, which saw threats to its prize assets: the Champions League and the European Championship.

Mr Infantino still built closer ties to Saudi soccer and the kingdom's Crown Prince Mohammed Bin Salman. Saudi Arabia will host the 2034 World Cup, and largely funded the revamped men's Club World Cup hosted in the US last year.

What does this mean for Infantino's future?

The financial success of the just-ended World Cup has made it likely that Mr Infantino will be re-elected unopposed next year for a fourth and final term in office through to 2031.

At his re-election in 2023 in Rwanda, Mr Infantino suggested any CEO delivering similar financial results would be kept in the job forever.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

Speculation has swirled for years that Mr Infantino might want a different global role in soccer beyond his FIFA presidency, which is due to end when he is 61.

The Times reported on Tuesday that a CEO-like commissioner role of the new FFE operation could be created for him.

"This has never been discussed," FIFA said in a statement on Wednesday (AEST). "However, the FIFA president and the FIFA administration will and must have leading roles in this entity — if approved."

There was no timetable suggested for debate and decisions by FIFA, its ruling Council chaired by Mr Infantino, and the 211 members.

FIFA is scheduled to hold an online congress on November 23 to confirm hosts of the Women's World Cup editions in 2031 and 2035.

AP

World.title: Quick hits: Record beaten five times in 10 minutes, pool haka thrills
World.content:
New Zealand swimmers pay tribute to a victorious teammate by performing the haka, a Pakistani lawn bowler fits in some work shifts and a weightlifting record falls a staggering five times.

Here are the quick hits from day five of the Commonwealth Games.

1. 'Super proud' New Zealanders

Lewis Clareburt and his New Zealand teammates perform the haka after his victory. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

New Zealand swimmer Lewis Clareburt received a double honour after winning the men's 400-metre individual medley final.

Aside from being awarded the gold medal, Clareburt was the recipient of a haka proudly performed by his New Zealand teammates.

The Tollcross International Swimming Centre crowd also appreciated the gesture.

"People really respect it [the haka] around the world and it makes me super proud to be a Kiwi," Clareburt told reporters.

The crowd erupted when the New Zealanders performed the haka. (Getty Images: Adam Pretty)

Clareburt won the men's 200m butterfly earlier in the swimming program.

2. Lawn bowler works double shift

Mohammed Ayub Qureshi competing in the lawn bowls. (Getty Images: Francois Nel)

No-one can accuse lawn bowler Mohammed Ayub Qureshi of not being a multitasker.

Qureshi competed for Pakistan in the men's singles event while also working at his restaurant in Glasgow.

Last Friday afternoon local time, he faced off against Scotland's Jason Banks before heading to the restaurant to work the evening rush.

Showing what the Commonwealth Games are all about, Qureshi invited Banks to drop by for a meal after the Scot sealed victory.

Loading Instagram content

"I was too scared before I played him in case he spiced up my food too much," Banks said.

It is the second time Qureshi has represented Pakistan at the Commonwealth Games in the city that has been his home for more than 50 years.

3. Record falls again and again

Hafizuddin Bin Roslin Muhammad ended a run of record-breaking lifts. (Getty Images: Lintao Zhang)

What could possibly be better than seeing the Commonwealth record broken at a Commonwealth Games?

Well, seeing the same one be beaten five times in the space of 10 minutes or so would probably do it.

That is exactly what happened in the men's 88-kilogram weightlifting competition, with Cameron McTaggart, Braydon Kennedy and Hafizuddin Bin Roslin Muhammad all achieving new standards in rapid succession.

New Zealander McTaggart started things off with a 154kg lift.

That was swiftly bettered by Canada's Kennedy, who lifted 155kg with his first attempt.

McTaggart tried to better that, but missed at 157kg with his final snatch.

Then Malaysian lifter Muhammad entered the chat.

Neither he nor Kennedy could get 160kg up on their first attempts at the weight, but Muhammad did so on his second.

Then Kennedy threw up 161kg, so Muhammad added another kilo for the newest and final record of 162kg.

4. Aussies snare two golds in an hour

Breanna Scott won gold on the beam. (Getty Images: Mattia Ozbot)

Breanna Scott already had a gold medal from this Commonwealth Games when she stepped out onto the balance beam on Tuesday.

After she flipped off it at the end of her routine, she had a second.

"It's pretty overwhelming to be honest, none of it has sunk in yet," she told Channel Seven after the final.

"The team gold was such a special medal for all of us, and that was really the main goal coming into this.

"All of us in finals now getting these extra little medals is just topping it off."

She, and the rest of the Australian team, barely had time to let it, to be fair.

Jesse Moore delivered a superb routine to secure gold. (Getty Images: Mattia Ozbot)

An hour or so later, Australia had a second gold of the session.

Jesse Moore broke his duck to claim a sensational gold on the parallel bars.

His was Australia's ninth gymnastics medal of these Games.

5. Athlete on track twice in 34 minutes

Howard Tapuaiga Siila competing in the men's 800m heats. (Reuters: Phil Noble)

Howard Tapuaiga Siila knew he had a full schedule on his hands when he arrived at the Scotstoun Stadium on day five.

The Tuvalu athlete was entered in both the men's 400m and 800m heats, which is a daunting task at the best of times.

But for Siila, there was only 34 minutes between the start of each race.

He took off in his 800m heat at 11:33am local time, finishing eighth in 2:32.38.

Siila was back on the track for the 400m at 12:07pm, finishing eighth via a time of 55.96.

Both were season-best times.

Competing in both events was planned, but there was one hitch.

"When I decided to enter the races we weren't sure of the scheduling," Siila told reporters in the mixed zone.

World.title: 'Biggest cheat in cricket history': Clicking scandal causes outrage
World.content:
An amateur cricket match in England has become a viral sensation after allegations of cheating were shared on social media.

A video, which claims to show a fielder clicking his fingers to imitate the sound of a bat connecting with the ball before a player is called out, has been viewed millions of times on X.

The poster of the video described it as "about the worst case of cheating I've ever seen in cricket".

Loading Instagram content

"First slip clicks his fingers to imitate an edge, bat nowhere near it and given out," the post read.

The video of a match involving North Yorkshire and South Durham Cricket League team Saltburn has been greeted with outrage online and generated headlines around the world.

TV presenter Piers Morgan weighed in, describing the player involved as the "biggest cheat in cricket history" and wondered how many batters' days "has he ruined?"

The league said in a statement on X that it had received a formal complaint regarding a game on Saturday, but did not reveal which teams were involved. However, it is understood the investigation is focused on the clicking.

"A full investigation has been initiated and until such time as the formal processes are complete no further comment will be made," it said.

There was no immediate response when The Associated Press contacted the league and Saltburn for comment.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

AP

World.title: 'The Aussies are on fire' on a night where that should've been impossible
World.content:
In the land of lochs, the announcer at Scotstoun Stadium couldn't figure out the first half of his name, but Lachlan Kennedy's performance on a sodden night in Glasgow ensured Australia will never forget it.

The weather on Tuesday night couldn't have been much more Scottish.

It was teeming basically all night, to the point the women's high jump final was halted for 45 minutes and the women's hammer throw probably should have been.

There were only two brief windows when the rain turned from a downpour to a drizzle, and it just so happened to be the moments "Lacklan" Kennedy was welcomed to the newly laid blue track.

The support crew was working overtime to make things vaguely manageable. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

It sounds like the sort of apocryphal tale told about Don Bradman in an era before the footage existed to prove your grandad was lying to you.

But it really happened.

To be clear, it wasn't dry, but no wetter than the night in March when he beat rising superstar Gout Gout in the 200m at the Maurie Plant Meet.

That established him once again as not just a fast runner, but a man capable of performing under the most intense pressure. A man plying his trade against a boy still figuring his out.

And Kennedy did it again on the biggest stage, winning Australia's first men's 100 metres medal at the Commonwealth Games with silver behind Cameroon's Emmanuel Eseme on the second night of an athletics program that has been backed to deliver so much for Australia.

After not running a heat, Lachie Kennedy came straight out and made a statement. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

"It's all about rising to the occasion. I'm a big believer in you've got to bring your best when it matters most," Kennedy said.

"That's what we've been training for all season. We've all been planning for this competition here and my coach has clearly outdone himself."

It seems extreme to say he obliterated the national record of Patrick Johnson by taking it from 9.93 down to 9.85, but 0.08 of a second means something different to folks like Kennedy than it does us mere mortals.

In the 58 years since Jim Hines broke the 10-second barrier in the 100 metres, only 232 more have people dipped into single digits.

Aussie sprinters storm to 100m medals Lachlan Kennedy and Torrie Lewis set new national records in claiming 100m medals, while a host of Australians take gold across athletics and swimming.

The margins are so fine in the jewel in the athletics crown that there have been 1,550 legal runs in 0.42 of a second between 10 flat and Usain Bolt's world record of 9.58.

Most are from the United States, Jamaica and spread across Africa, and just two from Australia, with Kennedy the only one since 2003.

Kennedy stands alone in some respects, but is proud to be part of a pack pushing each other towards greatness.

Gout's rise trained a spotlight on the team, whose performances with that attention have proved it warranted.

"Aussie track is clearly in the best spot it's ever been, our team is so strong … We're in a real golden age," Kennedy said.

That was clearly evident as Kennedy — after running alongside compatriot Eddie Nketia, who finished sixth in the final after laying down a PB of 10.03 in the semis — was still talking to the media in the mixed zone when Torrie Lewis won bronze in the women's final.

Loading...

"The Aussies are on fire," Kennedy said as he cheered Lewis on to the team's third of six medals on the night.

Lewis also set a new national record, but rather than breaking a record that had stood for 23 years, hers had barely stood for 23 hours.

Lewis's 10.99 in the women's final came after her 11 flat in the semi, which lowered her own record of 11.04 from a week prior.

All in an event she wasn't even sure she wanted to compete in.

Torrie Lewis followed Lachie Kennedy into the history books. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

Lewis is a beneficiary of the controversial automatic qualifiers into the semis of her pet 200m event, where she'll be hoping for more silver (or better) ware before the relays kick off in the ultimate representation of what this team can do.

"I have a day off tomorrow, luckily with the bye, then Thursday see how I pull up for the semifinal and hopefully I can do something special there as well," she said.

Lewis and Kennedy were the headlines due to Australia's historic lack of truly exceptional flat sprint talent since the days of Raelene Boyle.

We've jumped at a few false dawns and sometimes athletes have been unable to live up to those expectations, while field sensations like Steve Hooker, Nina Kennedy, Eleanor Patterson, Matt Denny, Nicola Olyslagers and a cavalcade of women's javelin chuckers have been consistently brilliant.

The anachronisms of the Commonwealth The Commonwealth Games continues to roll on despite calls to decolonise our lives, with Scotland of all places a strange venue to stage two celebrations of the British Empire over the past 12 years.

They were again on Tuesday night: Patterson and Olyslagers went 1-2 to continue their impossibly consistent excellence in the high jump, and 22-year-old Lara Roberts broke through for her first major international medal.

Patterson said it was "phenomenal" to see the runners joining the jumpers and throwers in contention for medals.

"I was out there and you get to have a lay of the land and you understand what's going on," she said.

"I definitely took in my stride that there was a lot of Aussies there and seeing how well everyone was doing.

"Athletics in Australia, it's going off. I want the whole of Australia to know that we're taking it to the world, we're representing Australia very well and we're not bad, we're pretty bloody good."

Back on the track Ky Robinson kicked off the stunning hour and a half with victory in the 10,000m.

Australian athletics has had a number of these special nights of late, so much so that it risks becoming expected.

Australians have become so used to success in the pool that we have become somewhat blasé about the brilliance of our aquatic elite, but for now, on relatively dry land in Scotstoun there really is no other word for it.

That was special.

Tech.title: The Ferrari Luce has at least 500 fans
Tech.content:
is a news writer covering all things consumer tech. Stevie started out at Laptop Mag writing news and reviews on hardware, gaming, and AI.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Just two months after a bumpy launch earlier this year, Ferrari has reportedly already hit its 2026 sales goal for its polarizing, Jony Ive-designed Luce EV. Ahead of Ferrari announcing its quarterly earnings on Thursday, the Financial Times reports that Ferrari was aiming to sell “just under 500” Luce units this year, and reached that target this month.

Luce sales so far were reportedly driven by “strong demand from China,” where EV sales have already taken off from makers like Geely, Lynk & Co, and Zeekr. The Financial Times says Ferrari was trying to “reach a new generation of wealthy buyers” with the Luce, particularly in China and “tech hubs like Silicon Valley,” adding that their sources say US tech entrepreneurs have had “positive” feedback on the €550,000 EV.

Long term, Ferrari is reportedly hoping to sell around 2,500 Luce units by 2030, or roughly 600 each year, making up about 5 percent of the company’s annual sales. It’s also auctioning off the first production model of the Luce next month, which could sell for upwards of $1.1 million.

Tech.title: Remarkable’s refurbished bundle is an awesome deal that’s over $350 off
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

A lot of us here at The Verge are fans of Remarkable’s digital note-taking tablets, and right now one of its higher-end options is much cheaper than usual. The Remarkable Paper Pro normally sells for $629 on its own, but Woot is currently offering a refurbished bundle for $449.99 through July 31st. It includes the tablet, a Marker Plus stylus, and a Book Folio, saving you $368 compared to buying new. The same refurbished bundle costs $649 from Remarkable and comes with a longer one-year warranty versus Woot’s 90-day warranty.

The 11.8-inch Paper Pro offers a paper-like writing experience, along with a rich color display. Unlike the monochromatic Paper Pure —Remarkable’s latest tablet that retails for $399 — it features an adjustable front light, making it easier to read and keep working after the lights go down. It also supports (but does not include) the optional $229 Type Folio keyboard, allowing you to switch between handwriting and typing.

Writing feels remarkably smooth — more so than similar devices from Boox, Kobo, and even Kindle Scribe models — while Remarkable’s software lets you organize notebooks with folders and tags, write directly on PDFs, and quickly convert handwritten notes into typed text. Although it supports basic sketching features like layers and shading, an iPad Pro is a better tablet if you’re serious about drawing. The Paper Pro’s color display was made with productivity in mind, serving as a distraction-free experience for reviewing slide decks, marking up reports, editing text, and organizing color-coded notes.

Tech.title: DoorDash is going airborne with new drone delivery division
Tech.content:
is transportation editor with 10+ years of experience who covers EVs, public transportation, and aviation. His work has appeared in The New York Daily News and City & State.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

DoorDash is launching a new drone delivery program called DoorDash Air. The largest food delivery app in the US said that it has approval from the Federal Aviation Administration that clears the way for drone delivery in the near future.

DoorDash said it has received a Part 135 air carrier certification from the FAA that enable it to delivery small packages via drone. Other companies to receive this designation include Alphabet’s Wing, Zipline, and Amazon.

Previously, DoorDash worked with Alphabet’s drone delivery division Wing on a number of pilots in places like Dallas-Fort Worth, Virginia, and Australia. Now the company says it will deploy its own drones, designed specifically for food delivery. The drones will be designed and assembled within the company’s DoorDash Labs division, which houses its robotics and AI teams responsible for building its Dot sidewalk delivery robots.

“We’re designing an aircraft purpose-built for the gaps we see in local commerce, and it complements the short- and long-range designs our partners are scaling,” the company said in a press release. “Our drone is also proudly American-designed and built, with the majority of components made right here in the U.S.” (To be sure, the vast majority of drones are manufactured in China.)

In addition, DoorDash says it will also build all the necessary ground-level infrastructure to enable restaurants to hand off their deliveries to drones. As seen with other drone delivery pilots, there is a complex system of structures and additional equipment that needs to be built on the ground to enable drones to pickup their payloads before embarking on their deliveries. And there are flight plans, airspace management, and drop-off logistics that needs to be established to track the drones in flight. DoorDash says its committed to building all that infrastructure itself.

“The aircraft is what everyone sees,” the company says. “The harder problem is the infrastructure and integration on the ground, and that’s our advantage. Solving hard physical-world problems for local businesses is our focus, from real-time inventory reconciliation to universal handoff systems for drive-throughs, rooftops, or merchant back doors. We are building that complete end-to-end system.”

DoorDash says drone delivery could solve the problem of midrange deliveries that still end up taking longer because couriers are hard to find. The company says more than 20 percent of its orders involve distances of three to five miles, but that those orders can take on average nearly 25 percent longer than shorter deliveries, largely because finding a courier takes longer for these mid-range trips.

“Routing mid-range deliveries to drones lets Dashers focus on the orders they often favor: shorter deliveries that can be done quickly, staying near a high concentration of merchants for optimal routing, and maximizing their earning potential by getting them to their next order faster,” the company says.

DoorDash didn’t reveal which markets it was targeting for its initial launch, noting that it would announce more details in the months to come.

Tech.title: The Nothing Ear 3A look great… and sound good enough
Tech.content:
is a senior reviewer covering TVs and audio. He has over 20 years experience in AV, and has previously been on staff at Digital Trends and Reviewed.

Nothing has had a strong visual identity since the Ear 1 were released in 2021 for $99 and challenged the notion that a highly featured headset requires a high price. The Ear 3A have the same transparent look as Nothing’s previous earbuds, with a clear case and stem design accented by a solid-colored body — this time adding a striking pink alongside yellow, black, and white options. And Nothing continues to improve both ANC and audio performance. But the Ear 3A also share the buggy performance that has plagued Nothing earbuds. While $99 is an attractive price for them, be ready to deal with some minor adaptive ANC and call quality issues.

The Ear 3A have 12mm dynamic drivers and support the high-res LDAC codec, along with SBC and AAC. Their default sound is very heavy on the bass, and while it gives bass lines extra punch, the midrange — which includes vocals and guitars — gets covered by the excessive low end. Bassheads might enjoy it, but it’s far too much for my taste, and I expect that will be the same for most people. Where I might ding some points for this on other earbuds, the Nothing 3A save themselves from that because of the robust EQ in the app. There’s a simple interface with four presets and a custom 3-band EQ, a nice 8-band parametric EQ that gives you more advanced adjustments, and some additional EQ profiles from users curated by Nothing.

In less than a minute I was able to adjust the EQ to something far more balanced to my ear (I added a downward slope to the bass below 115Hz, mid boost between 220–540Hz, another slight cut to the shouty frequencies between 2–3.5kHz, and some extra highs above 6.6kHz for a more open sound). It gave Chris Robinson’s voice more presence on “Thorn in My Pride” and his brother Rich and Marc Ford’s guitars nice crunch and bite as the song builds through the solo. And even with the cut to the low end, Johnny Colt’s bass supports the band throughout.

Nothing added a pink color to go along with yellow, white, and black options.

ANC performance is improved over previous Nothing earbuds, with solid cancellation particularly in the lower mids and bass range, so low drones like air conditioners or plane cabin noise get filtered out very well. For $99, they also do a decent job with higher frequencies, but if you plan to use them consistently in a coffee shop you’ll still hear orders being called out a bit. And if the high ANC setting is too much for you, there are mid and low settings that let in a bit more of the low end to ground you in reality.

There’s also an adaptive ANC setting, but here’s where some of the minor issues I encountered started. While out on walks around the neighborhood, occasionally (maybe two or three times during an hour walk) the ANC intensity would quickly adjust to let in much more ambient noise and then switch back to its previous level. The whole experience lasted maybe two seconds each time and was disorienting. I tried to take note of what might have triggered it, but couldn’t find a consistent situation that would cause it to happen. In general, whenever the adaptive ANC makes a change to the intensity, it’s sudden instead of the more gradual change that my Apple AirPods Pro 3 or Sony WF-1000XM6 do — for hundreds of dollars more.

The one issue I was able to figure out, also about volume attenuation, was with my call quality. While talking to a friend I regularly call when testing earbuds, if I was just listening to him, he couldn’t hear anything from my side at all. No traffic, no wind, no breathing, nothing. At one point he wondered aloud if the call had disconnected.

When I was talking, I sounded clear and natural to him if I started talking when there wasn’t a lot of ambient noise around me. When the sound around me got louder — such as more cars driving by — a bit of that sound leaked through, although my voice still sounded natural. But if I started talking while there was a lot of noise around me, my voice sounded dark as the earbuds strongly filtered out upper-mid and high frequencies, including doing a great job tamping down the loud ambient sound.

The Ear 3A have the same transparent design Nothing has used since the introduction of the Ear 1 in 2021. The Nothing X app includes controls for ANC intensity, a great parametric EQ, and customized controls.

Both the ANC and call quality issues could be addressed with future firmware updates (my testing was with firmware 1.0.1.59), and if you use one of the static ANC settings instead of adaptive ANC, or don’t plan on making calls in noisy areas, then they’re a nonissue anyway.

The Nothing Ear 3A also include 32MB of on-device storage, allowing them to record up to two hours of a call or take an audio snapshot (Nothing’s term) of up to one minute. When you then access the app, you can transfer the recordings onto your device. When beginning a call recording, a message plays to notify everyone. I can easily see the use of recording an important call to make sure you don’t miss any information (although this can also easily be done through your phone), but I have yet to find a reason for the audio snapshot. It only records up to a minute of what you’re listening to, not anything around you using the earbuds’ microphones, at lower fidelity. It’s unique to the Nothing 3A, but also gimmicky.

I’m glad the Nothing Ear 3A returned to a price under $100 after the $179 Ear 3. Nothing is at its best when it’s challenging what can be done for less — and I’m more forgiving of its minor flaws. While the sound wasn’t my taste out of the box, the fact you can make meaningful adjustments and tune it to your preferences makes them more versatile than most earbuds at the same price.

Photography by John Higgins / The Verge

Tech.title: Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8 feels like the future
Tech.content:
is a news editor with over a decade’s experience in journalism. He previously worked at Android Police and Tech Advisor.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Is this the future of foldable phones?

Samsung clearly thinks so. The company has given its new wide foldable the “Z Fold 8” name, positioning the phone not as a widescreen oddity, but as the new normal, the default design for foldables going forward. Rumor has it that Apple feels the same way, with a similar squat shape widely predicted for the first foldable iPhone, expected to launch in September.

Whether you want to give the credit to Apple, Samsung, or even Huawei (which got here first with the Pura X Max), I think they might be onto something. After a week, the Z Fold 8 feels comfortable, natural, and normal, despite being the shortest and widest phone I can remember using. And thanks to the 4:3 inner display — better suited to both reading and watching video — I’m using this as a foldable more than I ever have with previous models.

It isn’t perfect. Not every app plays nicely with the short outer screen, though issues are pretty rare. And the drop from three cameras on last year’s model to two cameras on this year’s feels like a real downgrade for an $1,899 phone.

We won’t really know the future of foldables until Apple enters the market. But with the Z Fold 8, Samsung has already made a good case that this design should stick around.

Until now, foldables have mostly been one of three shapes: flippy, foldy, and more recently (and rarely) trifoldy. Samsung has played a large part in defining those categories. But the Galaxy Z Fold 8 is among the first of a new wave of wider models.

The 5.5-inch outer display is both shorter and wider than typical phones, almost the exact same dimensions as a standard passport, with a 10:16 aspect ratio. It looks a little odd when closed, but makes sense when you open the phone up to see its 7.6-inch, 4:3 inner screen — not coincidentally the exact aspect ratio used by most iPads. This feels more like a foldable tablet than any previous Z Fold yet, and perhaps because of that I’ve found myself opening it up more than any foldable I’ve ever reviewed.

A little less content fits vertically on the outer screen, but it usually looks fine. Though some pages, even One UI’s default Quick Settings, require extra scrolling. Opened up, the Z Fold 8’s inner screen is a great shape for movies, though still has letterboxing. It’s arguably even better for reading in portrait.

This stretched shape is more natural for watching TV and movies, giving you a wider screen without too much letterboxing. It’s much better suited to this than the Z Fold 8 Ultra, which barely gives you any extra screen space for video when held vertically and has its selfie camera cutout in the way if you rotate it into landscape. The Z Fold 8 is arguably even better for reading, giving a convincing facsimile of the dimensions of a book when you hold it in portrait.

The shape takes more getting used to when closed, but less than you might think. Even when I tried the phone for an hour or so at Samsung’s press briefing I was surprised by how natural it felt, and a week with the Z Fold 8 has only cemented that feeling. After a while this doesn’t feel like an especially short or wide device, it just feels like a phone.

There are occasional errors that give away that Android wasn’t designed with these dimensions in mind. Once or twice Instagram has failed to fully load, leaving a white bar in the extra space on the right-hand side of the screen; the Withings app once crunched two rows of content together in an effort to fit things in vertically; and even Samsung’s default One UI Quick Settings panel is too long, requiring you to scroll to reach the bottom.

The Z Fold 8 Ultra is in Samsung’s classic foldable shape, taller and thinner. The squarish Ultra might be better for multitasking, but it’s worse for most content.

I’m not saying this squat screen is better than a regular slab phone, because it probably isn’t. You have to scroll a little more often because of the lost vertical space, and it can be a stretch to reach the phone’s far side. But there are advantages too: the extra width makes two-handed typing more comfortable (it’s not been much remarked, but this is a pretty similar size and shape to the classic BlackBerry); and because it’s so short, reaching the top of the phone is easier than ever. Anyone lamenting the death of the small phone may, perhaps paradoxically, find they’re a fan of the Z Fold 8.

It helps that all that reduced size keeps the Z Fold 8 light. At 201g, it’s Samsung’s lightest Z Fold yet. It’s slim too. At 9.7mm thick when shut, this is just a little chunkier than last year’s Z Fold 7, or this year’s Ultra, but it’s still far thinner than 2024’s Z Fold 6. Those dimensions put it within reach of a standard smartphone; an iPhone 17 Pro, for instance, is 206g and 8.8mm thick.

The Z Fold 8 is barely thicker than an iPhone 17 Pro. And almost as thin as its USB-C port when open.

Despite its slimness, the Z Fold 8 actually packs a bigger battery than any Z Fold bar the new Ultra, with a capacity of 4,800mAh. That’s thanks to Samsung finally adopting silicon-carbon batteries, a more energy-dense design that just about every Chinese phone manufacturer has long since adopted.

Samsung has been duly cautious in its approach, emphasizing stability and longevity as it’s incorporated more reactive silicon into the battery anode. Silicon-carbon batteries have a tendency to degrade faster than traditional designs, meaning the battery life gets worse more quickly over time, but Samsung says it’s managed to avoid that risk. It’ll take a year or more to learn just how well Samsung struck that balance, but for now I’m heading to bed with 40 percent of the battery left every night, so the extra capacity is doing its job.

Charging is fine, but less impressive. The Z Fold 8 has 45W wired charging and 20W wireless, both of which are good by US standards but sluggish compared to many Android phones available elsewhere. Unlike Google’s Pixel 10 Pro Fold, the Z Fold 8 lacks the built-in magnets required to support Qi2 wireless charging, though it is compatible with Qi2 cases. In fairness, that helps keep the phone itself thinner and lighter, and Samsung is likely betting that you were going to put a case on it anyway.

It really is uncannily close to a passport in size. It’s comfortable to hold in the hand. The lavender is muted, but attractive. Though I wish the phone had more than two cameras.

That’s a shame, because the phone looks great. It fits right into Samsung’s existing design language, which I’ve long been a fan of for its slick simplicity. I love my lavender model, in a simple, subtle purple, as well as the online-exclusive “pistachio” — though it’s really more of a grayish green than anything resembling the nut.

There’s no IP68 rating, which is a shame, with IP48 protection leaving the Z Fold 8 a little more vulnerable to dust and sand than rival foldables from Google, Oppo, and Honor. Samsung says the phone is sturdier overall thanks to new titanium infused layers under the display, which also make the crease on the inner screen subtler. It’s not quite as difficult to see or feel as on Oppo’s impressive Find N6, but the crease really is a complete non-issue now.

The cameras might be more of a concern. Samsung has downgraded the Z Fold 8 to just two rear lenses, a main camera and an ultrawide — no telephoto at all. And while the new 50-megapixel ultrawide is a significant improvement on what came before, the main camera uses a smaller sensor, lower resolution, and narrower aperture than the previous generation, making it worse in just about every respect.

Previous Next

























1 / 14 The Z Fold 8’s main camera is decent, but nothing special.

The photos it takes are fine. This is a similar main camera to the base Galaxy S26, with similar results, and roughly comparable to an iPhone 17. The low-light processing is better than I expected so long as subjects are mostly still, and colors are vivid but attractive. Like many Samsung cameras it finds fast-moving subjects tricky — almost every photo I’ve attempted of either of my cats has been blurry. The setup is improved by the ultrawide, which matches the main lens on quality in almost every shot, meaning there’s rarely a tradeoff for zooming out. But at this price, a telephoto lens wouldn’t go amiss.

Compared to previous generations of Z Fold, Samsung has kept the software updates fairly light. Google’s Gemini Intelligence Task Automation has rolled out to the phone, but isn’t yet available in the UK so I haven’t been able to test it. Then there’s My FanCam, an AI video editing feature which crops in to focus on a specific person. Now Nudge, Samsung’s take on Pixel phones’ Magic Cue, will suggest contextual actions you can carry out in split-screen, like adding an event to your calendar — though since it requires you to use Samsung Keyboard and specific messaging apps, it’s a little limited in practice.

I never expected to like this phone so much.

The foldable market is going to change for good in a month or two’s time. Apple’s entry into the space could be the push foldables need to go mainstream, or the final proof that they’ll be forever niche.

Either way, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 makes a good case that this might be the shape their future hopes rest in. It’s compact enough to feel small when folded and wide enough to feel expansive when open. It’s great for watching TV and movies, but just as good for reading, the two things most people might actually want a foldable for, leaving the Ultra for the multitasking productivity obsessives. If I was buying one of Samsung’s new foldables, it would be this one. But while this feels like the future of foldables, it still needs to get substantially cheaper to become the future of phones.

Photography by Dominic Preston / The Verge

Agree to Continue: Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Every smart device now requires you to agree to a series of terms and conditions before you can use it — contracts that no one actually reads. It’s impossible for us to read and analyze every single one of these agreements. But we started counting exactly how many times you have to hit “agree” to use devices when we review them since these are agreements most people don’t read and definitely can’t negotiate. To use the Galaxy Z Fold 8, you must agree to: Google Terms of Service

Google Play Terms of Service

Google Privacy Policy (included in ToS

Install apps and updates: “You agree this device may also automatically download and install updates and apps from Google, your carrier, and your device’s manufacturer, possibly using cellular data.”

Samsung End User Licence Agreement

Samsung Privacy Notice

Samsung Terms and Conditions There’s also a variety of optional agreements, including: Provide anonymous location data for Google’s services

“Allow apps and services to scan for Wi-Fi networks and nearby devices at any time, even when Wi-Fi or Bluetooth is off.”

Send usage and diagnostic data to Google

Google Gemini Apps Privacy Notice if you opt in to using Gemini Assistant

Turn on Samsung offline finding

Samsung news and special offers

Samsung personalized advertising

Bixby personal data intelligence

Samsung customization service Other features, like Google Wallet, may require additional agreements. Final tally: seven mandatory agreements and more than nine optional agreements.

Tech.title: Artists are lawyering up against AI slop, and some are even winning
Tech.content:
When The Atlantic published a searchable dataset of works used to train AI, Kirk Wallace Johnson, like a lot of artists, looked for his name out of curiosity. And, like a lot of artists, he found it. Essentially, his books, like The Feather Thief and The Fishermen and the Dragon — nonfiction tomes that he spent “five to six years researching, writing, and investigating” — had been pirated and fed to a chatbot. He says he felt a “cocktail” of emotions: “anger over the brazenness of the theft, worry over what this means for writers, and a healthy thirst for revenge on these massive corporations that have become galactically wealthy” using his intellectual property.

He proactively reached out to Susman Godfrey, the law firm already leading the case against Anthropic on behalf of authors, because he saw their suit as a “middle finger on behalf of everyone that has tried to create something.”

Johnson is just one of the dozens of authors, musicians, illustrators, and artists of all stripes taking the fight against AI to the courts. The lawsuits they’ve filed have primarily targeted the companies on copyright grounds, though some have sought other avenues, like terms of service violations. Some have dragged on for years, others settled comparatively quickly. Along the way artists have been dealt their fair share of wins and losses, especially around the definition of fair use.

“This does not seem to be a bus driven by a bunch of sane sober thinking people, and we’re all stuck in it.” — Kirk Wallace Johnson

Illustrator and cartoonist Sarah Andersen was one of the first and most outspoken to directly take on the AI giants. She describes her webcomic Sarah’s Scribbles as deeply personal. It’s a “complex culmination of my education, the comics I devoured as a child, and the many small choices that make up the sum of my life,” she wrote in a 2022 New York Times editorial. She, along with Karla Ortiz, Kelly McKernan, and several other visual artists, filed a class action suit against Stability, Midjourney, DeviantArt, and Runway AI. The case has been crawling its way through the court system since January 2023. That was just a few short months after Stability’s image generator Stable Diffusion and Midjourney were first released. At the time, generative AI was primarily a curiosity; ChatGPT had only just made its debut the previous November. Now it’s a matter of national security.

In the meantime, other artists, perhaps emboldened by Andersen’s efforts, have launched their own legal assaults on the biggest players in AI, including Meta, Google, Anthropic, and AI music generator Suno. By and large artists are optimistic about how their individual cases will pan out, and some believe that their efforts will help guide the courts toward legal guardrails. But they also harbor deep concerns about the approach taken by AI companies. “This does not seem to be a bus driven by a bunch of sane sober thinking people, and we’re all stuck in it,” Johnson says.

The problem, many seem to agree, is that the Big Tech CEOs and the people building AI models fundamentally don’t understand or respect art. Andersen says she felt “violated” and described it as “reducing my life’s work to an algorithm.” Author Andrea Bartz, a novelist known for books like We Were Never Here and The Spare Room and the lead plaintiff in Susman Godfrey’s suit against Anthropic, has a similar reaction. “I felt violated, shocked, alarmed,” she told The Verge. “I had a big emotional response to seeing that something I’d worked on for so many years and poured my heart and soul into was just one of hundreds of thousands or maybe millions of books that these Big Tech companies had just stolen for training their algorithm.”

“I felt violated, shocked, alarmed.” — Andrea Bartz

Sam Kogon would prefer to be best known for his Americana-tinged pop rock, but his name has been in the headlines recently as the lead plaintiff in the ongoing suit against Google’s Lyria AI music engine. “They’re devaluing our work,” he says, “They’re giving it away to people, for now, for free. And that’s going to disenfranchise and disempower a ton of musicians.” But, just as importantly, he views AI “art” as dehumanizing. Making fake music, he says, is “the most anti-human thing you could do.”

Kogon, along with a number of independent musicians, is accusing Google of violating its own terms of service. This makes their case slightly different from many of the other cases, which focus primarily on copyright infringement. Instead, Kogon’s lawyers argue that Google improperly used its Content ID system and YouTube data to train Lyria and ProducerAI. The company has mostly refused to comment on the specifics of the accusations, though it has filed a motion to dismiss. In the filing, Google claims that the YouTube terms of service give it broad rights to “reproduce, distribute, [and] prepare derivative works.”

“It’s pure bait and switch,” Kogon says, noting that YouTube regularly changes its terms of service. The dense, compulsory TOS is not a contract that can be negotiated, it’s a “take-it-or-leave-it situation.” Google seems to be arguing that anything uploaded at any point rightfully belongs to the company for training purposes. Kogon counters that that makes “technology that wasn’t even invented, and wasn’t even a glimmer in anyone’s eye at the time of putting your things on YouTube, is now fair game.”

Krystle Delgado, an entertainment and IP lawyer who runs the YouTube channel Top Music Attorney, takes serious issue with Google’s claims. She says, “I don’t think that anyone uses YouTube thinking that you are giving the rights to remake your content,” but when digging into the TOS, she discovered the uploader grants YouTube an “irrevocable perpetual license, meaning you can’t ever take it back.”

Google spokesperson Jack Malon responded by telling The Verge that “as we’ve said for several years, we use content uploaded to YouTube to improve the product experience for creators and viewers across YouTube and Google, including through machine learning and AI applications.”

Artists I spoke to viewed this as an abuse of Google’s position. Opting out of a platform as big as YouTube simply isn’t an option.

Those who stand to lose the most are independent artists and the creative working class. When novelist Richard Kadrey, comedian Sarah Silverman, writer Christopher Golden and several others sued Meta for using their books to train its Llama AI without consent, their filing argued exactly that. “While AI-generated books probably wouldn’t have much of an effect on the market for the works of Agatha Christie,” the complaint read, “they could very well prevent the next Agatha Christie from getting noticed or selling enough books to keep writing.”

Johnson says that “anyone that’s focusing on these world-famous authors and screenwriters, they’re missing the point.” The threat isn’t that AI is going to displace all great art. He says, “AI could never write The Godfather … But AI could write a mediocre film. AI could write a mediocre book. And there are tons of authors and screenwriters that live in that space. And it’s no judgment to them. They’re servicing a marketplace.”

The judge in Kadrey v. Meta dismissed many of the authors’ initial claims for failing to show evidence of market harm, but a narrower set of claims focusing on copyright infringement and the use of pirated materials is still working its way through the courts.

In Bartz v. Anthropic, the company was found to have violated copyright laws by using pirated ebooks downloaded from the internet to train Claude. In addition to paying out the largest settlement ever in a copyright case — $1.5 billion — the company also agreed to destroy its trove of pirated ebooks. But where things get complicated is with the trove of secondhand books — millions of them — the company bought and scanned to train its models under the name Project Panama. Judge William Alsup ruled that using those legally acquired books to train an LLM qualified as fair use because it was “quintessentially transformative.”

“The courts and the judges seem to be starting to lean our way, and the court of public opinion too.” — Krystle Delgado

“I strongly disagree with the judge on that part of the ruling … I very much hope that future courts will see the light,” Bartz says. “Even a library can’t buy a physical copy of a book, scan it, and start lending it out as an ebook,” she says.

Still, she doesn’t want to take away from the fact that her case against Anthropic is the first time a large AI company has been held accountable and faced consequences for using artists’ work without consent. She described the sizable settlement as the “first major win for creatives against an AI company … Hopefully that will guide us toward guardrails that are much needed in the industry.”

Delgado, who is leading the case against Suno and Udio on behalf of independent musicians, is equally optimistic. Despite the narrow setbacks in the case against Anthropic and Meta, she believes the pendulum is swinging in artists’ favor. “Right now with these companies, they’re really nervous,” she says. “Not only were they sued, but the courts and the judges seem to be starting to lean our way, and the court of public opinion too.” Polls have shown that people, at the very least, want transparency when it comes to AI.

Even if they win the legal battles, though, all the creators and lawyers I spoke to are concerned about the artists’ ability to continue making a living in the face of an ever-growing tide of AI.

“There’s been so much money spent on marketing to us this idea that AI is inevitable,” Bartz says, “and it’s very convincing and it’s very loud and it’s very pervasive. But I would just encourage people to think about the damage that these companies are doing to the arts, to our critical thinking, to our environment, to the world economy, as they continue to amass power and money.”

Tech.title: OpenAI’s rogue AI agent didn’t stop at hacking Hugging Face
Tech.content:
is a London-based reporter at The Verge covering all things AI and a Senior Tarbell Fellow. Previously, he wrote about health, science and tech for Forbes.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.
